documents.title: A quantitative review of the effects of biochar application to soils on crop productivity using meta-analysis
documents.summary: A 2011 meta-analysis of biochar applied to soil, by Simon Jeffery, Frank Verheijen and colleagues. It pools published trials to find a mean crop response. The reader gets an average across soils and crops, not one site, with the caveat that averages hide trials where biochar did nothing.
documents.abstract: Jeffery, Verheijen, van der Velde and Bastos pooled published trials of biochar added to soil to estimate its mean effect on crop productivity. The paper appeared in Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment in 2011, early in the field, when most data came from pots or short field runs. A meta-analysis weights each trial, then reports an average response across soils, crops and rates, with a spread around it. Responses differ between soil types, so the average hides cases where biochar did nothing or cut yield. It is a useful starting point for a grower asking what the literature says on balance, and a reminder to check the soil match before assuming a gain. Later meta-analyses with more field data have refined its conclusions.

documents.title: Agronomic values of greenwaste biochar as a soil amendment
documents.authors: Chan, ZWIETEN, Meszaros, Downie and Joseph
documents.summary: Radish was grown in pots of hardsetting Alfisol in Australia with greenwaste biochar at 10, 50 and 100 tonnes a hectare, with or without 100 kilograms of nitrogen. Without nitrogen, yield did not rise at any rate. With it, extra dry matter grew from 95 per cent in the control to 266 per cent at 100 tonnes. Tensile strength fell as well.
documents.abstract: Radish (Long Scarlet) was grown in pots of hardsetting Alfisol (Chromosol), a soil with a long cropping history, using greenwaste biochar at 10, 50 and 100 tonnes a hectare, with or without 100 kilograms of nitrogen a hectare. With no nitrogen, biochar did not lift yield even at 100 tonnes, and the 10 tonne rate trimmed dry matter slightly for reasons not understood. With nitrogen, the added dry matter rose from 95 per cent in the nil-biochar control to 266 per cent at 100 tonnes, so the char made fertiliser work harder. Above 50 tonnes, soil pH, organic carbon and exchangeable cations went up, tensile strength dropped, field capacity rose. Those changes matter on soils that set hard. Pots, not paddocks, and 100 tonnes is far beyond any commercial rate.

documents.title: Biochar and its effects on plant productivity and nutrient cycling: a meta‐analysis
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 371 independent results from 114 published studies. On average biochar raised aboveground productivity, crop yield, microbial biomass, rhizobia nodulation, soil phosphorus, soil potassium, total nitrogen, total carbon. The amount of biochar added did not predict productivity. Effects on downstream environments were unknown.
documents.abstract: Biederman and Harpole pooled 371 independent comparisons drawn from 114 published manuscripts. On average, biochar raised aboveground productivity, crop yield, microbial biomass, rhizobia nodulation, plant potassium, soil phosphorus, soil potassium, total soil nitrogen, total soil carbon, and nudged pH upward. Belowground productivity, mycorrhizal colonisation, plant tissue nitrogen and soil inorganic nitrogen showed no mean response. Soil and climate added variability. No link appeared between the rate of biochar and aboveground productivity, so more char was not better. The paper called biochar a possible win for energy, carbon storage and ecosystem function, but flagged downstream non-target environments as an open gap. Averages like these describe the literature, not any one paddock.

documents.title: Biochar boosts tropical but not temperate crop yields
documents.summary: A global meta-analysis of biochar and crop yield. Temperate soils showed no average yield effect. Tropical soils gained 25 per cent, through liming and fertilising effects in acidic, low-fertility soils with little fertiliser applied. High-nutrient biochars outperformed low-nutrient ones. For temperate farms, the gains lie in lime and fertiliser savings, not in yield.
documents.abstract: Jeffery and colleagues ran a global meta-analysis to sort out where biochar lifts yield. Split by latitude, the answer was clear. In temperate regions biochar had no average effect on crop yield. In the tropics it raised yield by 25 per cent on average. The tropical response came from liming and fertilising effects, which fit the low pH, low fertility, low fertiliser inputs of many arable soils there. Within the tropics, nutrient-rich biochars lifted yield well above nutrient-poor ones, which supports the fertiliser explanation. Temperate soils are moderate in pH, higher in fertility, receive more fertiliser, leaving little room for a further gain. The yield benefit is therefore not universal. For temperate farmers the case for biochar rests on lime and fertiliser cost savings, greenhouse gas control, other ecosystem services.

documents.title: Does biochar improve soil water retention? A systematic review and meta-analysis
documents.summary: A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis from Fatemeh Razzaghi, Peter Obour and Emmanuel Arthur asking whether biochar improves soil water retention. Published in Geoderma, it pools measurements to test directly one of the most quoted reasons for using biochar on dry land.
documents.abstract: Razzaghi, Obour and Arthur ran a systematic review and meta-analysis in Geoderma, 2019, built around one question: does biochar improve soil water retention? Water holding is among the most quoted reasons for using biochar on dry farmland, and the review checks it against pooled measurements, not single trials. Results depend on soil texture, because a coarse sand has more room to gain than a clay already holding water. Biochar properties plus rate also matter. For dryland growers, turf managers or anyone irrigating light soils, it is the place to see how often retention rose, then decide whether water holding alone justifies buying biochar.

documents.title: Biochar applications influence soil physical and chemical properties, microbial diversity, and crop productivity: a meta-analysis
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 59 studies published from 2012 to 2021. Biochar raised soil pH by 46 per cent, cation exchange capacity by 20 per cent and organic carbon by 27 per cent. Bulk density fell 29 per cent, porosity rose 59 per cent. Crop productivity rose in fine and coarse soils only, not in medium-textured soils.
documents.abstract: Singh and colleagues extracted global data from 59 studies published between 2012 and 2021 on soil physical, chemical, microbial properties and crop productivity. Biochar raised soil pH by 46 per cent, cation exchange capacity by 20 per cent, organic carbon by 27 per cent, with larger effects in coarse and fine soils. Chemical effects varied with feedstock. Bulk density fell 29 per cent, porosity rose 59 per cent. Biochar made above 500 degrees Celsius did better on physical properties: bulk density down 31 per cent, porosity up 66 per cent. Biochar made below 500 degrees had a bigger effect on microbial diversity, bacteria in medium and coarse soils, fungi in fine soils. Crop productivity rose only in fine and coarse textured soils, with the yield response following the change in physical properties. Long-term field trials are needed to show how biochar ages, when to reapply it.

documents.title: Biochar effects on phosphorus availability in agricultural soils: A meta-analysis
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 108 paired comparisons on plant-available phosphorus in agricultural soils. Biochar raised availability by a factor of 4.6 overall, 5.1 in acid soils and 2.4 in neutral soils, with no effect in alkaline soils. Only rates above 10 tonnes a hectare and pyrolysis below 600 degrees Celsius worked. The effect lasted at least five years.
documents.abstract: Phosphate rock is finite, so slow-release phosphorus sources are of interest. Glaser and Lehr pooled 108 pairwise comparisons of biochar against unamended soil. Biochar increased plant-available phosphorus by a factor of 4.6 (95 per cent confidence interval 3.4 to 5.9), regardless of feedstock. Two conditions mattered: application above 10 tonnes a hectare, pyrolysis below 600 degrees Celsius. Soil pH set the size of the response. Acid soils (pH below 6.5) rose 5.1-fold, neutral soils (6.5 to 7.5) 2.4-fold, alkaline soils (above 7.5) showed no significant change. The effect held for at least five years, so biochar acts as a short, medium or long-term phosphorus source. The rates needed are high, so the cost per tonne decides whether it pays. Availability is not the same as a measured yield response.

documents.title: Biochar effects on crop yields with and without fertilizer: A meta‐analysis of field studies using separate controls
documents.authors: Ye, Arbestain, Shen, Lehmann, Singh and Sabir
documents.summary: Field studies pooled by Lili Ye and colleagues, all with separate controls and biochar at 20 tonnes a hectare or less. Biochar with inorganic fertiliser lifted yield 15 per cent over fertiliser alone, while biochar by itself did nothing. Over three or more years yield rose 31 per cent. Rates above 10 tonnes a hectare added nothing.
documents.abstract: This meta-analysis of field studies used separate controls, so biochar could be compared with fertiliser alone as well as with untreated soil. Biochar rates were 20 tonnes a hectare or less. Fertiliser alone raised yield 26 per cent over unfertilised ground, and biochar with fertiliser raised it 48 per cent. Against fertiliser alone, adding biochar gave a 15 per cent gain (confidence interval 11 to 19 per cent). Biochar on its own did not lift yield against either control. A separate analysis of studies running three years or more found a 31 per cent gain, pointing to benefits beyond liming, such as cation exchange capacity. Rates above 10 tonnes a hectare gave no extra yield in the short term. Fertiliser use, mostly nitrogen, mattered more than climate or soil type. Data limits stopped feedstock or production effects being separated.

documents.title: Effects of biochar application on root traits: a meta‐analysis
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 2108 paired observations from 136 articles on how biochar changes plant roots. Root biomass rose 32 per cent, length 52 per cent, surface area 39 per cent and nodules 25 per cent. Root phosphorus concentration rose 22 per cent. Effects were larger in annual plants than in perennials.
documents.abstract: Roots are where biochar meets the plant, so Xiang and colleagues pooled 2108 paired observations from 136 articles covering 13 root variables. Root biomass rose 32 per cent, volume 29 per cent, surface area 39 per cent. Root length rose 52 per cent, root tip number 17 per cent, far more than root diameter at 9.9 per cent. Biochar favours fine, exploring roots over thick ones, a pattern suited to nutrient or water shortage. Root nitrogen concentration did not change, root phosphorus rose 22 per cent (most with nitrogen fertiliser), root nodules increased 25 per cent. Annual plants responded more than perennials, with soil texture and pH altering the result. Pyrolysis temperature and time mattered more than the feedstock source. The figures are averages across many trials, not a promise for a given paddock.

documents.title: Heterogeneous global crop yield response to biochar: a meta-regression analysis
documents.summary: A meta-regression of 84 studies asking which soils give a yield response to biochar. Low cation exchange capacity and low organic carbon predicted a positive response. Yield response grew with time since application. The largest gains were projected for highly weathered soils of the humid tropics, the smallest for the rich soils of major farming regions.
documents.abstract: Crane-Droesch and colleagues combined meta-analysis with missing-data and semiparametric methods on 84 studies, to explain why crop yield responses to biochar differ so much. Soil cation exchange capacity and organic carbon were strong predictors, with low values of both linked to a positive response. Yield response also grew with time since first application, relative to unamended controls. High clay content and low soil pH were weaker predictors of a larger response. None of the biochar properties in the dataset (biochar pH, carbon content, pyrolysis temperature) predicted yield change. The fitted model was then projected onto a global soil database. The largest gains appear in highly weathered soils such as those of the humid tropics, while richer soils in the major agricultural areas are less likely to benefit.

documents.title: Biochar addition persistently increased soil fertility and yields in maize-soybean rotations over 10 years in sub-humid regions of Kenya
documents.summary: Ten years of maize-soybean rotation at three sites in Kenya, with Acacia biochar applied at 50 plus 50 tonnes a hectare over the first two seasons. Biochar added about 1.2 tonnes a hectare to maize yield, 0.4 to soybean, with or without mineral fertiliser. The gain lasted the full decade. About 40 per cent of the biochar carbon was lost.
documents.abstract: Field trials were set up at three sites in sub-humid Kenya in 2006, possibly the longest biochar trials in sub-Saharan Africa. Biochar made mainly from Acacia was applied at 50 plus 50 tonnes a hectare over the first two seasons. Maize and soybean were then grown in rotation with or without mineral fertiliser. Biochar slightly raised soil porosity, pH, plant-available phosphorus, water-holding capacity. Yield responded at every site. The average seasonal gain was around 1.2 tonnes a hectare for maize, 0.4 for soybean, the same with or without fertiliser, so the effects added together. Mineral fertiliser alone lifted maize 1.6 tonnes a hectare, the following unfertilised soybean 0.6. The biochar yield effect persisted across all 10 years. Topsoil carbon analysis showed about 40 per cent of the biochar carbon was lost to mineralisation, erosion or movement down the profile. The rate was very high by farm standards.

documents.title: Effect of banded biochar on dryland wheat production and fertiliser use in south-western Australia: an agronomic and economic perspective
documents.authors: Blackwell, Krull, Butler, Herbert and Solaiman
documents.summary: Four dryland wheat experiments in Western Australia and South Australia, with woody biochar banded beside the seed row at about 1 tonne a hectare. Banding held yield with less fertiliser, and lifted yield where fertiliser was short. A 12-year cash flow puts break-even biochar cost at AU$40 to 190 a hectare, assuming a 50 per cent phosphorus saving or a 10 per cent yield gain.
documents.abstract: Four experiments on dryland wheat in Western Australia and South Australia tested biochar placed in bands near the roots. Banding limits wind erosion risk. The chars were made at high temperature from woody materials, giving stable, low-nutrient products. A low rate of about 1 tonne a hectare changed yield and fertiliser requirement in a useful direction: yield held at reduced fertiliser, and rose when fertiliser rates were low. The response is put down to better nutrient uptake through more arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal colonisation in dry seasons and low-phosphorus soils, not to nutrients or water held in the char. A 12-year farm cash flow, with benefits fading in a straight line to nil, gives a break-even cost of AU$40 to 190 a hectare. It allows for a 50 per cent phosphorus fertiliser saving, a 10 per cent yield gain, or both. Carbon trading accreditation could cut the net cost.

documents.title: Enhanced biological N2 fixation and yield of faba bean (Vicia faba L.) in an acid soil following biochar addition: dissection of causal mechanisms
documents.summary: A subtropical field trial of faba bean in rotation with maize on a rhodic ferralsol, comparing two biochars (one from papermill waste) with compost or lime. Lime gave the highest nitrogen fixation, tracking molybdenum uptake. Biochars gave the bigger yield gains: papermill biochar eased acidity and aluminium toxicity while supplying phosphorus.
documents.abstract: Field study into why biochar boosts legume nitrogen fixation in acid soil. Faba bean was grown in rotation with maize on a rhodic ferralsol after amendment with two contrasting biochars, compost or lime. Soil parameters, plant nutrient uptake were measured alongside stable nitrogen-15 isotopes to separate the causes. Biological nitrogen fixation followed plant molybdenum uptake, which rose as soil acidity fell under lime and papermill biochar. Crop yield followed plant phosphorus and boron uptake, plus relief from pH constraints. Papermill biochar did this best, since it dealt with acidity as well as low soil nutrient status. Lime produced the highest nitrogen fixation, yet the biochars gave greater yield benefits by addressing phosphorus nutrition and aluminium toxicity. Earlier support for these mechanisms came mostly from glasshouse work, so a field dissection is the useful part for growers on acid soils.

documents.title: Multi-year double cropping biochar field trials in Nepal: Finding the optimal biochar dose through agronomic trials and cost-benefit analysis
documents.authors: Pandit, MULDER, Hale, Zimmerman, Pandit and Cornelissen
documents.publisher: The Science of The Total Environment
documents.summary: Three years of maize and mustard on a moderately acidic silty loam in Rasuwa, Nepal, with biochar at 5 to 40 tonnes a hectare. The first year showed no yield effect. In year two maize rose up to 93 per cent, mustard up to 134 per cent. Cost-benefit analysis put the best dose at 15 tonnes a hectare.
documents.abstract: Field trials in Rasuwa, Nepal, tested six biochar doses (control, 5, 10, 15, 25, 40 tonnes a hectare) on a moderately acidic silty loam, double-cropping maize with mustard for three years. Biochar had no significant effect on grain yield in the first year, then positive effects (p < 0.01) in years two and three. In year two at 15, 25 and 40 tonnes, maize yield rose 50, 47 and 93 per cent, mustard 96, 128 and 134 per cent. The analysis counted farm inputs, labour, biochar production, health costs (under 2 per cent of preparation cost), methane emitted in production (up to 30 per cent of biochar cost, depending on carbon price). Income was crop sales plus carbon credits. The best dose was 15 tonnes a hectare at every carbon price, lifting gross margin 21 per cent with no carbon price, 53 per cent at US$42 a tonne of CO2. Only the zero price is realistic for Nepali farmers now.

documents.title: Biochar addition reduces salinity in salt-affected soils with no impact on soil pH: A meta-analysis
documents.authors: Wang, Ding, Han, Tan, Ge and Nan
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 660 paired observations from 99 articles on biochar in salt-affected soils. Electrical conductivity fell 13.2 per cent, cation exchange capacity rose 17.0 per cent, with no change in pH. The salinity cut showed only in severely salinised soils, not slight or moderate ones.
documents.abstract: Meta-analysis of 660 paired observations drawn from 99 peer-reviewed articles, testing biochar on salt-affected soils. The drop was clear in severely salinised soils, but not in slightly or moderately salinised ones. Cation exchange capacity rose 17.0 per cent, while pH did not change. Model selection ranked initial salinity level and biochar feedstock as the main controls on how ECe responded. Biochars vary widely, so results depend on the product. Fuller characterisation is needed. Few studies compare salt-tolerant with non-salt-tolerant plants, so crop response is thinly covered. For a saline paddock, the evidence favours biochar where salinity is already high, with no reason to expect a pH shift.

documents.title: Benefits of biochar, poultry manure and biochar–poultry manure for improvement of soil properties and sweet potato productivity in degraded tropical agricultural soils
documents.summary: Field experiments in 2019 and 2020 at two sites in southwest Nigeria, on degraded Alfisols. Biochar at 0, 10, 20 and 30 tonnes a hectare was crossed with poultry manure at 0, 5 and 10 tonnes. Biochar at 30 with manure at 10 gave the highest sweet potato tuber yield, 220 per cent above the control, 89 per cent above manure alone at 10 tonnes.
documents.abstract: Two-year field experiments in 2019 and 2020 at two sites in southwest Nigeria tested biochar on severely degraded Alfisols. The design was factorial: biochar at 0, 10, 20, 30 tonnes a hectare, poultry manure at 0, 5, 10 tonnes, in a randomised block with three replications. Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) was the crop. Biochar at 30 tonnes with manure at 10 tonnes gave the best tuber yield at both sites. Averaged over two years it beat the control by 220 per cent, sole manure at 10 tonnes by 89 per cent, sole biochar at 30 tonnes by 108 per cent. Bulk density, porosity, moisture, pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium all influenced yield. The interaction shows biochar raising the efficiency of the manure. The biochar feedstock is not given.

documents.title: Biochar improves the nutrient cycle in sandy-textured soils and increases crop yield: a systematic review
documents.summary: A systematic review of 92 articles (1609 observations) on biochar in sandy-textured soils. Biochar cut nitrous oxide emissions by 29 per cent, mineral nutrient leaching by 38 per cent. Publication bias played a minor role, so the figures are not an artefact of what got published.
documents.abstract: Nine meta-analyses were run on 1609 observations from 92 articles, drawn from peer-reviewed papers plus grey literature, screened in two stages with validity checks. In sandy-textured soils, biochar cut nitrous oxide emissions by 29 per cent (confidence interval minus 48 to minus 3) and mineral nutrient leaching by 38 per cent (minus 56 to minus 13). Corrected and uncorrected averages were close, so publication bias is a minor concern, though meta-regression showed some sign of it. Sandy soils respond to biochar in varying size and direction across the literature, which the wide confidence intervals reflect. The leaching result matters most on light soils where nutrients move quickly below the root zone.

documents.title: Biochar field testing in the UK: outcomes and implications for use
documents.authors: Hammond, Shackley, Prendergast‐Miller, Cook, Buckingham and Pappa
documents.summary: Seven field experiments on five working UK farms from 2009 to 2011, using wood biochar on arable, legume, horticultural and root crops. Across 47 treatments, yield rose by 0.4 tonnes a hectare on average. Rates of 20 tonnes a hectare or less gave the larger benefit.
documents.abstract: Wood biochar was applied from 2009 to 2011 in seven experiments on five working UK farms. Results by trial were mixed: three showed no significant yield effect, two gained 5 to 6 per cent, one doubled yield, one lost 2 to 16 per cent. A meta-analysis of all 47 treatments found a significant positive effect, averaging 0.4 tonnes a hectare more yield. Application rates of 20 tonnes a hectare or under did better than heavier doses. Temperate trials were scarce before this work, which shows biochar can pay in cool-climate farming under some conditions. With one trial doubling yields while others did nothing, the average hides wide variation between sites.

documents.title: Long-term effects of adding biochar to soils on organic matter content, persistent carbon storage, and moisture content in Karagwe, Tanzania
documents.summary: A seven-year follow-up at Karagwe, Tanzania, on Andosols treated with biochar-based compost. Soil organic matter rose 14 to 17 per cent, soil organic carbon 8 to 10 per cent, soil moisture 4 to 6 per cent over untreated soil. The sanitation-based product beat the standard compost mix on all three measures, with every treatment improving the soil.
documents.abstract: A Latin rectangle field experiment with four replicates was sampled seven years on, with 96 soil samples taken. Two biochar-compost treatments were compared with untreated Andosols: carbonisation with sanitation (CaSa) and carbonisation with standard compost (CaSt). CaSa raised soil organic matter by 17.3 per cent, soil organic carbon by 10.0 per cent and soil moisture by 6.3 per cent. CaSt gave increases of 14.4, 8.4 and 4.0 per cent. Both treatments improved the soil, and CaSa was the stronger one. The data were analysed with one-way analysis of variance. These are biochar-compost mixtures, so the gains cannot be credited to biochar alone. Carbon and moisture benefits for smallholders lasted seven years in a volcanic soil.

documents.title: The Long-Term Effect of Biochar Amendment on Soil Biochemistry and Phosphorus Availability of Calcareous Soils
documents.summary: Two long-term field trials in calcareous soils in China, one on Fluvo-aquic soil for six years, one on Cinnamon soil for five, each given a single 20 tonne a hectare biochar application. Crop yield stayed 10.8 to 24.3 per cent higher throughout. Available phosphorus rose 13.1 to 49.1 per cent, so the gain looks tied to phosphorus release in alkaline ground.
documents.abstract: Biochar was mixed into the topsoil once at 20 tonnes a hectare on two calcareous soils in China: a Fluvo-aquic soil followed for six years, a Cinnamon soil followed for five. Treated plots were compared with untreated plots for soil fertility, phosphorus fractions, enzyme activity, plus the abundance of phosphorus-cycling genes. Yield stayed 10.8 to 24.3 per cent higher after five to six years. Soil organic carbon, available phosphorus (up 13.1 to 49.1 per cent) as well as available potassium all rose. Enzymes tied to carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus cycling were more active, the alkaline phosphatase genes phoD, phoX, plus nifH, were more abundant. The labile phosphorus pool grew. The feedstock is not stated in the material available here. Two soils in one country is a narrow base, so rates will not transfer to every calcareous paddock.

documents.title: Productivity gains in vegetables from rice husk biochar application in nutrient-poor soils in Timor-Leste
documents.summary: Vegetable trials at three sites in Timor-Leste with rice husk biochar, phosphate, local fertiliser. On the acid site, biochar lifted yields of chilli, tomato, soybean by 230 per cent on average over the control. Adding phosphate raised yields further. At the neutral and alkaline sites, biochar also beat the control. Phosphorus and zinc shortages were the main limits it relieved.
documents.abstract: Field trials on vegetable crops ran at three sites in Timor-Leste, using combinations of rice husk biochar, phosphate, local fertiliser, with a pot incubation of soil from the acid site. On that acid, nutrient-poor soil, rice husk biochar had a larger effect than any other fertiliser, raising chilli pepper, tomato, soybean yields by 230 per cent on average over the control. Phosphate on top of biochar lifted yields again in all three crops. At the neutral and alkaline sites, biochar still raised mean yield over the control. The main constraints relieved were phosphorus and zinc deficiency. The yield rises are among the highest reported for vegetables anywhere. A global meta-analysis cited in the paper shows no average yield effect in temperate regions but about 25 per cent in the tropics. Acid, low-fertility soils respond most, so the results suit Australian soils of that type better than fertile ones.

documents.title: Effects of biochar application on soil leaching of nitrogen and phosphorus
documents.publisher: IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science
documents.summary: Soil amended with 2 to 8 per cent biochar by mass, then measured for leaching. Total nitrogen leaching fell by 17.6 to 37.7 per cent, total phosphorus leaching by 12.0 to 26.0 per cent. The best rate was 8 per cent for nitrogen, 2 per cent for phosphorus. Eight per cent is high for a whole paddock but workable for turf, parkland or high-value crops.
documents.abstract: Huang and colleagues tested biochar at 2 to 8 per cent by mass in soil and measured what leached out. Total nitrogen leaching dropped by 17.6 to 37.7 per cent, total phosphorus leaching by 12.0 to 26.0 per cent. The best rate for nitrogen control was 8 per cent by mass, for phosphorus 2 per cent. At fertiliser rates operators already know, the biochar held a fair share of nutrients which would otherwise leach to groundwater or run into the dam. The 8 per cent rate is on the high side for a paddock-wide amendment, yet well within reach for sports grounds, parklands, high-value crops or compost windrows. Councils concerned about runoff to waterways have a use for the figures.

documents.title: Assessing the impact of biochar in the Herbert cane industry (SRA Grower Group Innovation Project GGP1102, final report)
documents.summary: A grower group trial in the Herbert River district near Ingham, Queensland, from 2012 to 2014, on a low cation exchange capacity cane soil. Biochar at 10 tonnes a hectare with 58 kg of nitrogen beat conventional fertiliser at 124 kg of nitrogen. Cane yield was 18.7 per cent higher in plant cane, 13.2 per cent in first ratoon.
documents.abstract: The Biochar Grower Group of Lannercost ran this Sugar Research Australia project west of Ingham in the Herbert cane region, from 2012 to 2014. The soil has a low cation exchange capacity, so it holds nutrients poorly. Biochar at 10 tonnes a hectare plus 58 kg of nitrogen out-yielded the conventional program of 124 kg of nitrogen, by 18.7 per cent in plant cane and 13.2 per cent in the first ratoon. Compost was also assessed in the farming system. The result is a halving of nitrogen with better yield, which is the number a cane grower will care about. It comes from a grower group trial on one soil type, not a replicated multi-site experiment, so it reads best as a strong local signal worth testing on your own blocks.

documents.title: Impact of biochar on the water holding capacity of loamy sand soil
documents.publisher: International Journal of Energy and Environmental Engineering
documents.summary: Laboratory measurements on biochar from mixed feedstocks, alone and blended into a loamy sand. Pure biochar held over 2.7 times its dry weight in water. Adding biochar at 9 per cent by mass doubled the soil's water-holding capacity. Gains are smaller in soils already heavy with clay.
documents.abstract: Yu, Raichle and Sink ran controlled lab tests on biochar made from a mix of feedstocks. They measured the water held by pure biochar, then the effect of blending it into a loamy sand at several inclusion rates. Pure biochar held more than 2.7 times its dry weight in water. At a 9 per cent mixture by mass, the loamy sand held twice as much water as it did untreated. In heavier soils the effect was smaller. These are laboratory figures from one soil, not field yields, and a 9 per cent mass blend is a heavy dose for a paddock. The paper is the source behind many water-holding claims in sales material, and it puts a measured number on a figure often quoted loosely. It gives the strongest support for biochar in sandy or sandy-loam soils.

documents.title: Maize yield and nutrition during 4 years after biochar application to a Colombian savanna oxisol
documents.summary: A single application of 0, 8 or 20 tonnes a hectare of biochar on a Colombian savanna oxisol, under maize and soybean rotation from 2003 to 2006. Maize yield did not rise in year one. At 20 tonnes it then rose 28, 30 and 140 per cent over the control in years two, three and four.
documents.abstract: Major and colleagues applied biochar once, at 0, 8 or 20 tonnes a hectare, to an acid savanna oxisol in Colombia, then grew a maize-soybean rotation from 2003 to 2006. Soil was sampled to 30 cm each year except 2005. Maize grain yield did not rise in the first year. At 20 tonnes, yields then exceeded the control by 28, 30 and 140 per cent in 2004, 2005 and 2006. Available calcium and magnesium in the soil were 77 to 320 per cent higher, soil pH rose, and exchangeable acidity trended down. Tissue tests showed calcium and magnesium were limiting in this system, so the gain is attributed mainly to those nutrients. The mechanism is a liming and nutrient effect on a poor, acidic soil, which limits how far the numbers carry to fertile Australian soils.

documents.title: Effects of biochar from slow pyrolysis of papermill waste on agronomic performance and soil fertility
documents.summary: An Australian trial of biochar made by slow pyrolysis from papermill waste, assessing crop performance plus soil fertility. Van Zwieten, Kimber, Morris, Chan, Downie and Rust published it in Plant and Soil in 2009. Papermill waste is an industrial residue, so the result speaks to waste-derived feedstocks in particular.
documents.abstract: Van Zwieten, Kimber, Morris, Chan, Downie and Rust tested biochar made by slow pyrolysis of papermill waste, a feedstock otherwise sent to landfill or burned. The 2009 paper in Plant and Soil looks at agronomic performance as well as soil fertility in Australian conditions. It sits in the early Australian biochar work from the New South Wales group, alongside the greenwaste radish trial by Chan and colleagues. Papermill waste differs from wood in ash content and nutrient make-up, so its effect on pH, nutrients and plant growth need not match a woody char. Anyone considering an industrial residue as feedstock should read it for the soil response, then check local rules on waste-derived products before committing.

documents.title: Biochar and Soil Physical Properties
documents.publisher: Soil Science Society of America Journal
documents.summary: A review of biochar effects on soil physical properties. Bulk density fell 3 to 31 per cent, porosity rose 14 to 64 per cent, wet aggregate stability rose 3 to 226 per cent, and available water rose 4 to 130 per cent. Sandy soils responded more than clays. Field-scale, long-term studies are still thin.
documents.abstract: Blanco-Canqui reviewed what biochar does to soil compaction, strength, structure, water movement and heat behaviour. Bulk density fell by 3 to 31 per cent, porosity rose by 14 to 64 per cent, and penetration resistance changed little or not at all. Wet aggregate stability rose by 3 to 226 per cent, while dry aggregate stability gave mixed results. Plant-available water rose by 4 to 130 per cent. Saturated hydraulic conductivity dropped in coarse-textured soils, rose in fine-textured ones. Few studies cover other properties, but biochar appears to lower tensile strength, alter infiltration, moderate soil temperature swings, and barely change water repellency. Sandy soils respond more than clayey soils, larger rates give larger effects, finer particles hold more water but slow saturated flow. The ranges are wide because studies differ in soil, biochar, rate. Long-term field trials covering these properties are still missing.

documents.title: Biochar amendment improves crop production in problem soils: A review
documents.summary: A 2018 review of biochar added to problem soils such as acidic, saline or degraded ground, from Haowei Yu, Weixin Zou and colleagues in the Journal of Environmental Management. Its title reports better crop production on these soils. Good soils have less room to gain, so the grower with a degraded paddock is the target reader.
documents.abstract: Yu, Zou, Chen and colleagues review biochar on problem soils in the Journal of Environmental Management, 2018. Problem soils here means ground limited by acidity, salinity, poor structure or low fertility, where crops struggle whatever the management. Biochar has most chance of a visible response on this kind of land, because it raises pH, adds cation exchange capacity, improves water holding in soils short of all three. A good soil may show little change. The review's headline is better crop production on problem soils, and the reader should check the underlying sections to see which soil types and biochars gave the gains. Match your own soil to theirs before expecting the same result.

documents.title: Biochar Impacts on Soil Physical Properties and Greenhouse Gas Emissions
documents.summary: A review of how biochar changes soil physical properties and greenhouse gas fluxes. Rates of 1 to 2 per cent by weight improved bulk density, water holding capacity. Data on surface area, aggregate stability, penetration resistance are scarce. Carbon dioxide emissions may rise at first, then ease over time.
documents.abstract: Mukherjee and Lal set out to collect the available data on soil physical properties, greenhouse gas emissions after biochar, offer mechanisms, list research priorities. Application rates of 1 to 2 per cent by weight improved soil bulk density, water holding capacity. Evidence on surface area, aggregation stability, penetration resistance is thin. On gas fluxes, biochar can raise carbon dioxide emissions at first, with suppression of greenhouse gases appearing over time. The review proposes a two-phase complexation hypothesis for how soil interacts with biochar. Most of the underlying work was short-term, so the 1 to 2 per cent range reflects what was studied rather than a tested optimum. Physical effects are better documented here than in many reviews, yet the paper shows how much remained unmeasured by 2013.

documents.title: Biochar Effect on Maize Yield and Soil Characteristics in Five Conservation Farming Sites in Zambia
documents.summary: Farmer-led maize trials on five soils in Zambia, with maize cob or wood biochar at 4 tonnes a hectare placed in conservation farming basins. On the coarse white sand at Kaoma, yield reached 444 and 352 per cent of fertilised plots. A red sandy clay loam near Lusaka gave 142 and 131 per cent, not statistically clear. Three other soils showed no effect.
documents.abstract: These pilot trials in Zambia paired a low biochar rate of 4 tonnes a hectare with conservation farming, in which hand-dug planting basins till only 10 to 12 per cent of the land. Placing biochar in the basins puts it where the roots are, much as fertiliser is placed. Maize cob and wood biochar were tested on five soils. At Kaoma, on coarse white aeolian sand, yield was 444 per cent (plus or minus 114) and 352 per cent (plus or minus 139) of fertilised reference plots. At the University of Zambia site, a red sandy clay loam, yield was 142 and 131 per cent, with no statistical support. Three other soils showed no significant effect. In the laboratory, 5 per cent biochar lifted Kaoma base saturation from below 50 to 60 to 100 per cent, cation exchange capacity from 2 or 3 to 5 to 9 centimoles a kilogram, plant-available water from 17 to 21 per cent.

documents.title: Biochar increases soil microbial biomass but has variable effects on microbial diversity: A meta-analysis
documents.authors: Li, Wang, Chang, Jiang and Song
documents.publisher: The Science of The Total Environment
documents.summary: A 2020 meta-analysis from Xiaona Li, Tao Wang, Scott Chang and colleagues in Science of the Total Environment. Biochar raises soil microbial biomass, but its effect on microbial diversity varies between studies. For a grower, bulk soil biology is the more reliable gain.
documents.abstract: Li, Wang, Chang, Jiang and Song pooled published studies to test how biochar changes the soil microbial community. The paper appeared in Science of the Total Environment, 2020. Its title gives two results: microbial biomass goes up after biochar, but diversity responds inconsistently, rising in some studies, falling or holding in others. More biomass means more living microbes per gram of soil, a useful sign for nutrient cycling, though it says nothing about which species are present. Differences in feedstock, pyrolysis temperature, soil type or study length are likely behind the variable diversity results. Biochar reliably feeds the soil microbes in bulk, while the shift in community is harder to predict.

documents.title: Fourfold Increase in Pumpkin Yield in Response to Low-Dosage Root Zone Application of Urine-Enhanced Biochar to a Fertile Tropical Soil
documents.authors: Schmidt, Pandit, Martinsen, Cornelissen, Conte and Kammann
documents.summary: A pumpkin field trial in Nepal on a fertile silt loam. Biochar from the invasive shrub Eupatorium adenophorum, made in a flame curtain kiln, was mixed 1:1 by volume with cow urine, then placed in the root zone at 750 kilograms a hectare. Yield reached 82.6 tonnes a hectare, over 300 per cent above urine alone, 85 per cent above biochar alone.
documents.abstract: Eupatorium adenophorum, a widespread invasive shrub, was pyrolysed in a low-cost flame curtain kiln. The biochar met all premium requirements of the European Biochar Certificate. In a pumpkin trial in Nepal, three treatments each sat on cow-manure compost: urine only, biochar only, or biochar mixed 1:1 by volume with fresh cow urine. All materials went straight to the root zone before seeding, with biochar at 750 kilograms of dry matter a hectare. Urine-loaded biochar gave 82.6 tonnes of pumpkin a hectare, more than 300 per cent above urine alone, 85 per cent above biochar alone. The proposed explanation is an organic coating of the inner pores from urine, which improved nutrient capture. The soil was already fertile, so the gain is notable, though this is one trial.

documents.title: Role of Biochar in Improving Sandy Soil Water Retention and Resilience to Drought
documents.authors: Li, Zhang, Novak, Yang and Wang
documents.summary: A review of how biochar changes water holding in sandy soils, written with drought-prone regions such as New England in mind. Mixing biochar into sand adds surface area plus micropores, lifting water retention and cutting fertiliser drainage. It covers mechanisms rather than field rates.
documents.abstract: Review of the fluid mechanics behind biochar's water holding in sandy soils, prompted by more frequent drought, warming in regions including New England, USA. Sandy soils hold little water, buffer temperature poorly. Adding biochar raises surface area, adds micropores, opens more gap space, though hydrophobicity is stronger at lower production temperature. Higher water retention reduces fertiliser drainage, which can lift crop productivity while cutting nutrient leaching. The review sets out sandy soil properties (surface area, pore size, water characteristics) and links them to plant growth, development, yield. It closes with research priorities: soil water retention, plant water use efficiency, crop drought resistance, yield. Most of the evidence is mechanistic, so rates for a particular farm still need local trials.

documents.title: Cost‐benefit analysis of using biochar to improve cereals agriculture
documents.authors: Dickinson, Balduccio, Buysse, Ronsse, Huylenbroeck and Prins
documents.summary: A cost-benefit model of biochar for cereals in north-western Europe and sub-Saharan Africa, built from field trial yields and costs from feedstock to soil application. Net present value was positive in sub-Saharan Africa in several scenarios, but only where the yield effect lasted 30 years. Every north-western Europe scenario came out negative.
documents.abstract: Economic assessment of biochar as a long-term improver of arable soils, published in 2014. Cost models followed biochar from feedstock acquisition to soil application in two generalised settings: north-western Europe, sub-Saharan Africa. Benefits came from a meta-analysis of published field trials, giving cereal grain gains of 0.07 tonnes a hectare a year or more in the first, 0.18 to 1.00 tonnes in the second. A single application was assumed to hold its yield effect without decay for a varied number of years. The extra grain was valued at projected commodity prices. In sub-Saharan Africa, net present value was positive in several scenarios once the effect ran 30 years. In north-western Europe it stayed negative even with benefits stretched indefinitely. The answer hinges on how long the yield effect lasts, an assumption rather than a measurement.

documents.title: The effect of biochar, lime and ash on maize yield in a long-term field trial in a Ultisol in the humid tropics
documents.publisher: The Science of The Total Environment
documents.summary: Seven planting seasons of maize on a degraded, strongly acidic Ultisol (pH 3.6) in the humid tropics, treated once with biochar, lime, ash or washed biochar. Maize yield averaged seven times the control with biochar, five times with lime, five with washed biochar and eight with ash. The effect held across all seven seasons.
documents.abstract: Multi-season field trial in Indonesia on a degraded, strongly acidic Ultisol (pH 3.60 in KCl, exchangeable aluminium 2.4 cmol per kilogram, exchangeable calcium 0.99), treated once at the start with biochar, lime, ash or washed biochar, then planted to maize for seven seasons. Every treatment lifted yield, averaging seven times the control for biochar, five for lime, five for washed biochar, eight for ash. The effect held through all seven seasons. Every treatment also raised soil pH and cut exchangeable aluminium, lowest with lime and ash. Ash added the most potassium, phosphorus and magnesium. Biochar beat lime although lime had the highest pH, lowest aluminium, which points to the potassium, magnesium, phosphorus the biochar supplied. Part of the benefit is a liming effect, part is nutrients. For smallholders, making biochar from farm waste lifts yields while storing carbon.

documents.title: Biochar enhances soil hydraulic function but not soil aggregation in a sandy loam
documents.summary: An 8-year field trial on a sandy loam in the North China Plain, with maize-cob biochar at 4.5 or 9.0 tonnes a hectare each year against straw return, plus a control. High-dose biochar raised plant-available water by 17.8 per cent, low dose by 10.1 per cent. Aggregate stability did not improve, so the gain is in pores, not structure.
documents.abstract: Eight-year trial on a sandy loam in the North China Plain, testing yearly additions of maize-cob biochar at 9.0 tonnes a hectare (high) or 4.5 (low), straw return, plus an untreated control. Measurements in the top 10 centimetres covered aggregate distribution, three-dimensional pore structure by CT scanning, hydraulic conductivity, water retention. Biochar raised soil organic carbon by 61.0 to 116.3 per cent. The high dose lowered bulk density. Total porosity rose, as did macroporosity (pores above 30 micrometres). Water retention improved across the gravitational, capillary and hygroscopic ranges at the high dose. Plant-available water rose 17.8 per cent (high) or 10.1 per cent (low). Neither dose increased macroaggregates or aggregate stability. Straw return did the reverse: it improved macroaggregate water stability without a gain in porosity or retention. Biochar in coarse-textured soil gave better drainage and water holding, but not better structure.

documents.title: Legacy of soil health improvement with carbon increase following one time amendment of biochar in a paddy soil – A rice farm trial
documents.summary: A rice farm trial on a clayey paddy soil, sampled in 2015 after a single 10 tonne a hectare biochar application in 2009. Soil carbon storage sat 45 per cent above the neighbouring unamended field six years on. Aggregate stability rose 25 per cent, grain yield 10 per cent, with less swing between years.
documents.abstract: Topsoil from a biochar-amended rice field (10 tonnes a hectare, applied once in 2009 from crop residue) was compared in 2015 with an adjacent field given no biochar. Soil carbon storage was 45 per cent higher. Total and available nitrogen rose by about 30 per cent, bulk density fell, pH held steady. Mean weight diameter of water-stable aggregates increased 25 per cent. Microbial biomass nitrogen was up about 30 per cent, as were enzyme activities. Total bacterial abundance rose 32 per cent, with fewer fungal pathogens. Earlier work on the same farm recorded 10 per cent more grain with less year-to-year swing in yield. The comparison is one pair of fields, so it shows a legacy on this farm rather than a replicated result. It does show a single dose still working six years on.

documents.title: Biochar increases plant-available water in a sandy loam soil under an aerobic rice crop system
documents.summary: Eucalyptus wood biochar at 0, 8, 16 and 32 tonnes a hectare, worked into the top 15 centimetres of a sandy soil under aerobic rice. Plant-available water rose by about 0.8 per cent for every tonne applied, two and three years later. Rice yield did not respond, because rainfall during the critical period topped 650 millimetres.
documents.abstract: Eucalyptus biochar (slow pyrolysis at about 450 degrees, milled below 2 millimetres) was applied at 0, 8, 16 and 32 tonnes a hectare to a sandy Dystric Plinthosol under aerobic rice, then measured two and three years later on 16 plots. Plant-available water in the upper layer rose in proportion to the rate, by about 0.8 per cent per tonne. Saturated moisture rose 0.5 per cent per tonne, macroporosity 1.6 per cent, so the gain came from more pore space in a sandy matrix. Rice yield did not change, since rainfall in both seasons exceeded 650 millimetres in the critical period, leaving no water shortage for biochar to relieve. The water benefit is real but only pays where a crop runs short. Very high rates need an economic check.

documents.title: Biochar and urease inhibitor mitigate NH3 and N2O emissions and improve wheat yield in a urea fertilized alkaline soil
documents.summary: A wheat field trial in Pakistan with urea at 150 kilograms of nitrogen a hectare, 10 tonnes a hectare of biochar and a urease inhibitor. Biochar cut ammonia loss by 27 per cent, nitrous oxide by 24 per cent. Adding the inhibitor took the cuts to 69 and 53 per cent. Grain yield rose 13 per cent with biochar.
documents.abstract: A randomised block trial with four replicates in Pakistan (34.01 degrees north) tested urea at 150 kilograms of nitrogen a hectare against urea with 10 tonnes a hectare of biochar, then urea with biochar plus a urease inhibitor (1 litre a tonne). Against urea alone, biochar cut ammonia emissions by 27 per cent, nitrous oxide by 24 per cent. With the inhibitor added, the cuts were 69 and 53 per cent. Biochar with urea lifted grain yield 13 per cent, shoot biomass 24 per cent, nitrogen uptake 12 per cent. The inhibitor added a further 22 per cent in grain, 38 in biomass, 27 in nitrogen assimilation. The soil was alkaline, where ammonia loss from urea is high, so results may be smaller on acid soils.

documents.title: Biochar Improves Soil-Tomato Plant, Tomato Production, and Economic Benefits under Reduced Nitrogen Application in Northwestern China
documents.authors: Guo, Yu, Kharbach, Zhang, Wang and Niu
documents.summary: A greenhouse experiment at Yangling in Shaanxi, China, growing drip-irrigated tomatoes on silty clay loam at biochar rates of 0, 30, 50, 70 tonnes a hectare, with nitrogen from 170 to 250 kilograms. Biochar at 50 tonnes with a 24 per cent nitrogen cut gave the highest yield. The mix recommended for local farmers is 35 tonnes of biochar with 200 kilograms of nitrogen.
documents.abstract: The greenhouse trial in Yangling, Shaanxi province, crossed four biochar rates (0, 30, 50, 70 tonnes a hectare) with four nitrogen rates (170, 190, 210, 250 kilograms a hectare) on silty clay loam under drip irrigation. Where nitrogen was cut by 16 per cent or 24 per cent, biochar raised microbial abundance, soil enzyme activity (urease, phosphatase, catalase), leaf gas exchange, biomass, tomato growth. The highest yield came from 50 tonnes of biochar with nitrogen cut by 24 per cent. Too much biochar (70 tonnes) or too deep a nitrogen cut (32 per cent) gave poor results for growth, yield, quality, returns. Weighing yield, sugar-acid ratio, vitamin C content, economics, the recommendation is 35 tonnes of biochar with 200 kilograms of nitrogen. These rates are high, and the trial ran in a greenhouse, so open-field economics at lower biochar rates need separate checking.

documents.title: Water cost savings from soil biochar amendment: A spatial analysis
documents.summary: A model linking biochar properties to soil water holding capacity, mapped across US counties with an irrigation cost model attached. Sandy soils in the southeast, far north, northeast and west stand to gain most. For an instrumented site in Nebraska, the model predicts irrigated water use falling 37 per cent.
documents.abstract: A meta-analysis related biochar properties and application rates to changes in water holding capacity, by soil texture. Limited data confined the analysis to sandy soils. Results were mapped across US counties, with an economic model converting water holding gains into irrigation expense. Biochar looked most effective for sandy soils in the southeast, far north, northeast and western United States. In a prototype run for an instrumented site in Nebraska, the model predicted a 37 per cent cut in irrigated water use. This is a prediction built on pooled studies, not a measured field result, and it covers sandy soils only. The approach is meant for farmers weighing a biochar purchase, and for placing future field experiments. The logic carries over to sandy irrigated country in Australia.

documents.title: Boosting soil health and crop nutrients with locally sourced biochar and compost in Sacramento urban agriculture
documents.authors: Gao, Medina, Gonzalez-Ospina, Burce, Burce and Melbourne
documents.summary: Two urban farms in Sacramento, California, one season of corn. Pistachio shell biochar at 12.5 tonnes a hectare, green waste compost at about 25 tonnes, a mix of the two, and an untreated control. Biochar and the mix raised soil water holding capacity, organic matter, cation exchange capacity. Corn kernels carried more phosphorus, magnesium, calcium, iron. One season only.
documents.abstract: Field trials ran on two urban farms in Sacramento, California, in a randomised block design with four treatments: an untreated control, compost at about 25 tonnes a hectare, pistachio shell biochar at 12.5 tonnes a hectare, and a compost-biochar mix. The biochar and compost rates were matched at 10 tonnes of carbon a hectare, with the mix carrying 20. Compost came from green waste produced on site, so the system recycled local organic material. Soil was sampled mid-season, then late in the season, with corn kernels analysed for nutrients. Biochar and the mix lifted water holding capacity, organic matter, cation exchange capacity. Soil nitrate plus available phosphorus ran higher under biochar. The mix raised microbial metabolic activity and community evenness, with overall diversity unchanged. Kernel phosphorus, magnesium, calcium, iron rose in both biochar treatments. The result covers a single season, so the longer-term pattern is untested.

documents.title: Effects of Biochar on Properties of Tropical Sandy Soils Under Organic Agriculture
documents.summary: Farmer fields on tropical sandy soil where biochar from local farm waste had been used for over three years. Amended soils had higher cation exchange capacity, field capacity, plant-available water and aggregate stability than unamended soils. Each difference was significant at p below 0.05 in a paired comparison.
documents.abstract: Biochar from local agricultural waste had been used in organic farmer fields for more than three years. Amended sandy soils were compared with unamended ones using a paired samples t-test. Cation exchange capacity, exchangeable potassium, available phosphorus, field capacity, plant-available water, water-stable aggregate fractions, median aggregate size and aggregate stability all differed at p below 0.05. Physical properties responded most strongly. Biochar particle size affects how clay arranges on the surface, while the grains give fungi a habitat and food source. Both build water-stable aggregates and hold more water. These are working farms with conservative soil management alongside the biochar, so the effect is a combined one. Sandy tropical soils hold water and nutrients poorly, which makes the result useful for similar country.

documents.title: Wood Vinegar Promotes Soil Health and the Productivity of Cowpea
documents.summary: A two-year field study in Ghana comparing wood vinegar applied as a soil drench or a foliar spray on cowpea. Both raised shoot dry matter, nodulation, grain yield over the control. Soil drenching returned the best economics, followed by foliar spraying.
documents.abstract: Wood vinegar, a by-product of pyrolysis rich in pyroligneous acid, is used as a growth promoter, a biopesticide. The Ghanaian field trial measured nodulation, shoot biomass, grain yield, value to cost ratio, soil enzymes, respiration, microbial biomass nitrogen, permanganate-oxidisable carbon, mineralisable carbon, pH, available nitrogen, phosphorus. Soil drenching and foliar spraying both lifted shoot dry matter, nodulation, yield. Drenching gave the larger gains in permanganate-oxidisable and mineralisable carbon, while soil enzymes and microbial biomass nitrogen rose under both methods. Economic returns beat the control, with drenching first. Two years in Ghana.

documents.title: Biochar Effects on Soil Water Retention and Water Movement
documents.summary: A 2026 American Biochar Institute briefing on how biochar changes soil water retention, movement, aimed at irrigation efficiency. Finer biochar particles raised plant-available water in silt loam, clay. It sets out where effects are strong, where they are weak or absent, what decides the difference.
documents.abstract: Irrigation takes the largest share of consumptive freshwater use in United States agriculture, so soil holding more usable water between irrigations is worth chasing. The briefing summarises peer-reviewed work on two linked properties: retention (field capacity, wilting point, plant-available water) plus movement (infiltration, redistribution, drainage). Plant-available water, the gap between field capacity and wilting point, is the measure that counts for irrigation. Finer biochar raised it in silt loam, clay. Guidance is given by soil texture, since light soils respond differently from heavy ones. Growers on sandy ground should read the texture sections separately from those on heavy clay, then check the rate, particle size of their own biochar against the studies cited.

documents.title: Biochar Guidelines for Agriculture Applications
documents.summary: A 2026 practical guide from the American Biochar Institute with the Nebraska Forest Service on applying biochar to annual or perennial crops. It cites a wheat trial on an acid soil where biochar at 8 tonnes an acre raised yields by 280 per cent over two years, against 200 per cent for lime. Advice is organised around the 4Rs: source, place, rate, timing.
documents.abstract: The guide borrows the 4Rs of nutrient stewardship, applying them to biochar. On source, it recommends local waste feedstocks such as poultry litter, rice hulls, corn stover, vine prunings, coconut husks, woodchips, bagasse, warning that biochar from biosolids or construction waste can carry contamination. Growers are told to know the feedstock, have the product analysed first, weigh the cost of distant supply. The headline trial figure is a wheat crop on an acid soil, where 8 tonnes an acre (about 20 tonnes a hectare) lifted yield by 280 per cent over two years, with lime giving 200 per cent. That is an acid-soil result, so do not expect it on a neutral paddock.

documents.title: 2023 Impact of Biochar on Soil Chemical Properties and Corn Yield and Quality
documents.summary: A replicated corn silage trial at Borderview Research Farm, Alburgh, Vermont, in 2023, on a rocky silt loam. Pine biochar at 17 tons an acre (about 38 tonnes a hectare) went on with urea, injected dairy manure, broadcast dairy manure or no added fertility. Biochar treatments generally gave more digestible silage by the 30-hour fibre test. Soil pH stayed within the recommended range for corn. A single season.
documents.abstract: University of Vermont Extension ran a randomised split plot trial with four replications. Main plots were urea at 200 pounds an acre (about 224 kilograms a hectare), injected liquid dairy manure, broadcast dairy manure, an unfertilised control. Each had a biochar subplot, a no-biochar subplot. The biochar came from Wakefield Agricultural Carbon in Georgia, made from Southern Yellow Pine in a continuous flow pyrolysis system above 1,300 degrees Fahrenheit (about 700 degrees Celsius). It was spread on 9 June, worked in by disc, then corn (Pioneer P8820Q) was planted on 14 June at 34,000 seeds an acre. Silage was chopped on 6 October, adjusted to 35 per cent dry matter. Quality was measured by near infrared analysis: protein, fibre, digestibility, net energy for lactation. Differences were tested at the 0.10 level. One year at one site means the pattern needs repeating before it is a recommendation.

documents.title: The Potential for Biochar to Improve Sustainability in Coffee Cultivation and Processing: A White Paper
documents.summary: A 2018 white paper from the International Biochar Initiative on coffee growing, drawing on trials in producing regions. Young Arabica seedlings given 2 per cent woody biochar grew 14 per cent more root fresh weight, 18 per cent more shoot fresh weight, 21 per cent more shoot dry weight than other rates tested. These are seedling results, not orchard yields.
documents.abstract: Kathleen Draper of the Ithaka Institute updated a 2015 white paper for the International Biochar Initiative, with funding from the Biochar for Sustainable Soils Project. It sets out the coffee growing challenge, then works through uses of biochar on farm: soil amendment, disease management, composting, water filtration, energy. It also covers biochar made from coffee residues, production technologies, carbon pathways, the economics, demonstration projects including one in Brazil. The one hard trial figure in the opening pages comes from Arabica seedlings. Those given 2 per cent woody biochar had 14 per cent more root fresh weight, 18 per cent more shoot fresh weight, 21 per cent more shoot dry weight than seedlings on other rates. Seedling pots say little about mature bearing trees, so read the field demonstrations before committing to a rate.

documents.title: The Potential for Biochar to Deliver Greater Sustainability for Maize Cultivation and Processing: A White Paper
documents.summary: A 2018 International Biochar Initiative white paper reviewing maize evidence. On highly acid soils, maize yields rose by more than 60 per cent on average with biochar. In Nepal, 2 per cent biochar with one third of the recommended fertiliser gave higher nutrient availability than the full rate. On fertile soils with high cation exchange capacity, yields fell by 7 per cent on average.
documents.abstract: Kathleen Draper of the Ithaka Institute wrote this white paper in July 2018 with funding from the Biochar for Sustainable Soils Project. It reviews the maize growing challenge, then the case for biochar: yield, disease resistance, lower air pollution, less groundwater pollution, energy, economic growth, residue management. The yield evidence depends heavily on the soil. Highly acid soils gave average gains above 60 per cent. A Nepal study found 2 per cent biochar with one third of the recommended fertiliser lifted nutrient availability beyond the full fertiliser treatment. The same body of work records an average yield drop of 7 per cent on fertile, high-CEC soils. For an Australian grower the lesson is to match biochar to a soil constraint such as acidity or low fertility, rather than applying it to good soil.

documents.title: Biochar Field Studies: An IBI Research Summary
documents.summary: A ten-page 2013 International Biochar Initiative summary of field studies by Josh Laufer with Thayer Tomlinson. A meta-analysis found a grand mean crop productivity increase of 10 per cent. Rice yields rose 12 per cent at 10 tonnes a hectare of biochar, 14 per cent at 40 tonnes, in unfertilised plots.
documents.abstract: The summary covers crop yield, economic performance, fertiliser interactions, water uptake, mycorrhizal colonisation, microbial activity, greenhouse gas flux. It draws on published literature to May 2013, written for the general public. Across a meta-analysis the grand mean productivity gain was 10 per cent. In unfertilised rice plots, 10 tonnes a hectare lifted yield by 12 per cent, while 40 tonnes lifted it by 14 per cent, so a fourfold rate bought only two extra points. The summary flags a gap in the evidence: many trials did not describe their biochar properly, which makes differences in results hard to explain. The paper is dated now, but the rate response and the call for consistent reporting still hold.

documents.title: Nitrogen dynamics following field application of biochar in a temperate North American maize-based production system (Güereña et al.)
documents.authors: Güereña, Lehmann, Hanley, Enders, Hyland and Riha
documents.publisher: Cornell University (Lehmann lab), Plant and Soil
documents.summary: A 15N tracer study of maize in a temperate North American cropping system, with biochar applied at 12 tonnes a hectare. Under full nitrogen fertiliser, leaching losses were 82 per cent lower after biochar. The share of applied nitrogen held in organic soil pools rose to 35 per cent from 15 per cent, so less fertiliser left the root zone.
documents.abstract: Güereña and colleagues applied biochar at 12 tonnes a hectare to a maize-based production system in a temperate part of North America. The fertiliser nitrogen was labelled with 15N, which let the team follow it into the crop, into soil pools, out through leachate. At full nitrogen fertilisation, nitrogen lost by leaching was 82 per cent lower where biochar had been added. The share of applied nitrogen retained in soil organic pools rose to 35 per cent, from 15 per cent without biochar. The result points to biochar acting as a nitrogen holding agent in the soil, which has a cost and an environmental side for any grower buying fertiliser. It is a temperate maize system on one site type, so sandy, low-rainfall or irrigated Australian soils may behave differently. The paper appeared in Plant and Soil in 2013.

documents.title: Soil and pasture responses to poultry litter biochar combined with fertiliser (Agronomy Australia conference)
documents.publisher: NSW DPI and Australian universities (Agronomy Australia Proceedings)
documents.summary: A pasture trial on a degraded red Vertosol at Tamworth, NSW, with poultry litter biochar at 10 tonnes a hectare mixed into the top 10 centimetres. Biochar with urea lifted digit grass herbage mass by 13 to 19 per cent in the 2010 to 2011 season, and improved nitrogen efficiency by 21 per cent at 50 kilograms of nitrogen a hectare. Without fertiliser, biochar did nothing for yield.
documents.abstract: NSW DPI set out 24 plots, each 9 by 7 metres, on a degraded red Vertosol at Tamworth on the North-West Slopes. Half received biochar made from wood-based poultry litter at 550 degrees Celsius, spread at 10 tonnes a hectare in December 2009. Digit grass (Digitaria eriantha cv. Premier) was sown the following January. Before any fertiliser went on, biochar plots grew 5664 kilograms of dry matter a hectare against 4935 without. Urea then went on at 0, 50 or 100 kilograms of nitrogen a hectare a year, with superphosphate at 200 kilograms a hectare on every plot. From September 2010 to May 2011, biochar plus nitrogen raised dry herbage mass by 13 to 19 per cent, more at 50 kilograms than at 100. Water use was similar across treatments, with a trend to better water use efficiency on fertilised biochar plots. Topsoil carbon was higher where biochar went on. One soil, one site, a four-page conference paper.

documents.title: Guidelines on Practical Aspects of Biochar Application to Field Soil in Various Soil Management Systems
documents.summary: A 23-page guide from 2010 by Julie Major, then IBI extension director, to the practical side of putting biochar on field soil. It covers rates, timing, incorporation methods across different soil management systems. Testing, regulations, storage, handling, wind loss also get sections.
documents.abstract: Julie Major wrote the guidelines for the International Biochar Initiative, with input from turfgrass, tree care, agricultural research, farming specialists in Asia, the United States, Britain, Australia (including NSW DPI). The contents run from characterising biochar through regulations to best practice for storage, transport, soil application. Wind loss of fine biochar gets its own section, with methods to avoid it. The remainder sets out rates, timing, incorporation for various soil management systems. The guide is version 1.0 from November 2010, written before most of the field evidence now available existed. Farm managers or contractors planning a first spreading job will find the handling detail useful, but should check rates against current trial results.

documents.title: Biochar for agronomic improvement and greenhouse gas mitigation (fact sheet)
documents.summary: A six-page CSIRO summary from 2010 of the national biochar research program, funded by GRDC and DAFF. The program characterised more than 70 biochars from different feedstocks and temperatures. It describes biochar as chemically and biologically stable, with value for crop productivity as well as carbon storage. It reports no yield numbers.
documents.abstract: CSIRO's fact sheet introduces two linked projects: a GRDC-funded one led with the University of Western Australia to tune fertiliser use alongside biochar, and a DAFF-funded national initiative on biochar properties, soil interactions, greenhouse gas effects, life cycle analysis. Both share the analysis of more than 70 biochars, measured for carbon, nitrogen, pH, electrical conductivity, water holding capacity, cation exchange capacity, trace elements, ecotoxicity. High-ash feedstocks tend to give more nutrients but lower stability, so biochars suited to productivity differ from those suited to carbon storage. Planned outputs included a calculator for farmers to estimate crop responses. The sheet explains why controlled application is the most reliable way to use biochar. It is a 2010 program overview, so read it as background, not a source of rates.

documents.title: Biochar: Potential for climate change mitigation, improved yield and soil quality (Grassland Society of NSW)
documents.publisher: NSW Department of Primary Industries (Van Zwieten et al.)
documents.summary: Early NSW DPI work, presented in 2008 to the Grassland Society of NSW. Cattle manure biochar raised plant nitrogen uptake by 23 per cent, phosphorus uptake by 36 per cent, without added nitrogen. Feedlot biochar lifted the yield response to nitrogen by 13 per cent. It is a four-page conference paper from the first years of field work.
documents.abstract: The paper covers pyrolysis basics, then results from glasshouse and field trials. NSW DPI managed 158 field plots with biochar in cropping, pasture, perennial tree crops. Biochars made at 400 to 700 degrees Celsius vary widely: higher temperatures raise alkalinity but lower available nutrients, while manure biochars carry more nutrients than woody ones. In a 47 day pot trial on a Krasnozem, poultry litter biochar and green waste biochar were each mixed in at 10 tonnes a hectare. Poultry litter biochar supplied more available phosphorus and nitrogen, while both raised soil carbon. Cattle manure biochar lifted plant nitrogen uptake by 23 per cent, phosphorus uptake by 36 per cent, with no added nitrogen. Feedlot biochar raised the yield response to nitrogen by 13 per cent. These are early pot and plot results from 2008, so confirm them against later field work.

documents.title: Nitrogen retention and plant uptake on a highly weathered central Amazonian Ferralsol amended with compost and charcoal (Steiner et al.)
documents.authors: Steiner, Glaser, Teixeira, Lehmann, Blum and Zech
documents.publisher: Cornell University (Lehmann lab), J. Plant Nutrition and Soil Science
documents.summary: A field trial near Manaus in the central Amazon, growing sorghum on a highly weathered Ferralsol with a 15N tracer to follow the fertiliser nitrogen. Plants recovered 14.7 per cent of applied nitrogen where compost was added, against 5.7 per cent under mineral fertiliser only. After the second harvest, the charcoal plots held more nitrogen in the soil, which matters on soils that lose nutrients fast.
documents.abstract: Steiner and colleagues ran a field trial near Manaus, Brazil, on a central Amazonian Ferralsol, a deeply weathered soil with little capacity to hold nutrients. Sorghum was the test crop. The nitrogen applied carried a 15N label, so each share could be traced into plant biomass or soil. Compost and charcoal amendments were compared with mineral fertiliser alone. In the crop, 14.7 per cent of applied nitrogen was recovered with compost, against 5.7 per cent with mineral fertiliser only. After the second harvest, the charcoal-amended plots kept more nitrogen in the soil than the others. The work comes from the Cornell group studying terra preta, the dark Amazonian soils that stayed fertile for centuries. It covers one site, one soil type, two harvests, so the pattern needs its own test before anyone applies it to Australian sands or clays.

documents.title: Biological nitrogen fixation by common beans increases with bio-char additions (Rondon et al.)
documents.publisher: Cornell University (Lehmann lab), Biology and Fertility of Soils
documents.summary: A pot study by Rondon and colleagues at Cornell on common beans in a biochar-amended soil. Fixed nitrogen rose from 50 to 72 per cent of plant nitrogen with 90 grams of biochar a kilogram of soil, and bean yield rose 46 per cent over the control.
documents.abstract: Marco Rondon, Johannes Lehmann and colleagues grew common beans in pots with biochar added at rates up to 90 grams per kilogram of soil, published in Biology and Fertility of Soils in 2007. At the top rate the share of plant nitrogen that came from biological fixation rose from 50 to 72 per cent, and bean yield rose 46 per cent over the unamended control. The mechanism is worth knowing: biochar shifted the plant's nitrogen supply toward its root nodules, away from soil nitrogen, which matters for legume growers wanting to cut fertiliser bills. It was a pot study at a very high biochar rate, so it shows what is possible, not what a paddock rate will deliver.

documents.title: Use of Biochar from the Pyrolysis of Waste Organic Material as a Soil Amendment (final report)
documents.publisher: Washington State University Center for Sustaining Agriculture and Natural Resources
documents.summary: A 181-page final report from Washington State University's Center for Sustaining Agriculture and Natural Resources. Biochars from several waste feedstocks were tested in five Washington soils at 9.8, 19.5 and 39 tonnes a hectare. Optimal slow pyrolysis gave a biochar yield of 26 per cent, and the report works through pyrolysis economics.
documents.abstract: This report covers biochar from the pyrolysis of waste organic material as a soil amendment in Washington State. Biochars from several feedstocks were applied to five soils at three rates: 9.8, 19.5, 39 tonnes a hectare, roughly 4, 8, 16 tons an acre. The design lets a reader compare feedstock, soil, rate in one programme, which few single studies do. The report also costs the production side. It puts the optimal biochar yield from slow pyrolysis at 26 per cent, a figure setting how much feedstock a unit must handle to supply a given area. At 181 pages it is a full project record. Results differ by feedstock, so check the tables for a soil close to yours before taking a rate from it.

documents.title: OSU research shows biochar benefits persist over time
documents.summary: Dryland wheat plots at Pendleton, Oregon, on Walla Walla silt loam, with forest-waste biochar applied once in 2013 at three rates in a wheat and pea rotation. More than ten years on, soil pH was up by as much as 0.9 units, most at the higher rates. Soil organic carbon stocks were 95 to 207 per cent above unamended plots.
documents.abstract: Researchers from Oregon State University plus Washington State University revisited a field experiment set up in 2013 near Pendleton. Winter wheat with summer fallow, low residue return, years of ammonium fertiliser had left the soil losing carbon, turning acid. Biochar made from forest waste was applied once at three rates, then compared with no biochar, or nitrogen alone. The pH gain, up to 0.9 units, sat in the surface layer where the biochar was mixed in. It was strongest, longest lasting at higher rates. Cation exchange capacity, calcium, magnesium, potassium, zinc rose, while iron solubility fell. Carbon stocks were somewhat lower in later measurements than early ones, but the gains held. Early yields with biochar plus nitrogen beat nitrogen alone: modest in wheat at moderate rates, stronger in peas at the lowest rate. The highest rate added no yield, made wheat more variable. Results were published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems.

documents.title: Biochar Guidelines for Agricultural Applications, Part 1
documents.publisher: Nebraska Forest Service with US Biochar Initiative
documents.summary: An eight-page farmer guide from the Nebraska Forest Service with the US Biochar Initiative, built around the 4Rs: right source, place, rate, timing. It cites a wheat trial on an acid soil where biochar at 8 tons an acre (about 18 tonnes a hectare) lifted yields 280 per cent over two years, against 200 per cent for lime. A sound starting rate is 1 ton an acre.
documents.abstract: The guide applies nutrient stewardship thinking to biochar. For source, know the feedstock, have the biochar analysed, and be wary of biosolids or construction waste, which carry contamination risk. For place, poor soils (low pH, low organic matter, low cation exchange capacity, compaction, erosion) are more likely to respond than good ones. For rate, 1 to 10 tons an acre has given consistent gains, with 1 ton the lowest effective rate for soil organism habitat, 3 tons for organic matter. Potting mixes take 5 to 25 per cent by volume. Average cost has fallen to about US$350 a ton, with carbon credits offsetting some of it. For timing, apply after harvest with a cover crop, avoiding frozen ground. Charging biochar with nutrients or microbes first limits nutrient tie-up, which can cost yield in the first year. The 280 per cent figure comes from one cited trial, not the guide's own work.

documents.title: Biochar Manual for Small Farms in BC
documents.publisher: University of British Columbia student manual with Fraser Common Farm Cooperative
documents.summary: A student-written manual for small farms in British Columbia, drawing on fieldwork at Fraser Common Farm Cooperative in Aldergrove. A pot trial with chicken-manure biochar lifted radish yield by 42 per cent at 10 tonnes a hectare, against 96 per cent at 50 tonnes. A Quebec soybean trial grew 20 per cent more biomass in the biochar plot in year one.
documents.abstract: Jessica Dennis, an undergraduate at the University of British Columbia, wrote this manual for small farmers and gardeners.
