It rests on academic sources, the work of farmers and small biochar producers, and fieldwork at Fraser Common Farm Cooperative in Aldergrove, with funding from the Pacific Institute for Climate Solutions. A table of trial results gives the numbers. A radish pot trial with chicken-manure biochar raised yield by 42 per cent at 10 tonnes a hectare, rising to 96 per cent at 50 tonnes. A soybean trial in Quebec produced 20 per cent more biomass in the biochar plot in the first year. These are pots and a single season, so treat the rates as a guide to direction, not a recommendation. The manual says plainly that it does not set out to persuade anyone to use biochar.

documents.title: Biochar and Sustainable Agriculture
documents.publisher: National Center for Appropriate Technology (NCAT / ATTRA)
documents.summary: A farm guide on biochar from the National Center for Appropriate Technology in the United States, published in January 2018. It covers what biochar is, what it offers farmers and ranchers, on-farm bioenergy, economics, soil carbon, plus the limits of the climate claims. One worked example: a Swiss biochar with 0.8 per cent potash would supply 160 pounds of K2O an acre at 10 tons an acre.
documents.abstract: This ATTRA guide, written by agricultural economist Jeff Schahczenski for the National Center for Appropriate Technology, was published in January 2018 as publication IP358. It is aimed at farmers and ranchers. Sections cover what biochar is, its value on farms, on-farm or community bioenergy, economic potential, the link to climate change and soil carbon, then the limits of biochar as a climate tool. It describes biochar as a pyrolysis product made from biomass, with gases or oils produced alongside it. The worked nutrient example uses US units: a Swiss biochar with 0.8 per cent potash would deliver 160 pounds of K2O an acre at 10 tons an acre, roughly 180 kilograms a hectare from about 22 tonnes a hectare. Nutrient content varies by feedstock, so a lab analysis of your own biochar is the number to use. The guide is a starting point, not a trial result.

documents.title: How biochar works in soil (Wilson)
documents.summary: Kelpie Wilson sets out how biochar works in soil, starting from the Amazonian terra preta. Field trials range from large yield gains in some places to neutral or negative results in others. Soil, climate or biochar type can decide the outcome, so she works toward a mechanistic explanation in place of a single recipe.
documents.abstract: Wilson opens with the hypothesis that people in the Amazon built terra preta over centuries by adding biochar to organic and household waste, turning weathered topsoil into a productive soil. She notes that field research since then has produced a wide spread of results, from overwhelming yield gains in some places to neutral or negative outcomes in others, and that hype mixed with science has clouded the search for a mechanism. Biochar materials differ widely by soil, climate, feedstock, so the question becomes how biochar works rather than whether it does. The article then sets out the mechanisms behind the yield improvements reported in field work. For a grower the useful message is the caveat: match the biochar to the soil problem, such as low nutrient holding or poor water retention, and trial a strip before a whole paddock.

documents.title: Anatomy of a Field Trial: wood-based biochar and compost in a Pacific Northwest soil (SeaChar)
documents.summary: A volunteer-run field trial from the Seattle Biochar Working Group (SeaChar), testing wood-based biochar with compost on a Pacific Northwest soil at a local college. The group set it up because no biochar trials existed in the region, and early audiences were sceptical about putting fuel in the ground. The write-up reads as a model for community groups wanting local evidence.
documents.abstract: Jim Ippolito, Art Donnelly and Jim Grob describe how a small Seattle group called SeaChar came to run a scientific field trial. After the Amazonian terra preta soils reached the news in 2006, people worldwide took up biochar as a climate measure. SeaChar began by informing the public, then met scepticism about adding what most people saw as fuel to soil. With no regional trials to point to, they set up their own at a local college, testing wood-based biochar with compost on Pacific Northwest soil. The article, in The Biochar Journal, is framed as the anatomy of a trial: why it was done, how it was designed, what a volunteer group can learn from running one. For a council, school or landcare group, it is a template for generating local evidence. As a community trial it will lack the replication of a university study, so read its results with that in mind.

documents.title: Reforestation with biochar (Ecker)
documents.summary: Achim Ecker's account of restoring 7 hectares of barren land in the Alentejo, Portugal, with a terra preta approach. The block held a few old cork oaks and one eucalyptus. He demonstrated a method for making biochar and terra preta in the dry southern European climate, to build the humus needed to start reforestation. It is one farm's experience, not a replicated trial.
documents.abstract: Ecker bought 7 hectares of land called Retumbana-Nova in the Alentejo, Portugal, almost 20 years ago. It shares a boundary with Tamera. A ruined rammed earth farmhouse has since been refurbished, but the land around it was barren, with a few old cork oaks and one eucalyptus left, and he wanted to reforest it. His starting point is that farmers in deforested regions with depleted soils must create and store enough humus to begin the reforestation that eventually protects land from bushfires and drought. He has experimented with terra preta for some years, recently demonstrating a new method for producing biochar and terra preta in the demanding Mediterranean climate of Portugal. The piece gives practical lessons from one property. With no replication or control plots described, it shows what is possible rather than what to expect, but dry-summer regions in southern Australia face a similar problem.

documents.title: Dietary biochar as a feed additive for increasing livestock performance: A meta-analysis of in vitro and in vivo experiment
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of lab and live animal trials on biochar added to ruminant diets. Methane fell, digestibility rose, nitrogen retention improved, rumen fermentation shifted toward propionic acid. Feed conversion improved in the live animal data, though intake of dry matter and crude protein dropped slightly.
documents.abstract: The pooled trials covered rumen fermentation in the lab, plus feed intake, growth, blood measures, digestibility and nitrogen retention in live animals. Each study was a random effect in a mixed model, with biochar dose fixed. Methane fell in a curved dose pattern while total gas production rose. Volatile fatty acids, acetic acid in particular, dropped in the lab work, while propionic acid and ammonia tended to climb with dose. In live animals feed conversion improved, intake of dry matter, organic matter, crude protein, neutral detergent fibre came down, digestibility of the same fractions rose, as did nitrogen retention. Growth performance improved. Feedstock and dose varied between the source studies, so the result is an average across biochars, not a recipe for one product.

documents.title: Addition of pyroligneous extract (wood vinegar) to the diet of growing and finishing pigs
documents.publisher: Brazilian Journal of Animal and Environmental Research
documents.summary: Twenty-four crossbred pigs in Brazil were fed eucalyptus wood vinegar at 0, 0.5, 1.0 or 1.5 per cent of the diet over 72 days, from 31 kilograms to about 98 kilograms. Growth, carcass quality and faeces were unchanged at every level. Pigs reached slaughter weight about 10 per cent sooner, so wood vinegar is safe in feed up to 1.5 per cent.
documents.abstract: Twenty-four crossbred female pigs (Pietrain, Landrace, Large White lines) started at 31.2 kilograms and finished at 97.5 kilograms after 72 days. Daily feed intake, weight gain, feed conversion, carcass yield, carcass quality and a diarrhoea index were measured. Growth-phase results showed no linear or quadratic trend across treatments. Over the full period the 1 per cent group showed a linear effect on feed intake, but weight gain and feed conversion did not shift. Carcass measures matched the controls, as did the faeces. Wood vinegar is a by-product of making charcoal and biochar, so this is one possible outlet for it. One small group of animals, one trial: a larger run would be needed to confirm the faster finish.

documents.title: Biochar-Enhanced Diets in Naeemi Sheep: A Strategy for Enteric Methane Mitigation and Growth Optimization
documents.summary: Naeemi ewes fed a diet with sterile date-palm biochar, against a control on the standard diet. Methane fell by 70.8 to 74.2 per cent from a starting 1070 ppm. Treated ewes were heavier at 64.19 kg, with greater body length, girth and wither height.
documents.abstract: This book chapter reports a second trial with Naeemi ewes, using sterile date-palm biochar added to a standard diet. Methane at day 0 was 1,070 ppm. Biochar lowered emissions by 70.79 to 74.24 per cent. Treated animals weighed 64.19 kg, with body length of 80.49 cm, heart girth of 82.95 cm, height at the withers of 100.49 cm, all above the control group. The proposed mechanism is the large surface area of biochar, plus its cation exchange capacity, which takes up hydrogen ions released in the rumen. Microbes then shift toward ammonium rather than methane. Particle size, porosity and surface chemistry change how well this works, and earlier trials by others have shown mixed methane results by biochar type and dose. The figures sit close to the same group's earlier paper.

documents.title: Mara Seeds Biochar dairy trial
documents.summary: A trial across four South Australian dairies using Mara Seeds Biochar at about 1 per cent of the mixed ration. At one dairy, milk yield rose about 2 litres a cow a day, solids rose 0.1 kilograms a day, and extra profit was about $130,000 a year on a 250-cow herd. The other three dairies gained less.
documents.abstract: Rebbeck ran a biochar feeding trial on four dairies in South Australia, using Mara Seeds Biochar at about 1 per cent of the mixed ration. One dairy reached the headline result: roughly 2 litres more milk per cow a day, 0.1 kilograms a day more solids, and about $130,000 a year in extra profit on a 250-cow herd. The other three dairies saw smaller gains, so results are site-specific. The trial moved biochar in dairy from interesting idea to something worth piloting in the milking shed. The product differs from Possible Agriculture Biochar in feedstock and pyrolysis profile, which is a higher-grade hardwood made at higher temperatures. Equivalent or better results are expected, but replication with that product is pending.

documents.title: Biochar and dung beetles: adaptation, productivity, mitigation, regeneration (presentation)
documents.summary: A South Australian dairy feeding trial across four dairies of 250 cows each. One herd was fed biochar at 200 grams a head a day, two dairies had none, with milk yield, protein, fat and cell counts measured six weekly. The presenter reports milk up by about 1.5 litres a head a day.
documents.abstract: Melissa Rebbeck of Climate and Agricultural Support presented a South Australian feeding trial across four dairies of 250 cattle each. One dairy fed 200 grams of biochar a head a day, another used a different biochar product at 90 ml, and two dairies fed none. Milk yield, protein, fat and cell counts were measured every six weeks against long-term records, along with manure pH. The presenter reports milk yield up by around 1.5 litres a head a day, less fodder bought, and biochar passing undigested into the dung. An economic estimate at $600 a tonne is included. These are presentation slides, not a peer-reviewed trial, with no replication or statistics shown, so treat the figures as an operator's report.

documents.title: Feeding Biochar to Cows: An Innovative Solution for Improving Soil Fertility and Farm Productivity
documents.authors: Joseph, Pow, Dawson, Mitchell, Rawal, Hook, Taherymoosavi, Van Zwieten, Rust, Donne, Munroe, Pace, Graber, Thomas, Nielsen, Ye, Lin, Pan, Li, Solaiman
documents.summary: Three years on a 53-hectare farm in Western Australia, feeding cattle high-temperature wood biochar mixed with molasses. Dung beetles carried the excreted biochar into the soil, soil properties improved, pasture health rose, and the farmer's net returns went up. The biochar came through the gut intact, so the farmer spreads nothing.
documents.abstract: A three-year field study on a 53-hectare farm in Western Australia tested a different way to put biochar in the ground: feed it to cattle. The animals received high-temperature wood biochar mixed with molasses. Biochar passes through the rumen and gut largely intact, leaves in the dung loaded with nutrients, and dung beetles then bury it in the soil profile, to a depth of 20 to 60 centimetres. Soil properties improved, pasture health lifted, and farmer net returns increased. The design suits grazing and dairy operations with active dung beetle populations, since the beetles do the spreading. The team includes Stephen Joseph, Lukas Van Zwieten and Zakaria Solaiman.

documents.title: Effects of biochar on live-weight gain and methane emissions of cattle on a cassava-based diet
documents.summary: A cattle feeding trial on a cassava-based diet, with rice-husk biochar made at 900 degrees Celsius and added at 0.6 per cent of dietary dry matter. Live-weight gain rose 25 per cent, and feed conversion improved from 23.2 to 19.1. Enteric methane fell 22 per cent from biochar alone, and 41 per cent when paired with potassium nitrate.
documents.abstract: Leng and Preston fed cattle a cassava-based diet with rice-husk biochar, produced at 900 degrees Celsius, at 0.6 per cent of dietary dry matter. Live-weight gain rose 25 per cent, and the feed conversion ratio improved from 23.2 to 19.1. Enteric methane fell 22 per cent with biochar alone. Adding potassium nitrate as a non-protein nitrogen source took the cut to 41 per cent. The trial design is documented well enough to replicate, so an operator can run a smaller version on their own ration. The feedstock differs from hardwood biochar, but the high-temperature properties are similar, so the mechanism should transfer. For feedlot and dairy operators facing emissions reporting, the methane result is a welcome extra.

documents.title: Feed supplementation with biochar may reduce poultry pathogens, including Campylobacter hepaticus, the causative agent of Spotty Liver Disease
documents.summary: Two large trials on commercial layer farms tested biochar at 1, 2 and 4 per cent of the diet. The 2 per cent rate worked best. Gallibacterium anatis and campylobacters, including C. hepaticus, the cause of Spotty Liver Disease, were lower in the gut of fed birds. Feeding from hatch shifted gut microbes more at 48 weeks than starting at point of lay.
documents.abstract: Rules on antibiotic use in poultry are tightening, which raises the question of alternatives. A Central Queensland University team tested biochar in layer diets at 1, 2 and 4 per cent by weight, then ran two large trials on commercial layer farms. The 2 per cent inclusion gave the best anti-pathogen result. Gallibacterium anatis and campylobacters, including Campylobacter hepaticus, were lower in biochar-fed birds, with a shift in the gut microbiota. Timing mattered: birds fed from hatch showed a greater change in community structure at 48 weeks than birds supplemented from point of lay. The measure is gut bacteria, not disease cases or egg output, so the result does not yet show fewer Spotty Liver outbreaks.

documents.title: Effect of dietary inclusion of biochar on growth performance, haematology and serum lipid profile of broiler birds
documents.summary: A 56-day feeding trial with 120 day-old broilers fed 0, 2, 4 or 6 per cent biochar. Starter-phase growth did not differ. In the finisher phase, birds on 6 per cent had the best final weight, daily gain, feed conversion. Haemoglobin rose at both phases, cholesterol fell.
documents.abstract: One hundred and twenty day-old broilers were split into four groups of 30, with two replicates of 15 birds, then fed diets with 0, 2, 4 or 6 per cent biochar for 56 days. In the starter phase final weight, daily gain, feed intake or feed conversion did not differ. In the finisher phase, final body weight, daily gain, feed conversion differed between diets, with the 6 per cent birds best on all three. Haemoglobin concentration and red blood cell count rose at both phases, while white blood cell count and packed cell volume were unaffected. Triacylglycerol did not change. Cholesterol and low density lipoprotein fell at both phases. The trial was small, 6 per cent was the highest rate tested, and the biochar feedstock is not named.

documents.title: Corncob biochar supplementation improves nutrient digestibility, fattening performance and carcass characteristics of fattening sheep
documents.summary: Twenty-four Horro rams in Ethiopia were fed a daily concentrate plus corncob biochar at 0, 1.5, 3 or 4.5 grams a day over a 111-day trial. The 1.5 gram dose lifted intake, digestibility, daily gain, dressing percentage and rib eye area over the control. It is a small, cheap dose made from a waste product.
documents.abstract: Horro yearling rams averaging 18.6 kg were split into four groups of six. Every ram received 300 g a day of concentrate (wheat bran with Noug cake) plus local hay, with corncob biochar added at 1.5, 3 or 4.5 g a day for three of the groups. The growth trial ran 111 days, followed by a 10-day digestibility trial, then carcass measurements. At 1.5 g a day, dry matter intake, crude protein intake, dry matter digestibility and acid detergent fibre digestibility all beat the control. Daily weight gain and feed conversion improved. Dressing percentage, hindquarter, forequarter, rib, brisket weights and rib eye muscle area also rose, with organ weights staying in the normal range. The recommended dose is 1.5 g a day. One breed on one farm system, so the dose needs checking in other flocks.

documents.title: Role of Biochar as a Feed Additive on Animal Performance, Digestibility, Micro‐Biota Dynamics, and Reduction of Enteric Methane Production
documents.summary: A review of biochar fed to cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, layers and broilers. Reported methane cuts reach 30 to 40 per cent in cattle, with better digestibility and growth across species. Some weight gains were small: fattening bulls rose from 479 to 481 kg.
documents.abstract: Biochar made by pyrolysis in a rotary kiln is treated here as a feed ingredient, mostly blended into a mixed product. The review lists body weight outcomes by species: fattening bulls from 479 to 481 kg, dairy cows from 94.3 to 96.6 kg, broilers from 1.8 to 2 kg, pigs from 36.5 to 40.5 kg, goats from 17.4 to 18.6 kg, sheep from 22.1 to 25.2 kg. Enteric methane fell by 30 to 40 per cent in cattle, from 0.033 to 0.02 mL a gram in goats, from 101.3 to 55.1 mL a gram in poultry. Feed conversion, digestion, rumen microbe numbers all improved. The review draws on trials with different feedstocks, doses, diets, so the size of the effect varies by product. The bull and dairy cow gains are small.

documents.title: Investigating the impact of biochar on methane gas emissions and its effect on enteric fermentation
documents.summary: Two groups of 14 Naeemi ewes, one fed biochar with the basal ration, the other the ration alone. Methane emissions fell by 65.6 to 78.4 per cent from a starting 1082 ppm. Treated ewes finished heavier at 63.66 kg, with a body condition score of 3.56 against 2.83 for the control.
documents.abstract: Naeemi ewes were split into a treatment group and a control group of 14 each. The treatment group received biochar mixed into the basal ration. Methane readings at day 0 were 1082 ppm in both groups. Biochar cut methane by 65.58 to 78.39 per cent. Treated ewes reached 63.66 kg body weight, with greater body length, girth and height than the controls. Average body condition score rose to 3.56 against 2.83, put down mainly to extra fat gain. The paper reports better nutrient use, better feed efficiency, and altered digestion in the rumen. One flock of one breed, so the figures need confirming in other animals before they are used for carbon accounting.

documents.title: Biochar litter amendment concerning environmental health and immunity in broilers
documents.authors: Zied, Elsayed, Elkomy, Abdrabouh and El-Bahnasy
documents.publisher: Bulletin of the National Research Centre/Bulletin of the National Research Center
documents.summary: Sixty Cobb broiler chicks were raised for five weeks on sawdust litter, or sawdust with 10 or 20 per cent biochar made from poultry litter at 450 degrees. The 10 per cent mix cut bacterial, E. coli, Salmonella counts in the air and litter. Immune markers improved in both biochar groups, most clearly at 10 per cent.
documents.abstract: A control group sat on plain sawdust litter. Two treated groups had sawdust litter amended with 10 or 20 per cent biochar, produced by pyrolysing used poultry litter at 450 degrees Celsius. Over the five weeks, bacterial, E. coli, Salmonella counts rose weekly in the control, in the air as well as the litter. Biochar reduced them, with 10 per cent working best. Treated birds had more white blood cells, a lower heterophil to lymphocyte ratio (a sign of less stress), more CD4 and CD8 T-lymphocytes by flow cytometry. Serum IgA, IgY, IgM rose, spleen and thymus tissue looked healthier. Only 60 birds in one trial, with 20 per cent doing less well than 10 per cent, so the best rate is not simply the highest.

documents.title: Biochar in Poultry Houses: Scientific Basis for Ammonia Control and Litter Value
documents.summary: A broiler house trial in Rockingham County, Virginia, ran from 2023 to early 2026, with one of three houses dosed with biochar. By day 37 of the May 2025 flock the biochar house read no detectable ammonia, and in later flocks it held the lowest mid-flock readings. It is one farm with no replication, so treat it as a lead, not a result.
documents.abstract: The Virginia trial followed three broiler houses on one farm, one treated with biochar. Early dosing was three supersacks pulverised into the bedding. Later it became weekly surface additions of about 180 litres, which worked better: ammonia in the biochar house fell below the others after two to four weeks, and in the May 2025 flock it read nothing by day 37. The houses differed in size, ventilation and flock numbers, so weather confounds single comparisons. Bedding moisture did not fall clearly. The report also cites composting work: 5 to 10 per cent biochar in poultry litter cut ammonia loss by 30 to 60 per cent, while 3 per cent changed nothing. Dietary biochar at 2 to 4 per cent cut manure ammonia by up to 17 per cent in broilers, but a high dose of one blend cut final body weight by up to 7 per cent.

documents.title: The use of biochar in animal feeding
documents.summary: A veterinary review of biochar as a feed additive, drawing on the published trials. No adverse effects were reported within the recommended dosing ranges. Mycotoxin binding sits beside lower methane output and better feed conversion as a main mechanism, so a vet or feedlot nutritionist asking about safety in the ration can start here.
documents.abstract: A veterinary review of biochar as a feed additive. It covers safety, mechanisms, regulation, the published efficacy data. No adverse effects were reported within the recommended dosing ranges. Mycotoxin binding is one of the less noticed mechanisms: the char sequesters toxins in the gut before they harm the microbiome, which helps explain better feed conversion. Methane reduction is the other effect reported. The review is the veterinary companion to the Leng and Preston cattle work. Where Leng and Preston dealt with production economics, such as live-weight gain, this paper deals with whether the practice is safe. It suits a vet or a feed-mill operator.

documents.title: Use of biochar as feed supplements for animal farming
documents.summary: A review of biochar in the feed of poultry, pigs, sheep, cattle. Inclusion rates for non-cattle species run from 1 to 2.5 per cent of feed. Reported effects are less manure odour, better feed conversion, lower mycotoxin loading and immune support. Mixed operations get one additive working across stock classes.
documents.abstract: This review covers biochar inclusion across poultry, pigs, sheep and cattle. For species other than cattle the rates run from 1 to 2.5 per cent of feed. The effects reported are reduced odour in manure, improved feed conversion, reduced mycotoxin loading, immune-system support. The cattle research gets the headlines, but application rates differ by species, which makes this the reference for poultry, pig, sheep guidance. For a mixed operation the practical reading is one additive working across stock classes, not only the cattle. Check the full text before setting a ration.

documents.title: The use of biochar in cattle farming (Gerlach and Schmidt)
documents.summary: A vet's account of biochar in cattle farming, written for The Biochar Journal by Achim Gerlach and Hans-Peter Schmidt. Ninety per cent of biochar produced in Europe goes to livestock. Mixed into feed, bedded into litter or added to slurry, it is reported to improve animal health within a short time, with less smell and fewer nutrient losses.
documents.abstract: Gerlach, a practising vet, and Schmidt describe the use of biochar in cattle farming. They report that 90 per cent of European biochar production is used in livestock systems, in three main ways: in feed, in litter and in slurry treatment. According to the article, animal health and wellbeing improve within a short time. The author ties this to the gut, since the productivity of a cow depends on a properly working digestive tract, and he lists hormonal, chelating, antibiotic, carcinogenic and neural effects among the symptoms he meets in daily practice. Less odour and lower nutrient loss from manure are the other benefits named, with the aim of closing the cycle of organic matter on the farm. This is a practitioner article, not a controlled trial, so dose rates and health outcomes should be checked against feeding studies before a herd is changed over.

documents.title: Biochar in poultry farming (Gerlach and Gerlach)
documents.summary: Henning Gerlach and Hans-Peter Schmidt describe biochar in poultry coops. In litter it cuts ammonia, holds moisture steady, prevents foot pad dermatitis within days. In feed, it is reported to lift the growth of young animals by 17 per cent on average. The setting is industrial poultry houses with high stocking densities.
documents.abstract: Gerlach and Schmidt start from a problem in industrial poultry production: high animal densities raise pathogen pressure, stressed birds mount a weaker immune response, and ammonia in the litter feeds the cycle. Adding porous biochar to the litter lowers toxic ammonia in the coop and regulates litter moisture. Coop odour, they report, can be prevented within a few days, as can foot pad dermatitis. Biochar in the feed is said to deactivate toxins in the gut, support the intestinal flora, raise vitality, with an average 17 per cent improvement in the growth of young animals. The article is a practitioner account in The Biochar Journal, so the figures are reported outcomes rather than replicated trial data. A grower weighing the idea should trial it on one shed first, and check the biochar is clean and food-grade before it goes in feed.

documents.title: Long-term effects of biochar on soil chemistry, biochemistry, and microbiota: Results from a 10-year field vineyard experiment
documents.summary: A ten-year vineyard trial comparing a single dose, a double dose of biochar, untreated soil. Soil organic carbon rose from 12.7 grams a kilogram in the control to 17.3 on the single dose, 23.1 on the double. Soil pH climbed from 6.33 to 7.07 at the double dose. Microbial diversity held steady while fungal richness in the root zone increased.
documents.abstract: A long-running field experiment in an intensively managed vineyard tested two biochar doses, single (SB) and double (DB), against untreated soil (CK). After ten years the team measured soil chemistry and biochemistry, then sequenced the bacteria and fungi in bulk soil and the rhizosphere. Soil organic carbon rose from 12.7 grams a kilogram in CK to 17.3 in SB and 23.1 in DB. Bulk density fell slightly, and pH rose from 6.33 in CK to 7.07 in DB. Bacterial diversity did not change, although the mix shifted toward oligotrophic groups. The double dose raised fungal richness in the rhizosphere: Basidiomycota yeasts went from 9.4 per cent of the community in CK to 17.0 per cent in SB, 24.8 per cent in DB. Putative plant pathogens such as Phaeoacremonium and Aspergillus fell. No harm to microbial diversity or soil function appeared over a decade.

documents.title: Effects of Biochar Application on Tomato Yield and Fruit Quality: A Meta-Analysis
documents.authors: Lei, Xu, Wang, Sun, Yu-hua and Xu
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of tomato studies published before March 2024. Biochar raised yield by 29.55 per cent, soluble solids by 4.28 per cent, vitamin C by 6.77 per cent. Gains were largest on dense soils low in organic matter.
documents.abstract: Tomato literature to March 2024 was pooled to test how biochar properties, farm practice and soil type affect yield and fruit quality. Biochar raised tomato yield by 29.55 per cent, total soluble solids by 4.28 per cent and vitamin C by 6.77 per cent, with larger gains at higher application rates. Wood and straw biochar made at 401 to 500 degrees performed best. The benefit is strongest on soils with high bulk density, low organic matter or nutrient shortages. Gains may fade as biochar ages in the soil, so repeat applications could be needed. Outcomes varied widely between studies, which makes the soil and biochar pairing matter more than the average. Growers on depleted soils gain most.

documents.title: Biochar–compost mixture and cover crop effects on soil carbon and nitrogen dynamics, yield, and fruit quality in an irrigated vineyard
documents.summary: A four-year trial in an irrigated Merlot vineyard in the Okanagan Valley, British Columbia, 2017 to 2020. Biochar mixed 1:1 with compost went on at 22 tonnes a hectare in 2017 and 2019, with or without a cover crop. Soil carbon in the top 15 centimetres rose 11 per cent with the mix, 17 per cent with the cover crop added. Yield rose 32 per cent in 2020 only.
documents.abstract: Merlot vines in the Okanagan Valley, British Columbia, received a 1:1 mix of biochar and compost at 22 tonnes a hectare (dry weight) in May 2017 and May 2019. Plots followed a factorial design with four replicates: control, the mix, a cover crop of dryland forage plus bird's-foot trefoil, or the mix with the cover crop. Soil carbon at 0 to 15 centimetres rose 11 per cent with the mix, 17 per cent with the mix plus cover crop. Nothing changed at the lower depth. Soil nitrogen was unchanged by the mix, fell 12.5 per cent under the cover crop, then rose 4 per cent in the combined plots. Grape yield lifted 32 per cent in the combined treatment in 2020 only. The cover crop cut petiole nitrogen in one or two of three years. The vine response arrived late, in a single season.

documents.title: Co-application of biochar and salt-tolerant bacterial inoculants on vineyard saline-alkaline soils
documents.summary: A vineyard on saline-alkaline soil, treated with biochar plus the salt-tolerant bacterium Pseudomonas resinovorans B9. The combination shifted the root-zone bacterial community towards beneficial genera, improved grape shoot growth, lowered soil salinity, and lifted phosphorus and potassium in soil and plant. Biochar gave the inoculant somewhere to live.
documents.abstract: Li's team co-applied biochar with salt-tolerant bacterial inoculants (Bacillus subtilis B4 and Pseudomonas resinovorans B9) in a vineyard on saline-alkaline soil. The pairing reshaped the rhizosphere community, enriching Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus and Flavobacterium, and gave the strongest positive correlation rate in the microbial network analysis, at 67.69 per cent. Grape shoot growth improved, soil salinity fell, and phosphorus and potassium rose in plants and soil. The proposed mechanism is shelter: porous biochar gives the bacteria a microhabitat to attach to, so they persist against the resident microbes. Both strains produce extracellular polysaccharides, which bind soil aggregates. For irrigation-tail country in inland NSW, Victoria and South Australia, it argues for biochar with an inoculant over either input alone.

documents.title: Oasis Vineyard biochar trial — write-up, 7.15.20
documents.authors: Oasis Vineyard / California Healthy Soils Program
documents.summary: A California Healthy Soils Program trial on a Pinot Noir vineyard with sandy soil, using biochar at 10 tons an acre. First-harvest yield rose 45 per cent, about 1.3 tons an acre, with six more clusters per vine. Revenue gained US$2,600 an acre against a biochar cost of US$2,400, so it paid back in one season.
documents.abstract: This write-up covers a California Healthy Soils Program field trial on Pinot Noir grown in low-organic-matter sandy soil. Four treatments were compared: a control, biochar alone at 10 tons an acre, compost alone at 15 tons an acre, and compost with biochar. Irrigation and fertiliser were identical. At first harvest the biochar-only vines yielded 45 per cent more than the control, an extra 1.3 tons an acre, with six more clusters per vine. The Ravaz Index moved into the ideal range of 5 to 10, so yield and vine balance improved together. Revenue rose US$2,600 an acre against US$2,400 for the biochar. No extra irrigation water was used, which points to water-use efficiency as the mechanism. One harvest only, and costs are in US dollars. Sandy-soil perennial growers in Australia can read across.

documents.title: Biochar increases vineyard productivity without affecting grape quality: results from a four years field experiment in Tuscany
documents.summary: Four harvests from a non-irrigated vineyard in Tuscany, Italy, with biochar at 22 tonnes a hectare. Yield in treated plots ran up to 66 per cent above the controls. Grape quality showed no significant difference. The gain was tied to dry seasons, so wetter or irrigated sites should expect less.
documents.abstract: Genesio and colleagues at Italy's National Research Council followed a non-irrigated vineyard in Tuscany for four harvest years. Plots with biochar at 22 tonnes a hectare out-yielded their controls by up to 66 per cent, with the largest gains in the dry seasons. Measured grape quality parameters did not differ between treated and untreated vines. That matters for a grower, because a yield gain is worth less if fruit quality falls. It is one site in one climate, and the benefit is tied to dry years, so a vineyard with irrigation or reliable summer rain should expect less. The result suits Australian dryland vineyards facing hotter, drier seasons.

documents.title: Improving vineyard water efficiency by addition of biochar derived from grape stalks and vineyard prunings (Wine Australia project UA 1404, final report)
documents.publisher: Wine Australia (Australian Grape and Wine Authority), University of Adelaide
documents.summary: A University of Adelaide project for Wine Australia on biochar made from grape stalks and vineyard prunings. The prunings biochar held more than ten times the phosphorus of other unmodified biochars. It raised water holding in the trial soils.
documents.abstract: Muhlack and Kwong, at the University of Adelaide, made biochar from grape stalks and vineyard prunings for a Wine Australia incubator project on vineyard water efficiency. They tested it in trial soils. The prunings biochar carried more than ten times the phosphorus of other unmodified biochars, and it increased water holding in those soils. The practical idea is a closed loop: a vineyard turns its own waste into an amendment for its own rows. Check the full report for application rates before drawing on the water figures.

documents.title: Potential of Integrating Biochar and Deficit Irrigation Strategies for Sustaining Vegetable Production in Water-limited Regions: A Review
documents.summary: A review of biochar combined with deficit irrigation in vegetable crops, set against 134 deficit irrigation reports. Without biochar, yields fell in 52 per cent of cases. With biochar, yield losses were largely offset, with better water use efficiency.
documents.abstract: Deficit irrigation applies less water than crop demand, and 134 reports on vegetables showed significant yield loss at every deficit level in 52 per cent of cases. Only 44 per cent held yields close to full irrigation, usually under small deficits. Shallow-rooted vegetables are sensitive to water stress, which is why losses are common. The review then examined biochar used alongside deficit irrigation, covering growth, yield, physiology, water use efficiency across vegetable species. Biochar under deficit irrigation generally helped compensate for the lost yield. The evidence is a literature review, not one controlled comparison, so the size of the offset varies with crop, soil, biochar. It suits growers in arid or semi-arid regions weighing water savings against yield risk.

documents.title: Effects of Biochar, Lime, and Compost Applications on Soil Physicochemical Properties and Yield of Pomelo (Citrus grandis Osbeck) in Alluvial Soil of the Mekong Delta
documents.summary: A three-year pomelo trial from 2018 to 2020 in Hau Giang Province, Vietnam, on acidic Mekong Delta alluvial soil. Biochar at 5 tonnes a hectare a year lifted fruit yield about 1.5-fold over fertiliser alone. Profit rose by an average of USD 1,672 a hectare with biochar or compost.
documents.abstract: The trial ran for three consecutive years, 2018 to 2020, on raised beds in Hau Giang Province, in a Mekong Delta soil with high acidity and few exchangeable bases. Treatments were a control, biochar at 5 tonnes a hectare a year, lime at 2 tonnes, compost at 5 tonnes, all with the same NPK (400 kilograms of nitrogen, 300 of phosphate, 400 of potash). Biochar or compost raised soil pH, organic matter, exchangeable calcium and magnesium. Bulk density fell in topsoil and subsoil. Fruit yield was about 1.5 times that of fertiliser alone. Average profit rose by USD 1,672 a hectare. The acid, infertile soil is probably why the result is large, so expect a smaller response on better soils.

documents.title: The potential for biochar application in “Shatangju” (Citrus reticulate cv.) orchard on acid red soil: Biochar prepared from its organic waste in an orchard
documents.summary: Pot and orchard trials on Shatangju mandarin in acid red soil in China, using biochar made on site from orchard waste in a small furnace. The furnace gave a 37 per cent yield at 80 per cent carbon, enough for the orchard's yearly needs. In the field, 2.4 to 3.6 kilograms a tree gave the best soil, leaf nutrition, fruit quality. In pots, 1.5 to 3 per cent biochar improved soil.
documents.abstract: Shatangju mandarin (Citrus reticulata) on acid red soil in China was tested in pure soil, pots, the orchard, with biochar made from orchard waste in a simple small-scale carbonisation furnace. The finished biochar was about 37 per cent of feedstock weight, at roughly 80 per cent carbon, and the orchard could make enough to cover its own annual use. Biochar raised the availability of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, boron, lifted soil pH and organic carbon, and increased the number and variety of root and rhizosphere microbes. Fruit from every biochar treatment was better coloured, of higher quality than the control. In pure soil, 3 per cent biochar gave a stable, suitable pH with or without fertiliser, while 1.5 to 3 per cent helped in pots. In the field, 2.4 to 3.6 kilograms a tree worked best. The orchard rate was adjusted from the closed trials.

documents.title: Effect of biochar and organic amendments on improving soil quality and apple orchard productivity: a 2-year field study
documents.summary: Two years of biochar in a mature apple orchard in South Korea. Low-temperature biochar went on at 19.8, 99 and 198 cubic metres a hectare, against manure compost, pruned branch chips and a mid-temperature biochar. The low-temperature char improved water holding, cation exchange and bulk density, with less carbon dioxide released than from the chips. Apple yield rose with it, as it did with the manure compost.
documents.abstract: The trial ran for two years in a mature apple orchard in South Korea. Treatments were livestock manure compost, pruned branch chips, a mid-temperature biochar, plus a low-temperature biochar at 19.8, 99 and 198 cubic metres a hectare. The low-temperature biochar improved soil physical and chemical properties: higher cation exchange capacity, better water holding, lower bulk density. Carbon dioxide emissions were lower than from the pruned chips, which points to carbon held in the soil. Nitrous oxide emissions did not differ between treatments. Tree growth, fruit yield, fruit nutrient content all rose most with the manure compost or the low-temperature biochar. No cost figures are given, so whether the char pays at orchard scale stays open. The biochar feedstock is not stated.

documents.title: Winery Residues Transformed into Biochar and Co-Applied with Trichoderma Increase Grape Productivity and Soil Quality
documents.summary: Biochar made from winery waste, either grape stalks or fermentation residues, was applied with Trichoderma fungi to Malbec vines. Grape stalk biochar with Trichoderma hamatum lifted grape productivity. Fermentation residue biochar with the same fungus raised soil microbial biomass carbon by 569 per cent over the control. Soil pH, phosphorus, potassium and organic carbon all rose. It is the first field test of on-farm winery char with Trichoderma.
documents.abstract: Winery waste was pyrolysed on farm into two biochars, one from grape stalks, one from grape fermentation residues. Each was applied to soil under Malbec grapevines, alone or with Trichoderma aureoviride URM 5158 or Trichoderma hamatum URM 6656. Both biochars raised soil pH, phosphorus, potassium, organic carbon, microbial biomass carbon. Grape stalk biochar with T. hamatum gave the productivity gain. Fermentation residue biochar lifted enzyme activity per unit of microbial biomass, then with T. hamatum raised microbial biomass carbon by 569.23 per cent over the control. No application rate, vineyard location or yield figure is given, so the size of the grape gain cannot be judged. For a winery the loop is short: the waste stream becomes the amendment.

documents.title: Biochar Enhances Vineyard Resilience: Soil Improvement and Physiological Benefits for Sangiovese Vineyards in Varied Soils of the Chianti Classico (Tuscany, Central Italy)
documents.summary: Biochar at 16 tonnes a hectare fresh weight (about 10.4 dry) on three organic Sangiovese vineyards in Chianti Classico, Tuscany, measured one year later. Bulk density fell 5 to 16 per cent. Soil organic carbon rose about 50 per cent in medium to fine soils, over 200 per cent in the coarse one. Yield averaged 42 per cent higher, though one site showed no gain.
documents.abstract: The B-Wine project tested biochar on three organically managed Sangiovese vineyards in Chianti Classico, Tuscany. Biochar went on at 16 tonnes a hectare fresh weight (about 10.4 dry), with measurements over one growing season, a year later. Soil carbon, moisture, saturated hydraulic conductivity, bulk density, leaf water content, photosynthesis and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery were all recorded. Bulk density fell 5 to 16 per cent. Soil organic carbon rose about 50 per cent in medium to fine textured soils, past 200 per cent in the coarse-textured soil. Effects on hydraulic conductivity varied with soil, biochar type, moisture. Average yield rose roughly 42 per cent, but two sites drove the result while the third showed no measurable gain. Response depends on the soil. A single season is a short test.

documents.title: Biochar: what is its potential for vegetable production? (fact sheet)
documents.summary: A nine-page vegetable industry fact sheet from Hort Innovation, funded by grower levies. It sets out what biochar can do for soil carbon, nutrient retention, water retention and soil structure, with results varying by feedstock. Benefits run greatest on light sandy soils low in organic matter, so trial a small block first, ideally alongside compost.
documents.abstract: Hort Innovation published this fact sheet in March 2022 for vegetable growers. It explains pyrolysis, in which agricultural wastes, woody wastes, biosolids or industrial wastes are heated in low oxygen. The main message is variability. A table of 14 biochars from earlier studies, made at 350 to 500 degrees Celsius, shows pH from 6.25 to 9.66, carbon from 172 to 905 grams a kilogram, carbon to nitrogen ratios from 7 to 400. Hardwood biochar has larger chunks, which suit drainage. Bagasse biochar has more surface area, which suits cutting nutrient leaching. The sheet advises testing chemical composition before purchase, pairing biochar with compost, then starting on a small area before rolling out across a block or several farms. Existing research has produced mixed results, quality assurance standards are limited, and biochar can be made on the farm or bought. It reports no new trial data.

documents.title: Biochar: A Potential Substrate Amendment in Container Production (e-GRO Edible Alert E508)
documents.publisher: e-GRO (university nursery and greenhouse extension network)
documents.summary: A Cornell greenhouse trial of Caesar basil in 6-inch pots of peat-perlite mix, with three biochars at 5, 10, 20 per cent by volume over 30 days. Willow chip biochar at 10 per cent gave the biggest fresh weight gain, 63 per cent, with mixed hardwood at 10 per cent close behind at 60 per cent. Gains fell away at 20 per cent.
documents.abstract: Neil Mattson (Cornell) with Muhammad Shahid (University of New Hampshire) compared an organic certified commercial biochar, a locally made mixed hardwood biochar, a willow chip biochar. Large particles were ground, sieved to 2 millimetres, with limestone added to bring substrate pH to 5.5. Plants grew for 30 days at 25 degrees Celsius by day, 18 by night, fed a 21-5-20 fertiliser at 150 parts per million nitrogen. The commercial product peaked at 5 per cent, with a 30 per cent fresh weight gain. Height rose by about 20 per cent for the commercial product plus the hardwood, 10 per cent for willow. More branching was visible, which probably drove the yield gain. Benefits declined at 20 per cent, possibly from excess salts or altered water holding. This is one cultivar, one short crop, one greenhouse. Results differed by product, so run a small trial first.

documents.title: Biochar in Horticulture: Prospects for the use of biochar in Australian horticulture
documents.publisher: NSW Department of Primary Industries with Horticulture Australia Ltd
documents.summary: A 104 page review for Horticulture Australia (project AH11006), compiled by NSW DPI with Van Zwieten, Downie, Singh and others, for fruit, vegetable, nut, nursery and turf growers. It notes a published meta-analysis showing an average yield rise of 10 per cent irrespective of soil type. It dates from 2012, so newer trial data now exist.
documents.abstract: Horticulture Australia commissioned this review in 2012 to explain carbon amendments to growers, with focus on stable forms lasting more than 100 years, and their prospects in carbon trading. Authors include some of Australia's early biochar researchers, with external reviewers from soil science and pyrolysis. The book covers soil carbon, how different organic amendments behave, biochar production, effects on soil, horticultural yields, carbon trading, a chapter of frequently asked questions. Horticulture is the third largest sector of Australian agriculture by value, the fastest growing. The foreword says many questions on use remained open at that stage. The yield figure, an average rise of 10 per cent regardless of soil type, comes from a published meta-analysis. Results depend on the biochar, so the review points readers to feedstock and temperature rather than a single rate.

documents.title: Oasis Vineyard Field Trial with Biochar and Compost: 6th Harvest Report
documents.summary: A Pinot Noir vineyard trial on dune sand run by Pacific Biochar, now at its sixth harvest. The site summary reports that biochar plus compost lifted yield by 34 per cent and added $17,607 an acre in revenue, with no effect on wine quality. The summary is the operator's own.
documents.abstract: Pacific Biochar Benefit Corporation reports on the Oasis Vineyard field trial, a long-running comparison of biochar with compost on Pinot Noir grown in dune sand. By the sixth harvest, the site summary states that biochar plus compost lifted yields by 34 per cent and added $17,607 an acre in revenue, with no quality impact. Sandy soils drain fast but hold little, so a result on dune sand points to water retention as the likely mechanism. The biochar supplier publishes the report, with summary figures but no full data tables, so the revenue figure rests on prices and yields at that site. Vineyard managers on light soils will find the setting familiar.

documents.title: Topdressing Biochar Compost Mixtures and Biological Control Organism Applications Suppress Foliar Pathogens in Creeping Bentgrass Fairway Turf
documents.summary: A two-year field study on a creeping bentgrass fairway, with monthly biochar-compost topdressing plus weekly or fortnightly Bacillus subtilis QST713 sprays. The biochar-compost mix lifted turf quality in both years, then cut dollar spot severity in 2021. Monthly mix with weekly QST713 fully suppressed copper spot in 2021.
documents.abstract: Plots of creeping bentgrass (Agrostis stolonifera) on a fairway received monthly applications of a biochar-compost mixture, with the biocontrol bacterium Bacillus subtilis QST713 applied weekly or every two weeks. Disease severity, turf quality were rated every 14 days through the growing season, while bacterial populations on the leaf were measured by qPCR. The biochar-compost mixture raised turf quality in both years, reduced dollar spot (Clarireedia jacksonii) in 2021. Weekly QST713 cut copper spot more than fortnightly sprays in 2020. The monthly mixture with weekly QST713 suppressed copper spot completely in 2021. The mixture did not affect how well QST713 established, with no interaction between the two treatments. Biochar or biocontrol alone is less reliable than synthetic fungicide, so this reads as a season-long program, not a replacement spray.

documents.title: Effects of biochar combined with different nitrogen fertilization rates on turf quality and carbon footprint in a turf system
documents.authors: Shen, Pan, Hu, Yu and Yang
documents.summary: A turf trial with biochar at 40 tonnes a hectare under four nitrogen rates, from 0 to 300 kilograms a hectare. Biochar cut nitrous oxide and methane (global warming potential) by 17 to 33 per cent, more than doubling soil carbon sequestration. Biochar with 225 kilograms of nitrogen matched the 300 kilogram rate on turf quality, with lower emissions.
documents.abstract: Eight treatments crossed four nitrogen rates (0, 150, 225, 300 kilograms a hectare) with biochar at either none or 40 tonnes a hectare in a turf system. Biochar lowered cumulative nitrous oxide and methane fluxes by 17.37 to 32.73 per cent, depending on the nitrogen rate. Soil organic carbon sequestration rose by 129 to 139 per cent, total biomass by about 4 to 15 per cent. Turf greenness (NDVI) barely moved. Ecosystem respiration rose slightly, but the change was not significant. Within the biochar plots, 225 kilograms of nitrogen cut nitrous oxide by 12.85 per cent, methane by 11.47 per cent, the carbon footprint by 16.01 per cent against 300 kilograms, with no loss in biomass, soil carbon or greenness. For a turf manager, biochar opens room to trim nitrogen without a visible penalty.

documents.title: Biochar as an amendment in sports turf rootzones (Australian Turfgrass Management Journal 23.6, Agronomy)
documents.summary: A two-page agronomy review in Australian Turfgrass Management, 2021, on biochar in sand rootzones for sports turf. Biochar raises cation exchange capacity and nutrient retention. It also carries cautions on application rate, particle size and water repellence. This is a short practitioner review, not a new trial, written for turf managers weighing a supplier's claims.
documents.abstract: A turf agronomist writing in Australian Turfgrass Management (volume 23, issue 6) reviews biochar as a sand rootzone amendment. The article credits biochar with raising cation exchange capacity, which lifts nutrient retention, and cites studies finding better moisture retention, though results vary. It also points out that sellers talk up benefits while saying little about problems. The cautions are rate, particle size and water repellence. It suits a sports turf manager who wants a sceptical, Australian-context read before a trial, and who wants to know what to ask a supplier.

documents.title: Biochar-compost mixtures added to simulated golf greens increase creeping bentgrass growth
documents.summary: Biochar-compost mixtures were added to simulated USGA-specification golf greens, a 30 cm sand root zone over 10 cm of pea gravel, then planted to creeping bentgrass. Growth increased, with water and nutrient retention improved in the sand. Infiltration and drainage stayed within the range a sports turf green needs, at the inclusion rates tested.
documents.abstract: United States Department of Agriculture researchers built simulated golf greens to USGA specification: 30 cm of sand over 10 cm of pea gravel. They mixed different biochar-compost blends into the root zone, then grew creeping bentgrass (Agrostis stolonifera), the standard cool-season green species in the northern United States and on high-end Australian courses. Bentgrass growth rose with the amendment. Water and nutrient retention in the sand improved, while the infiltration and drainage rates a green depends on were maintained. The worry that biochar would wreck drainage did not appear at the inclusion rates tested. It is still the closest turf-species evidence for a superintendent weighing a pilot on a practice green or back-of-range fairway.

documents.title: USGA Recommendations for a Method of Putting Green Construction (2018 Revision)
documents.summary: The 2018 revision of the USGA method for building a putting green. It specifies sand particle size, drainage rates, root-zone media targets. Biochar is not mentioned anywhere in it. No product can be called USGA approved on the strength of this document, so the accurate claim for a biochar amendment is compatibility with the construction principles.
documents.abstract: The United States Golf Association publishes a standard method for building putting greens, last revised in 2018. It is a specification for sand: the spread of particle sizes, the drainage the root zone must deliver, the media targets a green is built to. Biochar does not appear in the 2018 text. Products sold as USGA approved for biochar amendments are misreading the document, because the USGA has never approved biochar specifically. For a superintendent in a procurement conversation, the defensible wording is that a biochar amendment is compatible with USGA construction principles, which is a claim about drainage and root-zone behaviour, not an endorsement. The evidence for that compatibility has to come from separate turf trials and water-holding measurements, such as the Vaughn bentgrass work on simulated greens and the Yu loamy sand study. This document is the reference for what a green must do, not for what biochar does.

documents.title: Biochar trials at Okehampton Golf Club: Enriched Biochar Lawn Improver
documents.summary: A green trial at Okehampton Golf Club in Devon, England, applying enriched biochar at 1 kilogram a square metre over 100 square metres of two greens in March 2017. The club reported 20 per cent less fertiliser over the year on the 5th green, a sandy green that leaches nutrient. The greens were also watched for fusarium patch.
documents.abstract: Okehampton Golf Club in Devon trialled Carbon Gold's Enriched Biochar Lawn Improver, a biochar blended with fungi, bacteria and trace minerals. In March 2017 the greens were hollow-tined to 100 millimetres, then 1 kilogram a square metre was brushed in over 100 square metres of each of two greens, in the way sand is brushed in. The 5th green is newly extended, very sandy, a heavy leacher of nutrient. The 12th is the disease indicator green, shaded by trees in the Ockment Valley. The club normally feeds five times a year. On the 5th green the team skipped one feed because the turf looked healthy, with no visible difference three weeks later. The club reported a 20 per cent cut in fertiliser use across the trial area over the year. Fungicide against fusarium patch goes on twice a year, sometimes four times. This is a club account published by the supplier, with no replicated plots.

documents.title: Enriched Biochar for Sports Turf: A Game-Changer in Turf Rootzones
documents.summary: A Carbon Gold explainer on enriched biochar in sports turf rootzones, covering golf courses, football pitches, rugby pitches, community grounds. It describes how biochar's porous structure aerates compacted soil, holds water and nutrients otherwise lost to leaching, and carries beneficial microbes. It cites IPCC and European Biochar Certificate work for residence times of centuries.
documents.abstract: Carbon Gold, a UK biochar supplier, wrote this page for turf managers. It starts from the usual problems of a playing surface: compaction from play or machinery, uneven moisture, heavy reliance on fertiliser, low microbial activity. It then describes enriched biochar, which is activated and inoculated with beneficial soil biology before use. The claims are mechanisms: pore structure improves aeration, high internal surface area holds water in dry spells and lets it drain in wet ones, while surface chemistry keeps nutrients from leaching. Because the carbon is stable, the company argues the effect carries across several playing seasons, citing IPCC AR6 Working Group III Chapter 7 for centuries of residence time in soil. The page gives no trial data or application rates, so superintendents should read it as supplier guidance and look to trials such as Okehampton for numbers.

documents.title: Biochar and Biosolids Increase Tree Growth and Improve Soil Quality for Urban Landscapes
documents.summary: Six treatments on tree saplings in three typical urban soils: biochar, biosolids, wood chips, compost, aerated compost tea, and a nitrogen plus potassium fertiliser. Biosolids and biochar gave the greatest tree growth, with the clearest changes in soil properties. Biochar raised total organic carbon. Nitrogen content explained growth for every treatment except biochar.
documents.abstract: Urban soils are often degraded, a hard substrate for trees. This experiment compared biochar, biosolids, wood chips, compost, aerated compost tea, and a nitrogen plus potassium fertiliser across three typical urban soils, with sapling growth as the test. Biosolids and biochar produced the largest changes in soil properties. Biosolids lowered pH, raised available nitrogen, nitrogen mineralisation and microbial respiration. Biochar raised total organic carbon. Leachate nitrate did not differ between treatments, though dissolved organic carbon in leachate was higher under biosolids and compost. Biosolids and biochar also gave the greatest, statistically clear growth gains. Growth was modelled from plant-available nitrogen plus microbial respiration. Nitrogen content tracked growth under every treatment except biochar, so biochar worked by another route. Biochar and biosolids are acceptable, and possibly preferred, alternatives to the usual fertiliser, compost or mulch.

documents.title: Impacts of organic matter amendments on urban soil carbon and soil quality: A meta-analysis
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of compost, biochar and biosolids in urban soils used for gardens, landscaping, recreation and reclamation. Amendments lifted soil organic matter by 3.6 per cent on average. Biochar lifted it by 6.5 per cent, compost by 3.1 per cent, while biosolids added the most nutrients. Few studies went below 30 centimetres.
documents.abstract: Malone, Berhe and Ryals reviewed the literature on organic matter amendments in urban soils managed for gardening, landscaping, recreation, reclamation. Amendments raised soil organic matter by 3.6 per cent on average. Biochar gave the largest rise at 6.5 per cent, compost followed at 3.1 per cent, while biosolids gave the smallest rise but the best nutrient benefits. Chemical and physical soil quality measures improved with amendment. Gaps remain: few studies covered urban gardens, depths beyond 30 centimetres, or how long the added organic matter persists. For parks, sports turf, reclaimed sites the result is a guide to relative performance, not a prescription for rate. The review concludes amendments are an effective way to improve urban soils, store carbon.

documents.title: Quantifying the benefits of incorporating biochar in green roof substrates: field study on the highrise rooftop in temperate climate setting
documents.summary: A field study on a highrise rooftop in a temperate climate, comparing green roof substrate with and without 5 per cent wood biochar by volume. Biochar lifted maximum water capacity by 7.7 per cent, plant-available water by 14.2 per cent. Hydrus-1D modelling put the gain in evapotranspiration at 23.5 per cent, the drop in runoff at 54.7 per cent. Vegetation cover rose where biochar was used.
documents.abstract: Two green roof sections on a highrise building were compared, one with standard substrate, one with 5 per cent wood biochar by volume. Laboratory tests of hydrophysical properties were paired with in-situ soil moisture sensors, weather data, vegetation monitoring, then fed into a Hydrus-1D water balance model. Biochar made small changes to grain size, adding to the 0.01 to 0.1 millimetre fraction, and lowered bulk density. Maximum water capacity rose 7.7 per cent. Plant-available water rose 14.2 per cent. Substrate moisture was higher, with more vegetation cover where biochar was present. The model estimated 23.5 per cent more evapotranspiration plus 54.7 per cent less runoff. Those two figures are modelled, not measured directly. The study compares two roofs, not replicated plots, so site differences could account for part of the gap.

documents.title: Addition of Biochar to Green Roof Substrate to Enhance Plant Performance: A Long-Term Field Study
documents.summary: A one-year field trial of six green roof test beds in Australia, planted to wallaby grass, common everlasting, billy buttons. Biochar went in at different rates, by different methods, in different particle sizes. Medium-sized particles at 15 per cent by volume gave the best plant height, cover, dry weight. Substrate temperature also fell, pointing to lower building energy use.
documents.abstract: Six green roof test beds were monitored for a year, measuring plant height, coverage area, dry weight. The native species were wallaby grass, common everlasting, billy buttons. Beds differed in biochar amendment rate, application method, particle size. Biochar improved plant growth across setups and species. The best performer used medium biochar particles at a 15 per cent volume rate. Observed data also showed lower substrate temperature under biochar, which the paper links to reduced energy demand in the building below. Better plant performance could cut irrigation and maintenance costs, a real issue because high costs limit green roof uptake. With six beds over one year, the work gives guidance on rate and particle size for local natives, not a final specification. Longer runs would show whether the advantage holds through hot summers.

documents.title: An Arboriculture Treatment of Biochar, Fertilization, and Tillage Improves Soil Organic Matter and Tree Growth in a Suburban Street Tree Landscape in Bolingbrook, Illinois, USA
documents.summary: A three-year trial on 75 street trees (honey locust, Chinese elm, red maple) in compacted, fine-textured soil at Bolingbrook, Illinois. Biochar with fertiliser and tillage lifted total soil organic matter to 6.00 per cent, against 5.29 per cent for tillage alone. Red maple height growth was 28.9 per cent against 13.3 per cent. The soil gain looks short-lived.
documents.abstract: The experiment ran three years on a suburban street in Bolingbrook, Illinois. It covered 75 trees of three species, honey locust, Chinese elm, red maple, growing in compacted, fine-textured soil. The treatment combined biochar, fertilisation, tillage, and was compared with tillage alone. Red maple relative height growth was 28.9 per cent with the combined treatment against 13.3 per cent with tillage alone. Total soil organic matter reached 6.00 per cent against 5.29 per cent, particulate organic matter 9.73 per cent against 7.23 per cent, and a soil quality index 70.2 against 60.8. All differences were statistically clear at the 5 per cent level. The rise in organic matter faded fairly quickly, though it tracked tree growth. Biochar was not tested alone, so its share of the effect is not separated out.

documents.title: Evaluation of Biochar as a Potential Filter Media for the Removal of Mixed Contaminants from Urban Storm Water Runoff
documents.summary: Column tests of biochar as a stormwater filter, using a 61 centimetre column of synthetic runoff. It removed 86 per cent of suspended solids, 86 per cent of nitrate, 75 per cent of lead. Removal of other metals was weaker, and E. coli was barely touched.
documents.abstract: A 7 centimetre wide, 61 centimetre long column filled with biochar was fed synthetic urban stormwater carrying suspended solids, nutrients, heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), E. coli. Effluent suspended solids fell by an average of 86 per cent, nitrate by 86 per cent, phosphate by 47 per cent. Metal removal varied with each element: lead 75 per cent, copper 65, zinc 24, chromium 19, cadmium 18, nickel 17. Of three PAHs tested, phenanthrene was removed almost completely, naphthalene by 76 per cent, benzo(a)pyrene not at all. Biochar did not remove E. coli well. This was a laboratory column with synthetic water, not a field system. A council would need to pair the filter with a disinfection step where pathogens matter, then check the metal mix of local runoff.

documents.title: The use of biochar made from biomass and biosolids as a substrate for green infrastructure: A review
documents.summary: A review of biochar from biomass and biosolids as a substrate for green roofs, green parking lots, green walls. Feedstock and pyrolysis conditions set the properties. Biochar improves plant growth, fertiliser efficiency and rainwater capture, though pollutant limits and environmental risks need checking before use in substrates.
documents.abstract: Novotny, Markovic, Racek, Sipka with colleagues reviewed biochar as a stable organic component of growing media for urban green infrastructure, especially green roofs, parking lots, walls. The paper covers feedstocks including sludges, food waste, wood and plant residues, along with pyrolysis technology, conditions and the resulting physical and chemical properties. These properties drive nutrient availability, absorption of pollutants and harmful gases, carbon storage, pH. Biochar improves plant growth, fertiliser efficiency, rainwater capture in the substrates reviewed. The conclusion weighs benefits against pollutant concentration limits, risks to water sources, effects of climate change. Biosolids char needs particular care over contaminants. The review draws on existing papers, case studies, so it maps the evidence rather than measuring new substrates.

documents.title: A pilot bioretention system with commercial activated carbon and river sediment-derived biochar for enhanced nutrient removal from stormwater
documents.authors: Sang, Huang, Zhang, Che and Sun
documents.summary: A pilot bioretention column experiment comparing commercial activated carbon with biochar made from river sediment, using semi-synthetic stormwater runoff. The sediment biochars removed more chemical oxygen demand and total nitrogen than activated carbon. Phosphorus went the other way: activated carbon removed 95 per cent, the two biochars 48 and 56 per cent. Both materials leaked some phosphorus at first.
documents.abstract: Bioretention cells treat urban stormwater, but nutrient removal in standard designs swings widely. This pilot used columns to compare media amended with commercial activated carbon or with biochar made from river sediment. Both additions leached chemical oxygen demand and total phosphorus. Under semi-synthetic runoff, the two sediment biochars controlled chemical oxygen demand and total nitrogen better than activated carbon. Activated carbon was the stronger phosphorus filter, with an average mass removal of 95 per cent (plus or minus 3) against 48 per cent (plus or minus 20) and 56 per cent (plus or minus 14) for the biochars. Nitrogen suits biochar, phosphorus suits activated carbon. The work was done in columns, not a field cell. Dredged river sediment gives a use for a waste material.

documents.title: Biochar Amendment in Green Roof Substrate: A Comprehensive Review of the Benefits, Performance, and Challenges
documents.authors: Nguyen, Chau, Kumar, Chakraborty and Muttil
documents.summary: A review of studies on biochar in green roof substrate. Most found better retention of runoff plus nutrients. Gains in plant performance, thermal insulation, microbial diversity, carbon storage, erosion control were mostly agreed on. The literature is thin and uneven, so no firm conclusion is drawn yet. Rate, method, form, particle size all change the outcome.
documents.abstract: Researchers at Victoria University in Melbourne reviewed published work on biochar-amended green roof substrates. Most studies reported greater retention of runoff and nutrients. Studies also mostly agreed on gains in thermal insulation, plant performance, microbial diversity, carbon storage, erosion control. The review treats the variables behind those results: amendment rate, application method, processed form, particle size. Each shifts how well biochar works. A firm verdict is not yet possible, since few studies exist on biochar green roof systems and research effort has been uneven across topics. The review closes with gaps for future work. For a council or building owner, the direction of effect looks favourable on water and nutrients, while rates and particle sizes still need local testing before a specification is written.

documents.title: Biochar-amended substrate improves nutrient retention in green roof plots
documents.summary: Two growing seasons of green roof plots, planted with a Sedum mixture or left bare, with biochar mixed into the substrate at different rates. Biochar cut the export of phosphorus, organic carbon, organic nitrogen in runoff, all high from standard substrate. Plant cover peaked at 5 per cent biochar by weight, lowest at 10 per cent. Water retention did not change.
documents.abstract: Replicated green roof plots were built with substrate carrying different biochar rates, some planted with a Sedum mixture, some unplanted. Over two growing seasons the plots were assessed for plant cover, water retention, nutrient export in runoff. Standard substrate leached a good deal of phosphorus, organic carbon, organic nitrogen. Biochar reduced all three. Water retention was unchanged. Biochar released a small amount of nitrate, but plants took up enough nitrogen to cancel this out, so planted plots lost little. Plant cover after establishment was highest at the middle rate of 5 per cent by weight and lowest at the top rate of 10 per cent. For a council weighing roof substrates, the finding concerns the quality of water leaving the roof, not the volume. The trial used small plots over two seasons, so performance on a full-size roof is untested.

documents.title: Nursery Runoff Treatment by Novel Biochar-Amended Bioretention Systems
documents.authors: Richardson, Luangphairin, Bhattacharjee, Nachabe and Ergas
documents.summary: Pilot bioretention systems treating nursery runoff, with biochar through the whole profile or in the unsaturated zone only. Biochar in the internal water storage zone removed more nitrogen, raised mean retention time by 34 per cent, tripled plant biomass. The best planted unit removed 84 per cent of nitrogen.
documents.abstract: Commercial nurseries produce runoff rich in fertiliser nutrients. Pilot-scale bioretention systems with an internal water storage zone (IWSZ) were built with biochar in two ways: through both layers, or in the unsaturated zone only. They were tested at three hydraulic loading rates (0.11, 0.22, 0.55 centimetres a minute), two IWSZ depths (44 or 69 centimetres), with or without muhly grass (Muhlenbergia capillaris). Biochar in the storage zone gave greater nitrogen removal (p = 0.031), reducing short-circuiting to lift mean retention time by 34 per cent. Above-ground plant biomass was 0.73 kilograms against 0.23 kilograms. The best result was 84 per cent nitrogen removal in the planted unit at 0.22 centimetres a minute with a 69 centimetre storage zone. A spreadsheet design tool, fitted by logarithmic regression, helps size systems to a nitrogen target. These are pilot units, not full-scale installations.

documents.title: Biochar Guidelines: Plant Survival
documents.summary: A guide for nurseries, greenhouses and turf managers on biochar in growing media and rootzones, with case notes from a United States golf green and a Kansas vegetable farm. The golf test packed columns of 90 per cent sand, 10 per cent biochar, and the superintendent reports better water and nutrient holding. It is one superintendent's test, and he says standards are still needed.
documents.abstract: This American Biochar Institute guide, produced with the Nebraska Forest Service, treats biochar as a replacement for peat, perlite or vermiculite in growing media. A usable biochar has pieces of 2 to 6 millimetres, holds moisture, carries few nutrients, and has the fines under 1 millimetre sifted out. Test pH first. At North Shore Country Club a superintendent pre-charged biochar with nutrients and microbes, mixed it 9 to 1 with USGA rootzone sand, then packed 12 inch columns over pea gravel. He reports better water retention, with nutrient holding from the biochar's cation exchange capacity. He cautions that replicable standards need more research. A Kansas vegetable grower layers biochar on hugel beds to carry tomatoes through hot dry summers. The guide quotes carbon credit prices of about US$200 a tonne. Treat the yield claims as indicative, since the case notes are not controlled trials.

documents.title: Biochar Stormwater BMP Guidebook
documents.summary: A design guidebook for stormwater practitioners, published in March 2026 by the Center for Watershed Protection. It covers bioretention with or without underdrains, swales, filter strips, green roofs, dry ponds and soil amendment. It recommends 10 to 20 per cent biochar by volume in bioretention media, with testing and handling rules for the biochar itself.
documents.abstract: The Center for Watershed Protection wrote this guidebook for the American Biochar Institute, with funding from the USDA Forest Service and the US Endowment for Forestry and Communities. It works through eight stormwater practices: bioretention with underdrains, bioretention without underdrains, high flow media filters, vegetated swales, soil amendment, filter strips, green roofs, dry ponds. For each one it shows where the biochar sits in the design. The recommended rate in bioretention media is 10 to 20 per cent by volume. Other sections cover classification, quality testing, submittals, sourcing, delivery, storage, handling, risk mitigation. It closes with specification templates a council can adapt. A companion technical basis report carries the research behind the numbers. The guide is written from United States practice, so check rates against local soils and media standards.

documents.title: Biochar in Stormwater BMPs: Technical Basis Report
documents.summary: A literature review with expert interviews from the Center for Watershed Protection, March 2026, on biochar in stormwater filter media. Mixing biochar at 18 per cent by volume cut total nitrogen and nitrate loads by 65 per cent against the same mix without it. Biochar media cut total nitrogen by 20 to 27 per cent against compost media.
documents.abstract: This report supplies the research behind the stormwater guidebook. It reviews published studies on biochar properties, then on performance inside real stormwater practices. Properties covered include cation and anion exchange capacity, porosity, surface area, hydrophobicity, particle size, pH, ageing. Performance sections cover heavy metals, nutrients, other pollutants. The headline numbers are a 65 per cent cut in total nitrogen and nitrate load at 18 per cent biochar by volume, and a 20 to 27 per cent cut in total nitrogen against compost media. Experts interviewed named supplier variability as the biggest obstacle to standard specifications. Many studies test one biochar in one practice, so general rules are hard to draw. A final section sets out where biochar may not suit a site. Most data come from United States studies.

documents.title: Specification: Biochar for Urban Tree Planting
documents.summary: A template specification for councils putting biochar into new urban tree plantings. It suits loamy sand, sandy loam or sandy clay loam, at 5 to 20 per cent biochar by volume. Class A hydrologic soils take the full range, while class B or C soils take 5 to 10 per cent. Tree pits get at least half their backfill from the site's own soil.
documents.abstract: This specification is written for council engineers, with bracketed text to adjust for region. It treats biochar as one of several soil amendments for harsh street or park sites, best matched to dry, sandy, well drained or low nutrient soil. Before specifying, take a soil sample for texture, nutrient and organic matter results, then check the hydrologic soil group. Class A soils can take 5 to 20 per cent biochar by volume. Class B or C soils take 5 to 10 per cent. Group D soils need local expert advice. Biochar is mixed through the soil removed from the tree pit, and at least 50 per cent of backfill must come from site soil to limit transplant shock. The root collar stays 2 to 3 inches above finished grade. Compost can be added where tests call for it. The rates come from United States practice, not Australian trials.
