documents.title: Specification: Bioretention In-Situ Media with Biochar
documents.summary: A template specification for building bioretention beds by working biochar and sand into existing soil, using 15 to 20 per cent biochar by volume. The mix needs at least 60 per cent sand, with under 20 per cent clay. Rates and depths are set to lift infiltration, porosity, nutrient retention in urban plantings.
documents.abstract: This specification from the American Biochar Institute, with the Center for Watershed Protection, describes in-situ bioretention, where biochar goes into the soil already on site. The biochar share is 15 to 20 per cent by volume, with the rest topped up with sand to match hydrologic soil group A. Sand follows ASTM C33 medium to coarse gradation, washed. Mixing depth is 6 to 12 inches under turf, or 6 to 24 inches for perennials or hardwoods. Over-mixing breaks biochar into fines, which cuts infiltration, so mixing is kept short. Work stops when soil moisture exceeds 40 per cent. Each area is mixed then stabilised within a day, to stop biochar washing or blowing away. Only one treatment area is open at a time. Soil tests for texture, bulk density, infiltration come first.

documents.title: Biochar in Urban Landscapes (Stormwater) State of the Science
documents.publisher: University of Delaware (P. Imhoff) for Chesapeake Bay Program STAC
documents.summary: A 2023 briefing from the University of Delaware's Paul Imhoff for the Chesapeake Bay Program, covering biochar in urban stormwater systems. Biochar cut heavy metals by 27 to 100 per cent, nitrogen and phosphorus by 32 to 94 per cent, and organics such as PAHs by 54 to 100 per cent. Most of the evidence is from laboratory work.
documents.abstract: Paul Imhoff presented this seventeen-slide state-of-the-science briefing in May 2023. It reviews research on biochar for urban stormwater, a field with fast-growing publication numbers. Every recommended use involves mixing biochar into existing engineered media or soil. Bioretention cells and sand filters are the most studied, followed by green roofs, infiltration trenches, wetlands, filter strips, swales. Across the studies reviewed, biochar removed 27 to 100 per cent of heavy metals, 32 to 94 per cent of nitrogen plus phosphorus, 54 to 100 per cent of organic pollutants such as PAHs. The ranges are wide. Most results come from laboratory columns, not working stormwater basins. Councils weighing biochar in raingardens should treat the figures as a guide to performance, not a guarantee.

documents.title: Biomass Utilization, Forest Restoration, and Soil Productivity Associated with Bioenergy Harvesting and Biochar Application
documents.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station
documents.summary: An eight-page project summary from the US Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station on turning forest thinning residues into bioenergy plus biochar. Biochar returned to forest sites is expected to raise soil carbon and water holding capacity, while the removed fuel cuts wildfire risk. It sets research goals, not field results. Removing too much biomass can run down future site productivity.
documents.abstract: This is a research plan for western conifer forests in the United States. Thinning leaves tops, limbs, small roundwood, which can be burned for energy or converted to biochar. The Station's first goal is to measure how much woody biomass can be taken before soil physical, chemical or biological properties suffer, then to test fixes: leaving slash, fertilising the site, adding biochar. The second goal is economic: working out when biomass use gives the greatest net benefit, counting sales revenue, avoided disposal costs, reduced air pollution, carbon stored in soil. The document says many advanced conversion technologies have never been used commercially in the forest sector. Little is known about their products, emissions, financial viability. Uncertainty is described as high. No measured results are reported, so treat it as a statement of the questions being asked about forest biochar.

documents.title: Biochar for Forest Restoration in Western States (Utah Forest Facts 034)
documents.publisher: Utah State University Extension with USDA Forest Service
documents.summary: A seven-page Utah State University Extension fact sheet, with the US Forest Service, on turning thinning slash into biochar in the western United States. Pinyon-juniper woodland covers about 19 million hectares. Slash is usually piled and burned, because harvest costs run well above what the wood sells for. A pilot field study cited in the sheet found biochar raised soil methane uptake and water holding capacity.
documents.abstract: Forest restoration in the Intermountain West leaves large volumes of small-diameter wood, tops, branches. Harvest and transport costs sit well above market value, so most of it is burned or left. The sheet argues biochar could make restoring expanded pinyon-juniper woodland affordable. It explains pyrolysis in four modes. Fast pyrolysis at about 500 degrees Celsius gives 75 per cent liquid, 12 per cent char, 13 per cent gas. Slow carbonisation at 400 to 500 degrees gives 30, 35, 35 per cent. Torrefaction at about 290 degrees gives 77 per cent solid. Chips are screened, then dried to 10 per cent moisture or less before the reactor. Syngas can fuel the drying, so the process largely powers itself. The Tucker RNG system is one commercial example. The field evidence is a single pilot study, so the agronomic claims are early.

documents.title: Stockholm Biochar Project (urban tree planting)
documents.publisher: City of Stockholm / Stockholm Biochar Project (hosted by IBI)
documents.summary: Stockholm's city programme collects garden and park waste, turns it into biochar, and sells the heat to the district heating system. The char goes into garden soils, parks and 300 new street tree beds in 2018. The pilot plant heated 80 apartments, with a full-scale plant planned for 400.
documents.abstract: Mattias Gustafsson, project manager and founder of the Swedish Biochar Association, presents the Stockholm Biochar Project. It won the Bloomberg Mayors Challenge in 2014, one of five winners from 155 European cities. Residents collect garden waste, as does the city, and it is pyrolysed in an oxygen-free plant run as a public and private partnership. The pyrolysis gas supplies renewable heat to the district network. The char goes to gardens, parks and tree planting. The pilot plant served 80 apartments with biochar carbon matching the emissions of 700 cars, while the full-scale plant is planned to serve 400 apartments with a carbon store equal to 3,500 cars. The city counted about 1,500 study visitors in 2018, the year it also won Sweden's award for best recycling facility. It is a programme presentation, so the figures are reported outcomes, not trial data.

documents.title: Terra Nostra four-year trial: enriched biochar in urban tree planting
documents.summary: A four-year independent tree trial by Terra Nostra in the Netherlands, comparing enriched biochar mixed with structural tree soil against plain biochar and a structural-soil control. Thirty lime trees were dug up at the end. Enriched biochar trees carried 1,028 metres of roots against 706 metres in the reference mix, and cation exchange capacity fell 11 per cent over two years against 40 per cent.
documents.abstract: Terra Nostra researcher Wendy Batenburg tested three batches of Amsterdam Tree Soil, a coarse sandy structural mix: a reference mix, plain biochar, and Carbon Gold's enriched biochar with mycorrhizal fungi and minerals. Each batch had ten 1 cubic metre samples planted with lime trees. After two years of measurement all 30 trees were lifted, roots intact. The enriched mix grew 1,028 metres of roots per tree against 706 metres in the reference. About 98 per cent of the extra length was fine root under 2 millimetres. Cation exchange capacity fell 11 per cent over two years in the enriched mix, against 40 per cent in the reference. The soil kept its strength. Trees also showed less stress, with less lime leaf wasp damage. Carbon Gold, which sells the product, republished the trial, so the original Dutch source is worth checking.

documents.title: Planting urban trees with biochar (Embren)
documents.summary: Stockholm has spent nearly ten years refining structured soils with biochar for street trees. The mix of crushed stone and biochar reaches about 40 per cent void ratio and saves up to 25 per cent in time and labour. In some cases six-year-old trees in these soils were five times larger than 30-year-old trees planted the traditional way.
documents.abstract: Bjorn Embrén describes the capital's near-decade of work to cut urban tree mortality, shorten replacement cycles and lower maintenance cost. Structured soils are gravel or crushed stone mixed with a small share of amendments such as peat, sand, clay or lava. Biochar is the one he reports with great success. The stone and biochar mix reaches a void ratio of about 40 per cent, leaving room for roots, air, water. It saves up to 25 per cent in time and labour at planting. In some cases six-year-old trees in structured soils with biochar were five times larger than 30-year-old trees in conventional plantings. Stockholm has tested a range of mixes for trees, bushes, perennials or grasses in urban and suburban sites. The five-times figure is a selection of cases, not a trial average. Councils with compacted street verges will find the method most relevant.

documents.title: Meta-Analysis of Biochar as an Amendment for Arsenic Mitigation in Paddy Soils
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 25 studies on biochar in arsenic-contaminated paddy soils, mostly from South Asia and Southeast Asia. Maize residue biochar and sewage sludge biochar cut arsenic availability and the arsenic reaching rice grain. Rice biomass and yield rose against controls, though high application rates mobilised arsenic in the field.
documents.abstract: Twenty-five studies were pooled to test how well biochar locks up arsenic in paddy soils, with attention to arsenic in the rice itself. The focus is South Asia and Southeast Asia, where rice is the staple and a strong arsenic accumulator. Biochars made from maize residue or sewage sludge lowered arsenic availability in the soil, plus the amount reaching the grain. Rice biomass and yield were higher than in untreated controls. Modified biochars cut availability further, probably through interactions with iron and calcium phases on or in the char. One caution stands out: at high dosages, arsenic was mobilised in field conditions, not locked up. The pooled result is therefore a case for moderate rates with local testing first, on flooded rice soils especially.

documents.title: Measurement and modelling of sorbent-amendment impacts on seasonal and long-term PFAS transport through unsaturated soil lysimeters
documents.summary: Field lysimeters in Sweden spiked with PFAS, tested for nearly a year with waste-derived biochar or commercial sorbents. Leachate fell by over 99 per cent for long-chain PFAS, 83 to 96 per cent for short-chain. Modelling predicted under 1 per cent of PFOS would leach over 100 years from soil treated with sewage sludge biochar.
documents.abstract: PFAS-spiked soil was placed in field-scale lysimeters in Sweden, then monitored for nearly a year through snowmelt, spring rain, heavy summer rainfall. Waste-derived biochars or commercial sorbents were mixed in. All sorbents reduced average leachate by over 99 per cent for long-chain PFAS, by 83 to 96 per cent for short-chain carboxylic and sulfonic acids. Sewage sludge biochar performed about as well as the commercial products. Long-chain compounds stayed evenly spread in the soil, while the more mobile short-chain ones collected in the lower layers. Leaching peaked in spring, then again in summer storms. A one-dimensional transport model found 30 to 65 per cent of PFOS held at the air-water interface in untreated soil. Over 100 years, nearly all PFOS would leach from untreated soil, against under 1 per cent from sludge biochar. The 100-year figure is a model projection.

documents.title: Stabilization of PFAS-contaminated soil with activated biochar
documents.authors: Sørmo, Silvani, Bjerkli, Hagemann, Zimmerman, Hale, Hansen, Hartnik, Cornelissen
documents.summary: Soils contaminated with PFAS, treated with activated biochar at 5 per cent application. Leaching fell by 98 to 100 per cent in low-organic-matter soils. Performance drops in soils rich in organic matter, so a site-specific pilot trial comes before any full-scale job.
documents.abstract: Sørmo's Norwegian team tested activated biochar for stabilising PFAS-contaminated soil. At 5 per cent application in low-organic-matter soils, PFAS leaching fell by 98 to 100 per cent, which is effectively complete stabilisation. Performance falls off in soils with high organic matter, so a site-specific pilot trial is recommended before treating a whole site. This is among the most cited recent papers on biochar for PFAS, and it is the peer-reviewed source to put in front of a council, fire station or airport weighing options. The biochar types described as most effective are high-temperature hardwood chars with activation, the profile of Possible Agriculture Biochar.

documents.title: Can biochar and designer biochar be used to remediate per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) and lead and antimony contaminated soils?
documents.authors: Silvani, Cornelissen, Smebye, Zhang, Okkenhaug, Zimmerman, Thune, Sævarsson, Hale
documents.summary: Shooting-range soils from Norway treated with designer biochars. Iron-enriched biochar at 20 per cent cut lead leaching by 99 per cent and antimony leaching by 40 per cent. Coconut-shell activated biochar at 1 per cent cut PFOS leachate by more than 96 per cent, in soils with 5.2 and 10.2 per cent organic matter.
documents.abstract: Silvani's team tested whether one biochar treatment could handle several contaminants in the same soil. They worked with shooting-range soils of two organic matter contents, 5.2 and 10.2 per cent. Iron-enriched designer biochar at 20 per cent application reduced lead leaching by 99 per cent and antimony leaching by 40 per cent. Coconut-shell activated biochar at 1 per cent application cut PFOS leachate by more than 96 per cent in both soils. The lesson is matching: activated coconut-shell for PFAS, iron-enriched for lead. It is a companion to Sørmo 2021 from the same Norwegian team. Councils with old shooting ranges or fire-training grounds can weigh these inclusion rates against excavation and disposal. The work is laboratory leaching tests, not a full-scale site treatment.

documents.title: Engineered/designer biochar for contaminant removal/immobilization from soil and water: Potential and implication of biochar modification
documents.authors: Rajapaksha, Chen, Tsang, Zhang, Vithanage, Mandal, Gao, Bolan, Ok
documents.summary: A review of engineered biochars for removing contaminants from soil and water. Modifications include acid or base treatment, steam activation, magnetic loading, and mineral impregnation. Sorption capacity rose 5 to 20 times over unmodified biochar, depending on the contaminant. Hydrogen peroxide oxidation lifted lead sorption 20 times.
documents.abstract: Rajapaksha's team, including Nanthi Bolan of the University of South Australia, review how biochar can be modified for a given contaminant. Methods covered are acid or base treatment, amination, surfactant modification, mineral impregnation, steam activation, and magnetic loading. Sorption capacity improved 5 to 20 times over unmodified biochar, depending on the target contaminant. For lead, hydrogen peroxide oxidised biochar reached 20 times the sorption of the plain char. The central message is that biochars are not interchangeable for remediation: the activation profile must match the contaminant. That is what makes biochar a defensible regulatory choice, and it is the reference for a council manager explaining why a treatment uses a specific engineered char. This is a literature review, so results come from many studies rather than one site.

documents.title: Biochar as a sorbent for contaminant management in soil and water: A review
documents.summary: A review of how biochar binds contaminants in soil and water, written by a group including Nanthi Bolan and Dinesh Mohan. It covers biochar as a sorbent for managing pollutants in both media. Sorption is the basis for most remediation uses, so it is a sensible first read for a consultant weighing biochar at a contaminated site.
documents.abstract: This 2013 review in Chemosphere looks at biochar as a sorbent for contaminant management in soil and water. Authors include Mahtab Ahmad, Anushka Rajapaksha, Nanthi Bolan and Dinesh Mohan, several of whom have published widely on remediation. Sorption is the mechanism behind most remediation uses of biochar: pollutants stick to the char surface, which makes them less mobile in the soil or less available to plants. The review treats soil and water together, so it suits a consultant comparing biochar with activated carbon or other amendments. Performance varies with feedstock, pyrolysis temperature and the contaminant in question, so site-specific testing should come before any field-scale use. It remains a standard reference in the remediation literature.

documents.title: A review of biochars’ potential role in the remediation, revegetation and restoration of contaminated soils
documents.authors: Beesley, Moreno‐Jiménez, Gomez-Eyles, Harris, Robinson and Sizmur
documents.summary: A 2011 review of biochar in the remediation, revegetation and restoration of contaminated soils, by Luke Beesley, Tom Sizmur and colleagues. It covers how biochar can lock up pollutants, then help plants re-establish on damaged ground. It suits a consultant wanting a first map of where biochar has been tried.
documents.abstract: Beesley, Moreno-Jimenez, Gomez-Eyles, Harris, Robinson and Sizmur review the use of biochar on contaminated land in Environmental Pollution, 2011. Their themes are remediation of pollutants, revegetation of bare ground, wider restoration of soil function. Biochar can hold metals plus organic contaminants on its surface, raise pH, and add organic carbon to poor substrates, which together help plants establish on sites such as mine tailings or old industrial land. Effects depend on the contaminant, since a char that immobilises one pollutant can mobilise another, for instance through a pH shift. Read it for the range of cases and the mechanisms, then test locally. Field-scale evidence was thin when it was written.

documents.title: Analysis of the long-term effectiveness of biochar immobilization remediation on heavy metal contaminated soil and the potential environmental factors weakening the remediation effect: A review
documents.summary: A review of how long biochar holds heavy metals in contaminated soil, drawing on field remediation work over several years. Most studies report effective immobilisation for 2 to 3 years, a few for 5. Acid rain, flooding, plant roots, earthworms, soil microbes can all weaken the effect over time.
documents.abstract: Published remediation results were reviewed for one question: how long does biochar keep heavy metals locked up? Attention went to agricultural land, plus field projects running several years. Biochar lowers the available metals in soil, in plants too, and most studies show the effect holding for 2 to 3 years, with a few showing 5. Several reports find it fading with time. Abiotic causes include acid rain, a flooded environment, shifts in pH, redox, dissolved organic matter, as well as changes in the char itself such as chloride and alkali leaching. Biotic causes include plant roots, earthworms, soil microorganisms, which can reduce immobilisation considerably. Long-term data remain thin. Anyone planning a remediation should expect to monitor for years, and may need to reapply, particularly on wet or acidic sites.

documents.title: Applications of Biochar and Modified Biochar in Heavy Metal Contaminated Soil: A Descriptive Review
documents.authors: Liang, Lin, He, Li, Zhu and Zhu
documents.summary: A review of biochar and modified biochar for heavy-metal-contaminated soil, covering feedstocks, pyrolysis temperature, additives, modification methods. Remediation works through adsorption, complexation, precipitation, ion exchange, electrostatic attraction. Modified chars generally outperform raw biochar, with monitoring needed after treatment on site.
documents.abstract: This review sets out how biochar is used to treat soil contaminated with heavy metals. It compares the raw materials used to make biochar, the way pyrolysis temperature, additives, modification methods change the finished product, plus the soil types and operating conditions for repair. Five mechanisms are described: adsorption, complexation, precipitation, ion exchange, electrostatic attraction. Which one dominates depends on the feedstock, the temperature, any chemical modification. Modified biochars are presented as a way to raise capacity beyond raw char. The paper covers the monitoring methods used after remediation, then ends with directions for future work, including simpler preparation methods. It is a descriptive review with no new field trial, so it helps a consultant shortlist a char, not set site-specific application rates.

documents.title: Biochar can be used to capture essential nutrients from dairy wastewater and improve soil physico-chemical properties
documents.summary: A review of batch sorption work on biochar in dairy wastewater, scaled to California. In 24 hours biochar took up 20 to 43 per cent of ammonium, 19 to 65 per cent of phosphate in flushed dairy manure, at 2.86 milligrams of ammonium and 0.23 of phosphate per gram. Scaled up, the state could capture 11,440 to 57,200 tonnes of ammonium-N a year.
documents.abstract: Biochar made from local excess biomass could pull nutrients out of dairy wastewater before they reach runoff. The work reviewed used batch sorption experiments on flushed dairy manure. Within 24 hours biochar adsorbed up to 20 to 43 per cent of the ammonium, 19 to 65 per cent of the phosphate. Capacity was 2.86 milligrams of ammonium, 0.23 milligrams of phosphate per gram of biochar. Assuming 10 to 50 per cent use of available excess biomass, the figures scale to California as 11,440 to 57,200 tonnes of ammonium-N, 920 to 4,600 tonnes of phosphate a year, with 8 to 40 million tons of biomass disposed of. Returning the nutrient-loaded char to soil would improve fertility. These are laboratory results scaled by arithmetic, not farm trials.

documents.title: Biochar as a sustainable product for remediation of petroleum contaminated soil
documents.publisher: Current Research in Green and Sustainable Chemistry
documents.summary: A review of biochar for petroleum-contaminated soil, covering how biochar is made, then used as an amendment or sorbent alongside bioremediation. Performance depends on feedstock plus pyrolysis conditions, which set the char's surface area and chemistry. Side benefits include carbon storage, better soil fertility, a use for farm waste.
documents.abstract: Petroleum reaches soil through production, storage, transport, accidental release, harming plant growth and human health. This review looks at biochar as a tool for cleaning it up, mostly by helping bioremediation, where microbes break down the hydrocarbons. It describes how biochar is made, then how it works as an amendment, ameliorant or sorbent. Its large internal surface area, physical properties and chemical properties let it hold contaminants, with each varying by feedstock and pyrolysis conditions. Wide availability of feedstock plus low cost are given as advantages. Side benefits include carbon sequestration, better soil fertility, recycling of agricultural waste. The paper is a literature review with no new field data, so it informs the choice of char for a remediation brief, not a dose.

documents.title: Influences of Biochar on Bioremediation/Phytoremediation Potential of Metal-Contaminated Soils
documents.summary: A review of plant-derived biochar for phytoremediation of metal-contaminated soil. Biochar neutralises acidic soil pH, feeds native microbes, which helps fast-growing plants establish and take up metals. Heavy contamination otherwise cuts plant biomass, slowing cleanup. The review gives mechanisms rather than field rates, so it guides trial design more than application.
documents.abstract: Metals build up in soil from human activity and weathering, persist, damage soil microbes, threaten groundwater and the food chain. Phytoremediation uses plants to pull out or stabilise them, but heavy contamination stunts growth, limiting the method. This review examines biochar made from plant and agricultural waste as a way around that. It describes biochar raising the growth and remediation performance of native and wild plants on polluted soil. The carbon-rich material neutralises pH, supplies nutrients, encouraging native microbial growth. Fast-growing, high-biomass plants suit phytoremediation best. No field rates or yield figures are given, so the review is best used to understand mechanisms, then to plan trials with local feedstocks and plants. It positions biochar as a soil conditioner for the plants doing the cleaning, not a standalone fix.

documents.title: Containing Contaminants: Harnessing Biochar for Effective Pollution Control (PFAS insight brief)
documents.summary: An eight-page 2024 International Biochar Initiative policy brief on biochar for PFAS contamination. It sets biochar out as a viable option for persistent chemical pollution, with real-world pyrolysis applications. It is aimed at policymakers, funders, with no trial numbers in the opening pages.
documents.abstract: The brief describes PFAS as synthetic chemicals used for their water-resistant, grease-resistant properties, detected in the blood of most participants in a 1999 United States national health survey, linked to organ damage, immune suppression. They break down very slowly, if at all. Biochar is offered as a means of immobilising or decomposing pollutants, with uses named for industrial runoff, agricultural residues, stormwater management, land remediation, erosion control. The brief asks policymakers to direct money to research, policy, and funders to back studies, pilot projects. It is advocacy, so remediation consultants should look to the cited trials for removal rates, contaminant mixes, the fate of the spent biochar.

documents.title: Biochar in Water Management Fact Sheet
documents.publisher: Australia New Zealand Biochar Industry Group (ANZBIG)
documents.summary: A two-page ANZBIG fact sheet from March 2025 on biochar in stormwater filtration, wastewater, drinking water treatment. Its Australian case is Logan Water in Queensland, where a biosolids plant processes 34,000 tonnes a year, cutting emissions by 6,000 tonnes of CO2-equivalent a year.
documents.abstract: The sheet lists three uses: stormwater filtration to remove heavy metals, nutrients or organic pollutants, wastewater treatment to adsorb contaminants and recover nutrients, low-cost drinking water purification. It also points to higher soil water holding capacity as a way to cut runoff. The Logan Water project in Queensland, run by Logan City Council, Logan Water, Downer, ARENA, is the first in Australia to turn human wastewater biosolids into biochar. The plant handles 34,000 tonnes of biosolids a year, driven by rising disposal costs. Implementation advice is to assess existing infrastructure for retrofits, use biochar meeting contaminant standards, involve councils and water authorities. It is an overview with references to other sources, not a trial report, so it gives no removal rates.

documents.title: Waste water treatment and biochar (Draper)
documents.summary: Kathleen Draper argues that carbonising wastewater residuals suits municipalities as land application of biosolids is restricted. Sewage sludge carries nitrogen, phosphorus, micronutrients, plus harmful contaminants. Wastewater treatment accounts for nearly 3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, so pyrolysis offers a way to cut those emissions as well as the disposal problem.
documents.abstract: Draper treats organic residuals from wastewater treatment as one of the world's most renewable, yet underused, waste streams. Land application, a common end use, is increasingly restricted, so communities worldwide are looking for other ways to manage biosolids. Treating residential, commercial or industrial wastewater is costly for the municipalities running the plants. Sewage sludge holds useful nitrogen, phosphorus, micronutrients, along with harmful components. Carbonising it may solve several biosolids problems while offering a route to decarbonise an industry responsible for nearly 3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. The article is a position piece in The Biochar Journal. For a council or water utility, the open questions are contaminant fate in the char, such as metals and persistent chemicals, plus the cost of drying the sludge first, so pilot data come before any commitment.

documents.title: Compost and biochar — combined value in soil amendment
documents.summary: A synthesis from the International Biochar Initiative on adding biochar to compost windrows at 5 to 15 per cent by volume. It cut nitrogen volatilisation, held phosphorus against leaching and reduced odour. The finished compost released more slowly, with more biological activity. Operators already composting manure or green waste have the easiest entry point here.
documents.abstract: The International Biochar Initiative synthesis on combining biochar with compost, at 5 to 15 per cent biochar by volume in the windrow. Nitrogen volatilisation fell, phosphorus stayed bound instead of leaching, odour dropped sharply. The finished compost released nutrients more slowly, with more biological activity. The combination outperformed either input alone. The reason is physical: porous biochar adsorbs nutrients, odour compounds and water from the active compost, so ammonia stays in the windrow. For a mixed-livestock operator the loop is simple. Feed biochar to the cattle, run the manure through an amended windrow, spread the finished compost back on pasture.

documents.title: Synergisms between Compost and Biochar for Sustainable Soil Amelioration
documents.publisher: Management of Organic Waste (InTech book chapter)
documents.summary: A 2012 book chapter on biochar in poultry-litter composting. Ammonia emissions fell by up to 64 per cent and total nitrogen losses by up to 52 per cent. Biochar adsorbs volatile nitrogen during active composting, so more stays in the windrow. Feedlots, dairies and poultry sheds with a large manure stream are the obvious fit.
documents.abstract: Fischer and Glaser mapped the science of why compost with biochar beats either alone. In poultry-litter composting, biochar cut ammonia emissions by up to 64 per cent and total nitrogen losses by up to 52 per cent. The mechanism is adsorption: the porous surface holds ammonia and other volatile nitrogen compounds in the windrow during active composting. The result is a denser, more nutrient-rich compost, with the biochar entering the soil already carrying the compost microbial community. The combination follows the terra preta approach of stable carbon plus immediate nutrient value. The chapter has been cited more than 380 times. It suggests 10 to 20 per cent biochar in the windrow before turning. It is a book chapter, not a field trial on Australian manure.

documents.title: The roles of co-composted biochar (COMBI) in improving soil quality, crop productivity, and toxic metal amelioration
documents.summary: A review of biochar added at the start of composting, known as co-composted biochar or COMBI, with uses on farmland, contaminated soil. Co-composting improves both the compost and the char, lifts soil health, raised crop yields by up to 300 per cent in some cases. Evidence is still thin, with a few drawbacks listed.
documents.abstract: Antonangelo, Sun and Zhang reviewed the production of co-composted biochar, made by adding biochar at the start of composting, plus its use in agriculture. Co-composting changes both materials: the compost process improves and the biochar surface chemistry shifts as it ages. Benefits over compost or biochar applied separately, or mixed afterwards, include better soil health, higher yields (up to 300 per cent in a few cases) and lower availability of toxic metals in contaminated land. A few drawbacks and side effects appear, but the review judges them outweighed. The number of studies is limited. The review calls for research on long-term effects, surface chemistry, nutrient adsorption and release as the char ages, environmental outcomes.

documents.title: Complementing compost with biochar for agriculture, soil remediation and climate mitigation
documents.summary: A review of how composting changes when biochar goes into the heap, and what the finished biochar-compost does in cropped and contaminated soils. Compost supplies nutrients plus microbes, while biochar adds stable carbon with a large reactive surface. A rice case study closes the chapter, using a mineral-enhanced biochar and a biochar-compost.
documents.abstract: A book chapter on making and using biochar-compost. It covers production methods for biochar, compost and the blend, then their use in farm soils and contaminated sites. Compost supplies labile carbon, nutrients, microbes. Biochar brings stable carbon, and its large reactive surface holds nutrients from the feedstock and the surrounding soil. It also alters the chemistry and microbial activity of the heap during composting. Metal and organic contaminants have their own sections. The chapter ends with a case study on making and field-testing a mineral-enhanced biochar plus a biochar-compost to lift rice yield. It is a review, so the figures come from the studies it draws on, not from one trial. For an operator with manure or green waste to process, the reading is simple: the blend is expected to give a more stable, more nutrient-rich conditioner than compost alone.

documents.title: Ammonia volatilization from composting with oxidized biochar
documents.summary: A seven-week composting test of poultry manure and straw with oxidised biochar, unoxidised biochar, or none. Unoxidised biochar lost twice the nitrogen of oxidised biochar. Oxidised biochar cut ammonia loss relative to carbon dioxide by 55 per cent, doubled the composting rate, and held 16.0 milligrams of nitrogen a gram of char against 6.1.
documents.abstract: Composting loses much of its nitrogen as ammonia gas. This test composted poultry manure and straw for seven weeks with oxidised biochar, unoxidised biochar, or none. Total nitrogen loss from the unoxidised treatment was twofold higher than from the oxidised one. Reported losses were 307, 142 and 51 milligrams per gram of starting nitrogen for unoxidised, oxidised, and no biochar. Judged against carbon dioxide loss, ammonia loss from oxidised biochar was 55 per cent lower than from unoxidised (82 per cent lower on a mass balance). Oxidised particles recovered after seven weeks held 16.0 milligrams of nitrogen per gram, against 6.1 for unoxidised. Oxidised biochar also raised microbial activity, doubling the rate of composting. Surface oxygen groups, added artificially or acquired by weathering, appear to drive the effect.

documents.title: Methane and nitrous oxide emissions during biochar‐composting are driven by biochar application rate and aggregate formation
documents.summary: Dairy manure composted with 5 or 20 per cent biochar by mass in California, using walnut shell, almond shell and almond clipping char. The 20 per cent rate cut nitrous oxide and ammonia but raised methane, still giving a net drop in warming impact. The 5 per cent rate delivered a similar net benefit without the methane rise, so lower rates make sense.
documents.abstract: Harrison, Gao, Thao, Gonzales and colleagues measured methane, nitrous oxide and ammonia during composting of dairy manure with biochar at 5 or 20 per cent by mass. The chars came from walnut shells, almond shells or almond clippings. Feedstock made little difference to emissions. Application rate did. At 20 per cent, methane emissions rose, nitrous oxide and ammonia fell, with global warming potential down overall. The team puts this down to biochar promoting compost aggregates, which probably acted as pockets without oxygen where methane formed and denitrification ran to completion. Biochar may also have shuttled electrons inside the aggregates. At 5 per cent the net reduction in warming impact was similar, with no methane increase. The study is a single composting system, so the rate effect should be tested on other manures.

documents.title: Biochar manure decreases ammonia volatilization loss and sustains crop productivity in rice paddy
documents.authors: Canatoy, Cho, Galgo, Park and Kim
documents.summary: Rice paddy trial in South Korea with swine manure applied at 12 tonnes dry weight a hectare as fresh, composted or biochar manure. Fresh and composted manure raised seasonal ammonia loss, but biochar manure did not. Composted manure lifted grain yield, while biochar manure did not, so ammonia per unit of grain was lowest with biochar.
documents.abstract: Canatoy, Cho, Galgo, Park, Kim with colleagues compared three swine manure forms in flooded rice: fresh, composted and biochar. Each went on at 12 tonnes a hectare (dry weight) before transplanting, under a standard fertiliser program of 90 kilograms nitrogen, 45 phosphate and 57 potash. Ammonia was measured with static chambers. Ammonia fluxes jumped after urea was applied in every treatment, more sharply where manure was present. Fresh or composted manure raised seasonal ammonia loss against the control, but biochar manure did not. Composted manure lifted rice yield through its higher nitrogen content. Fresh and biochar manure did not, with fewer panicles per hill and fewer grains per panicle. Ammonia per unit of grain was therefore lowest with biochar manure. The yield cost of biochar manure in this trial is a real limit.

documents.title: Biochar in Compost: Improve Compost and Save Money
documents.publisher: American Biochar Institute with Nebraska Forest Service
documents.summary: A draft 2026 guide from the American Biochar Institute with the Nebraska Forest Service on adding biochar to compost. It recommends 5 to 10 per cent biochar by volume, warning against going past 20 or 30 per cent. Composters report shorter processing time, fewer pile turnings, a product richer in nitrogen.
documents.abstract: The guide says biochar goes into the pile like any other ingredient, using existing equipment. It credits biochar with stimulating microbial activity, which raises temperature, shortens composting time, speeds stabilisation. The recommended range of 5 to 10 per cent by volume comes from the scientific literature plus composters' experience. Excess biochar can interfere with biodegradation, so 20 to 30 per cent is flagged as too much. The economic case rests on less turning, which saves fuel, labour, on higher nitrogen in the finished compost. These are reports from operators, not controlled trial data, and the document is a first draft. Compost makers can pair it with the Biochar Atlas cost-benefit tool to test the numbers on their own site.

documents.title: Biochar + Compost (white paper)
documents.summary: A sixteen-page white paper from Pacific Biochar on blending biochar with compost, drawn from published studies. Co-composting with biochar raised grape weight by 16 per cent and must acidity by 9 per cent. Compost with biochar lifted extractable nitrogen by 44 per cent, with available potassium up 26 per cent.
documents.abstract: Charlie McIntosh and Josiah Hunt of Pacific Biochar Benefit Corporation wrote this paper in January 2023. It reviews studies on adding biochar to compost early in the process. Biochar surfaces adsorb nutrients, so nitrogen losses fall by more than half in many studies, with more of the nitrogen held as nitrate than as ammonium. Emissions drop as well: methane by more than 80 per cent in some work, nitrous oxide by more than 50 per cent, ammonia by up to 60 per cent. The paper cites a grape study in which co-composting raised grape weight by 16 per cent and must acidity by 9 per cent, and another in which compost plus biochar lifted extractable nitrogen by 44 per cent, with available potassium up 26 per cent. The company sells biochar. The paper collects favourable results, so read the figures as upper ranges.

documents.title: Compost-biochar combination lab test
documents.summary: Bench-scale measurements of nitrogen retention, microbial activity, nutrient release at different biochar inclusion rates in compost. It is lab data, not a paddock result. The numbers give a baseline for setting targets and measurement points before committing a windrow or paddock to an on-farm trial.
documents.abstract: Quantitative bench-scale work on biochar in compost, covering nitrogen retention, microbial activity, the nutrient release profile across a range of inclusion rates. It sits underneath the International Biochar Initiative reference set: the IBI document is the bibliography, this is the bench data. Use it to set trial parameters, such as which inclusion rate to target, what nitrogen retention to expect, how to measure microbial activity, what the curing time looks like at different ratios. Read it with the IBI bulking-agent paper before committing a windrow or paddock to a serious trial. Lab conditions will differ from a working farm.

documents.title: Compost_biochar_IBI_references
documents.summary: A reference list of peer-reviewed work on biochar in compost, compiled by the International Biochar Initiative. It is a bibliography, not a study, so it carries no results of its own. Council briefs, ACCU project documents or grant applications can cite it as a single evidence base for biochar in composting.
documents.abstract: A compiled reference list from the International Biochar Initiative covering peer-reviewed work on biochar in compost. It is a bibliography with full citation detail, not a standalone study, so it reports no measured results of its own. Its use is practical. A council procurement officer or grant assessor asking about the evidence for biochar in composting can be sent this document, which saves chasing individual papers. It suits council briefs, ACCU project documents or grant applications needing a broad evidence base. Read it alongside the IBI synthesis on compost with biochar, and the bench data in the compost lab test, which give the findings behind the citations.

documents.title: Biochar as bulking agent for poultry litter composting
documents.summary: A review of biochar as a bulking agent in poultry litter compost, at 10 to 20 per cent by volume. Nitrogen losses from volatilisation and leaching fall, and so does odour. The finished compost has a better nutrient profile, more microbial activity, and slower nutrient release than litter-only compost.
documents.abstract: This review looks at biochar mixed into poultry litter windrows at 10 to 20 per cent by volume. Litter is a high-nitrogen, high-phosphorus, high-odour stream, usually handled as a disposal problem. With biochar in the pile, nitrogen loss through volatilisation and leaching drops substantially, odour falls, and the composting cycle speeds up. The finished compost shows a better nutrient profile, higher microbial activity, and slower-release nutrients than litter-only compost. It also has better structure, which helps when spreading through standard farm equipment. For a poultry operator, the practical point is that more of the nitrogen and phosphorus reaches the paddock rather than the air or groundwater.

documents.title: The Use of Biochar in Composting (IBI technical paper)
documents.summary: A five-page technical guide from 2015 on adding biochar to compost, written by Marta Camps of Massey University with Thayer Tomlinson. Mixing 20 per cent biochar by mass into poultry litter cut the ammonia concentration in emissions by up to 64 per cent. Nitrogen losses fell by up to 52 per cent.
documents.abstract: This International Biochar Initiative paper was reviewed by Mariluz Cayuela and M. A. Sanchez-Monedero. It explains how biochar can speed composting, lower greenhouse gas emissions, cut ammonia loss, bulk up the heap, reduce odour. It also takes up the worry about competition for feedstocks, arguing compost makers and biochar producers can draw on the same waste streams. The headline numbers come from poultry litter. A 20 per cent biochar addition by mass reduced ammonia in emissions by up to 64 per cent, nitrogen losses by up to 52 per cent. Both figures are upper bounds, so expect less from a poorly matched biochar or a drier, cooler heap. Intensive poultry operations wanting to keep nitrogen in the pile will find the most use here.

documents.title: Poultry Litter Biochar - a US Perspective
documents.summary: A 2012 International Biochar Initiative paper on biochar made from poultry litter in the United States. An 80/20 mix of litter and biochar reduced nitrogen loss by up to 52 per cent, ammonia emissions by up to 64 per cent. The paper rests on existing research plus a limited number of demonstration projects.
documents.abstract: Kathleen Draper with Thayer Tomlinson set out the characteristics of poultry litter biochar, the benefits of producing it, the challenges for farmers, the uses beyond soil amendment. They note the feedstock shapes the product, as do temperature, residence time, heating rate. More than half the carbon in the feedstock can end up locked in stable form. The poultry-specific numbers come from a mix of 80 per cent litter, 20 per cent biochar, which cut nitrogen loss by up to 52 per cent, ammonia emissions by up to 64 per cent. Evidence for litter biochar was thin in 2012, so treat the paper as a starting brief. Broiler or layer operators holding large litter volumes get the clearest read on market options, alternatives to spreading raw litter.

documents.title: Biochar Compost Fact Sheet: Enhancing Composting Efficiency and Soil Health
documents.publisher: Australia New Zealand Biochar Industry Group (ANZBIG)
documents.summary: A two-page ANZBIG fact sheet from February 2025 on adding biochar to compost. It recommends 5 to 10 per cent biochar by volume at the start of composting, up to 15 per cent for manure, then 5 to 10 tonnes a hectare of finished compost in the field. Straw biochars adsorbed up to 36 per cent more nitrogen.
documents.abstract: The sheet draws on the ANZBIG Farmer's Guide to Biochar plus published compost work. Co-composting at 5 to 10 per cent is said to speed breakdown of woody material, cut odour, cut greenhouse gas emissions, reduce nutrient leaching. Straw biochars hold ammonia best, and particles of 4 to 10 millimetres cut methane from compost piles. High nitrogen feedstocks such as manure take up to 15 per cent biochar to stabilise nitrogen. Case notes include a California vineyard given a biochar compost mix at 7 tonnes a hectare, reported at 20 per cent higher yield. A Western Australian salt-affected site gets a mention, as do Portland green roofs. These are summaries, not full trial data. Mix the biochar in at the start of composting, then spread with standard compost equipment.

documents.title: Biochar Improves Manure Management
documents.summary: A four-page Nebraska Forest Service fact sheet on biochar in manure management. A University of California Merced study of dairy manure cut methane emissions by 79 per cent with one tonne of biochar to 15 tonnes of manure, about 6 per cent on a wet basis. Oregon on-farm trials from 2016 to 2018 reported less barn odour, and one ranch's composted manure held ten times the nitrate of plain manure.
documents.abstract: The sheet pulls together trial reports with farm case histories. Kelpie Wilson ran on-farm trials in Oregon with USDA from 2016 to 2018. At Michaels Ranch, Days Creek, biochar added to the barn floor gave composted manure with ten times the nitrate of plain manure. At Willow-Witt Farm, Ashland, the owners noted strong odour reduction. In poultry houses of 25,000 birds, biochar is used to hold ammonia down. Mixed into stored litter, it adsorbs nitrogen before rain can wash it out. One rancher on 756 acres (about 306 hectares) used sawmill boiler ash biochar, pH 8.4, as a liming agent. Early data showed more nitrogen retained in the biochar-manure mix. A 2022 University of Iowa study found biochar-manure slurry combinations could supply 604 pounds of phosphorus, 675 pounds of nitrogen an acre. Much of the evidence is farmer testimony or preliminary data, so weigh it accordingly.

documents.title: Treating liquid manure with biochar (Schmidt)
documents.summary: Hans-Peter Schmidt explains how biochar tames liquid manure. The smell of slurry is microbial decomposition running out of control, and much of the ammonia from urea escapes to the air at spreading in spring and autumn. Treating the manure with biochar and managing the microbes in the shed cuts odour and nutrient loss.
documents.abstract: Schmidt starts from the old assumption that a cowshed must stink. He argues the smell is a sign of microbial decomposition gone out of control, and a source of disease for the animals living there. The sharp odour at spreading time comes mostly from ammonia, formed from the urea in manure, which escapes to the air in large amounts and burns soil organisms and fine roots. Treating liquid manure with biochar, along with control of the microbial environment in the shed or pit, closes the nutrient cycle: the slurry becomes a more efficient, odourless fertiliser. Dairy and feedlot operators near neighbours have the most to gain from the odour side.

documents.title: Biochar stability in soil: meta‐analysis of decomposition and priming effects
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of 128 biochar decomposition records from 24 isotope-tracer studies, plus 116 records on priming of native soil organic matter. About 3 per cent of biochar carbon is labile, with a residence time near 108 days. The other 97 per cent lasts about 556 years. Priming averaged a slight negative 3.8 per cent, though sandy soils lost 20.8 per cent more organic matter.
documents.abstract: Wang and colleagues pooled 128 observations of biochar-derived carbon dioxide from 24 studies using carbon-13 and carbon-14 tracers, to estimate how long biochar lasts in soil. Decomposition rose with the logarithm of time, then slowed. Two carbon pools fit the data: a labile pool of 3 per cent with a mean residence time of about 108 days, and a recalcitrant pool of 97 per cent lasting about 556 years. Feedstock, pyrolysis temperature, trial length and clay content all changed the rate. A second dataset of 116 observations covered priming, meaning whether biochar speeds or slows breakdown of native soil organic matter. The mean was a 3.8 per cent slowdown, with a confidence interval from minus 8.1 to plus 0.8 per cent, so not clearly different from zero. Crop-derived biochar (minus 20.3 per cent) and fast pyrolysis (minus 18.9 per cent) slowed it most. Sandy soils went the other way, up 20.8 per cent. Biochar persists for centuries.

documents.title: Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration after Biochar Application: A Global Meta-Analysis
documents.summary: A global meta-analysis of 64 studies with 736 treatments, where field trials ran 1 to 10 years at 1 to 100 tonnes of biochar a hectare. Field soil organic carbon stocks rose by 13.0 tonnes a hectare on average, or 29 per cent. Gains were larger in medium to fine-textured soils than in coarse ones.
documents.abstract: Meta-analysis covering 64 studies with 736 individual treatments. Field trials lasted 1 to 10 years with biochar at 1 to 100 tonnes a hectare. Soil organic carbon stocks rose by 13.0 tonnes a hectare on average, a 29 per cent gain. Pot and incubation experiments ran from 1 to 1278 days at 5 to 200 grams of biochar a kilogram of soil, lifting organic carbon by 6.3 grams a kilogram, or 75 per cent. Longer experiments stored more: over 500 days in pots, 6 to 10 years in the field. Organic fertiliser applied with biochar added further carbon. Biochar from plant material stored more than biochar from manure, linked to its higher carbon to nitrogen ratio. Medium and fine-textured soils gained more than coarse soils. Pot results run well above field results, so the field figure is the one to plan around.

documents.title: Quantifying the Effects of Biochar Application on Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Agricultural Soils: A Global Meta-Analysis
documents.summary: A global meta-analysis of 129 published papers on biochar's effect on soil greenhouse gases. Methane rose 15 per cent on average, carbon dioxide 16 per cent, while nitrous oxide fell 38 per cent. Global warming potential dropped 23 per cent, emission intensity 41 per cent, with crop yield up 21 per cent.
documents.abstract: Meta-analysis of 129 published papers measuring how biochar changes soil methane, carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide emissions from farmland. Across all studies, methane rose 15 per cent and carbon dioxide 16 per cent. Nitrous oxide fell 38 per cent. The effect varied with management, biochar properties, soil. Biochar characteristics accounted for 29 per cent of the variation in nitrous oxide, up to 71 per cent in carbon dioxide. Soil pH was the most influential variable for methane, the biochar carbon to nitrogen ratio for carbon dioxide, application rate for nitrous oxide. Across all three gases, global warming potential fell by an average 23 per cent, emission intensity (emissions per unit of output) by 41 per cent, while crop yield rose 21 per cent. Averages hide wide spread between sites, so match the biochar to the soil in question.

documents.title: Biochar application significantly increases soil organic carbon under conservation tillage: an 11-year field experiment
documents.authors: Ding, Li, Zhao, Lin and Wang
documents.summary: An 11-year field experiment on calcareous soil under conservation tillage, in a winter wheat and maize rotation with biochar at 0, 30, 60 or 90 tonnes a hectare. About 39 to 51 per cent of the biochar remained in the top 30 centimetres after 11 years. Native soil organic carbon rose, mostly in the stable fraction, but only in the top 15 centimetres.
documents.abstract: Eleven-year field trial testing biochar at 0, 30, 60 or 90 tonnes a hectare in calcareous soil under conservation tillage, across a winter wheat and maize rotation. Carbon already in the soil, separate from carbon added as biochar, was split into labile pools plus a recalcitrant pool. Its breakdown was tracked with soil basal respiration plus carbon-13 isotope measurements. After 11 years, 39 to 51 per cent of the biochar remained in the top 30 centimetres. Higher rates raised native soil organic carbon, particularly the recalcitrant fraction, while cutting the share of labile carbon. Biochar tended to raise indicators of microbial activity. At the two highest rates, more carbon dioxide came from maize-derived carbon, so mineralisation of native carbon also increased. Rate effects showed in the top 15 centimetres only, with no difference at 15 to 30 centimetres.

documents.title: Soil carbon increased by twice the amount of biochar carbon applied after 6 years: Field evidence of negative priming
documents.authors: Blanco‐Canqui, Laird, Heaton, Rathke and Acharya
documents.summary: Six years after wood biochar at 9.3 tonnes a hectare on a Midwestern US soil under no-till corn, switchgrass and prairie grasses. Soil carbon in the top 30 centimetres rose by 14.07 tonnes a hectare with biochar against 2.25 without, about twice the 7.25 tonnes of biochar carbon applied. Other soil properties barely moved.
documents.abstract: Field trial on a Midwestern US soil measuring soil carbon six years after biochar application. Main plots were no-till continuous corn, Liberty switchgrass, a low-diversity prairie mix (45 per cent big bluestem, 45 per cent Indiangrass, 10 per cent sideoats grama). Subplots received wood biochar at 9.3 tonnes a hectare (63 per cent carbon) or none. In the top 30 centimetres, biochar plots gained 14.07 tonnes of soil carbon a hectare against 2.25 on plots without. Biochar had supplied only 7.25 tonnes of carbon a hectare, so the gain was nearly double, which points to negative priming: biochar slowed the loss of native soil carbon, or aided its formation. The perennial bioenergy crops lifted soil carbon concentration by 79 per cent. They also improved aggregation and plant available water in the top 5 centimetres. Biochar did not interact with cropping system, with limited effect on other soil properties. One site, one rate, so treat the doubling as a result awaiting replication.

documents.title: How much is soil nitrous oxide emission reduced with biochar application? An evaluation of meta‐analyses
documents.summary: A review of 18 meta-analyses published between 2014 and 2022 on biochar and nitrous oxide from soil. Four found no clear effect, while the rest reported cuts of 10.5 to 54.8 per cent. Pooled, biochar lowered emissions by 38.8 per cent, with larger cuts at higher application rates.
documents.abstract: Eighteen meta-analyses on biochar and soil nitrous oxide were compared, with sample sizes from under 30 to over 1000 studies (mean 275). Four found no significant effect. The others reported reductions ranging from 10.5 to 54.8 per cent, so the headline number depends heavily on which review you read. A grand mean response ratio built from all of them gave a 38.8 per cent cut. The effect grew with biochar application rate and was shaped by the carbon to nitrogen ratio of the biochar. It strengthened over the first 18 months of an experiment, then faded. Nitrous oxide is the third most important long-lived greenhouse gas, with croplands a hotspot. The pooled figure beats any single review as a guide, but the fade after 18 months argues for treating it as a short-term result.

documents.title: Long-term biochar and soil organic carbon stability – Evidence from field experiments in Germany
documents.authors: Groß, Bromm, Polifka, Fischer and Glaser
documents.publisher: The Science of The Total Environment
documents.summary: Two long-term German field experiments sampled 12 and 14 years after biochar went on. On a loamy soil in Bavaria, 31.5 tonnes a hectare with compost held a soil carbon gain of 38 tonnes a hectare after eleven years. On a sandy soil, most of the gain was gone within nine years.
documents.abstract: Two German field experiments were resampled 12 and 14 years after application. On a loamy soil in northeastern Bavaria, compost plus 31.5 tonnes a hectare of biochar raised soil organic carbon stocks by 38 tonnes a hectare. The gain was still there after eleven years. On a sandy soil, 40 tonnes a hectare of biochar with digestate, compost or synthetic fertiliser lifted carbon stocks by 61 tonnes a hectare. Of that, 38 tonnes dissipated within four years, and after nine years the stock was only 7 tonnes above the control. Black carbon followed the same path. Persistence was set by the quality and amount of biochar, with compost or digestate adding little over the long term. Aged biochar lost its labile fractions but kept the stable ones. For sandy paddocks, expect the carbon credit to be far less durable than on loam.

documents.title: Flame curtain kilns produce biochar from dry biomass with minimal methane emissions
documents.publisher: The Science of The Total Environment
documents.summary: Methane measured from flame curtain kilns burning twigs and leaves. Dry feedstock under 15 per cent moisture gave 0 to 3.6 g of methane per kilogram of biochar. Wet feedstock over 40 per cent moisture gave more than 500 g, so drying comes first.
documents.abstract: Earlier reports of 30 g of methane per kilogram of biochar had held back carbon certification for flame curtain kilns. New measurements show almost none from dry twigs plus leaves: 0 to 3.6 g per kilogram. Wet feedstock produced more than 500 g per kilogram, so preparation decides the carbon balance. Even with dry feedstock, aerosols (21 to 82 g) plus carbon monoxide (40 to 118 g) per kilogram were substantial. Careful feedstock choice, with after-combustion of the syn-gases, is probably needed to control those. Certification of low-tech biochar from dry twigs plus leaves should not be refused over methane. Other dry feedstocks have not been measured yet, so the result holds for the material tested.

documents.title: Biochar for durable carbon removal: soil erosion reduction as a key mechanism
documents.summary: A global meta-analysis plus long-term Mediterranean vineyard trials on biochar and erosion. Across studies biochar cut runoff by 25 per cent and soil erosion by 16 per cent. In vineyards at 4 per cent biochar by weight, erosion fell by up to 65 per cent, stored water rose by up to 73 per cent and soil organic carbon by 85 per cent. Less erosion means the carbon stays put.
documents.abstract: Gholamahmadi and Kammann argue that erosion control belongs in the case for biochar carbon removal, because eroded topsoil carries its carbon away. A global meta-analysis shows biochar reduces runoff by 25 per cent and soil erosion by 16 per cent on average. Long-term Mediterranean vineyard experiments at 4 per cent biochar by weight showed erosion rates down by up to 65 per cent, including gravel erosion, stored water up by up to 73 per cent (up to 300 per cent in dry conditions) and soil organic carbon up by 85 per cent. The paper proposes erosion reduction be built into monitoring, reporting and verification methods, plus the IPCC carbon removal methodology report due in 2027. Counting erosion would cut uncertainty about how long the carbon lasts. The vineyard figures come from specific sites. The 4 per cent rate is high for broadacre use.

documents.title: Soil carbon accrual and yield response to biochar and compost in a four-year organic field study
documents.summary: A four-year organic field trial in southern Germany applied biochar carbon each year at 0, 500, 1,000 or 2,000 kilograms a hectare, co-composted with manure and grass-clover. Soil carbon rose by up to 10 tonnes a hectare, matching the carbon applied. Yields moved little: slightly lower for spelt and wheat early on, slightly higher for maize in year four.
documents.abstract: Biochar carbon was applied every year for four years at 0, 500, 1,000 or 2,000 kilograms a hectare on an organically managed field in southern Germany. It went on alone or co-composted with solid manure plus grass-clover biomass at 120 kilograms of nitrogen a hectare. The rotation ran spelt, grass-clover ley, winter wheat, silage maize. Compost lifted yields in spelt, wheat, maize (spelt rose from 3.21 to 4.20 tonnes a hectare). Co-composted biochar trimmed spelt slightly in the first year, marginally cut winter wheat, did nothing for the ley, nudged maize up in year four. Soil organic carbon stocks rose with compost as well as biochar, by up to 10 tonnes a hectare, in line with the carbon applied. The case here is carbon storage, not yield.

documents.title: Long-Term Low-Rate Biochar Application Enhances Soil Organic Carbon Without Affecting Sorghum Yield in a Calcaric Cambisol
documents.summary: A 12-year field experiment on a calcaric Cambisol growing sorghum, with low-rate biochar applied each year alone or with NPK fertiliser. Soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, available phosphorus, available potassium all rose. Sorghum yield did not change in 2020 or 2022, nor did soil bacterial diversity.
documents.abstract: Four treatments were run on a calcaric Cambisol: an unfertilised control, biochar alone, NPK fertiliser alone, NPK with biochar. Biochar went on at a low rate each year for 12 years, with sorghum yield, plant nutrient uptake, soil bacteria measured in 2020 and 2022. Soil organic carbon was higher wherever biochar was used, in both years. After 12 years, total nitrogen, available phosphorus, available potassium were also higher, with or without fertiliser. Sorghum nitrogen and phosphorus uptake was unchanged, and in 2022 plant nitrogen under NPK with biochar was lower than under NPK alone. Bacterial diversity and composition did not shift. The soil gained carbon and nutrients, but the crop did not respond. On this alkaline soil the case for biochar rests on carbon storage, not yield. The feedstock is not given in the material available here.

documents.title: Sustainable biochar to mitigate global climate change
documents.authors: Woolf, Amonette, Street‐Perrott, Lehmann and Joseph
documents.summary: A global modelling estimate of what biochar could do for the climate, using only biomass from sustainable sources. Net emissions could fall by up to 1.8 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year, 12 per cent of current human emissions, or 130 billion tonnes over a century. Burning the same biomass for energy saves less, except where fertile soils are treated with coal as the fuel offset.
documents.abstract: Woolf, with a team of co-authors, estimated the maximum technical contribution of biochar to climate mitigation. Biomass supply was limited to sources that leave food security, habitat and soil conservation intact. Pyrolysis of this biomass, with the char stored in soil, was compared with burning it for bioenergy. The model counts carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. Annual net emissions could fall by up to 1.8 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (as carbon), which is 12 per cent of current human-caused emissions. Over a century the total reaches 130 billion tonnes. Biochar beats bioenergy from the same feedstock in almost every case. The exception is fertile soil amended while coal is the fuel being displaced. These are ceilings set by technical limits, not forecasts of what will be built. They rest on assumptions about land, feedstock supply and char stability. The paper remains a common reference point for global estimates.

documents.title: Review of the stability of biochar in soils: predictability of O:C molar ratios
documents.summary: A review of black carbon degradation studies, finding the oxygen to carbon molar ratio predicts how long biochar lasts. Biochar with a ratio below 0.2 has a half-life of at least 1000 years in soil. The ratio reflects pyrolysis temperature, feedstock and any later oxidation, so it works better than temperature alone.
documents.abstract: Spokas reviewed biochar and black carbon degradation studies to find a simple predictor of stability. Biochar is not one material. Its chemistry varies with pyrolysis conditions and parent material, and so does the rate at which microbes break it down. The review points to the molar ratio of oxygen to carbon as the best guide. A ratio below 0.2 gives a half-life of at least 1000 years. Unlike production temperature, the ratio also picks up effects of feedstock and of post-production conditioning or oxidation. Volatile matter content is a weaker indicator. The relationship is drawn from a patchwork of existing studies, not a single controlled test, so it suggests a threshold rather than a guarantee for any given batch.

documents.title: Biochar in climate change mitigation
documents.summary: A 2021 review in Nature Geoscience on biochar as a climate mitigation tool, led by Johannes Lehmann with Annette Cowie, Caroline Masiello, Dominic Woolf and others. It weighs how much carbon biochar can keep out of the atmosphere, then sets out what limits the claim. A common reference for credit-linked projects.
documents.abstract: Lehmann and co-authors including Cowie, Masiello, Kammann, Woolf and Amonette assess biochar as climate mitigation in Nature Geoscience, 2021. The central question is how much carbon biochar can lock away, for how long, set against emissions from making it, the fate of the feedstock otherwise, and effects on soil emissions. Biochar carbon is far more stable than the plant material it came from, which is the basis for carbon removal claims. Net benefit depends on feedstock supply, kiln emissions plus the way the char is used, so each project needs its own accounting. Farmers, councils or developers weighing a biochar project with carbon income will find it a common starting reference.

documents.title: Greenhouse Gas Inventory Model for Biochar Additions to Soil
documents.authors: Woolf, Lehmann, Ogle, Kishimoto‐Mo, McConkey and Baldock
documents.summary: A greenhouse gas accounting method for biochar added to mineral soils, designed for farm, supply chain, national or global use. Biochar carbon content runs from 7 per cent for gasified biosolids to 79 per cent for wood pyrolysed above 600 degrees Celsius. Of the carbon applied, 63 to 82 per cent remains unmineralised after 100 years at the global mean cropland temperature of 14.9 degrees.
documents.abstract: Published in Environmental Science and Technology in 2021, this method turns biochar carbon storage into numbers for inventories, life cycle assessments and carbon markets. It uses simple parameters with activity data a farm or inventory compiler already holds. Woolf, Lehmann, Ogle, Kishimoto-Mo, McConkey and Baldock built it from a broad review of empirical work. Biochar carbon content varies with feedstock and production conditions, from 7 per cent for gasified biosolids up to 79 per cent for wood pyrolysed above 600 degrees Celsius. After 100 years in soil at 14.9 degrees, 63 to 82 per cent of the initial carbon is still unmineralised. The persistence figure is tied to that mean temperature, so warmer sites need their own calculation. The method covers mineral soils only.

documents.title: BIOCHAR AS A TOOL TO REDUCE THE AGRICULTURAL GREENHOUSE-GAS BURDEN – KNOWNS, UNKNOWNS AND FUTURE RESEARCH NEEDS
documents.publisher: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management
documents.summary: A review of biochar and farm greenhouse gases, mainly nitrous oxide and methane. It covers the mechanisms behind lower emissions after soil application, then wider options: pyrolysing manure, biochar as a fertiliser carrier, as a composting additive, as a feed or manure treatment additive. Life-cycle greenhouse gas assessments on nutrient-rich waste streams are the largest gap.
documents.abstract: Farming and land use change have raised atmospheric nitrous oxide and methane, the two main non-carbon-dioxide greenhouse gases. This review asks whether biochar can cut them, and how. It covers the proposed mechanisms behind lower emissions from soil, then looks at four other uses: pyrolysing manure as a cleaner alternative to spreading it raw, biochar as a carrier for fertiliser placed near the plant, biochar as a composting additive, biochar in animal feed or manure treatment. The aim is a lower emissions footprint per unit of product. Life-cycle assessments of biochar on nutrient-rich biomass wastes are named as the largest research need. In practice, a farm cannot yet count the net emissions saving without that accounting.

documents.title: Agroforestry and biochar to offset climate change: a review
documents.summary: A 2012 review of agroforestry and soil-applied biochar as ways to offset farming emissions. Most agricultural soils have lost much of their original organic carbon. Both practices can store large amounts over the long run while raising productivity, with payments to land managers for carbon or ecosystem services named as the route to adoption.
documents.abstract: Review of two land-use options for cutting the climate cost of farming. Agricultural expansion has raised greenhouse gas emissions. Most farmed soils have lost a large share of their original organic carbon, turning them into sources of carbon dioxide, and they can also emit nitrous oxide or methane. Conservation practices help in places but cannot be applied under every physical or biotic condition. Of the options reviewed, agroforestry systems plus soil-applied biochar are rated best, since both store large amounts of carbon over the long run, raise productivity, support ecosystem services. Payments to land managers for storing carbon or delivering ecosystem services are put forward as the main strategy for adoption. The argument is made from the literature, with no new field data.

documents.title: Biochar for Soil Carbon Sequestration: Current Knowledge, Mechanisms, and Future Perspectives
documents.summary: A review of how biochar builds soil carbon, covering feedstock, pyrolysis conditions, the mechanisms behind storage. Biochar is a stable carbon pool, it holds soil aggregates together, it shifts microbial activity. Application rate and biochar quality vary widely between studies, so long-term field trials, standard protocols, economic assessments are still needed.
documents.abstract: Li and Tasnady review the evidence for biochar as a soil carbon store. They start with biochar properties and production methods, then show how feedstock, pyrolysis temperature change the char. Three mechanisms are covered: the char itself resists breakdown, it protects other soil carbon by forming stable aggregates, it alters the soil microbial community. The review also sets out limits. Biochar properties vary a great deal between feedstocks. The best application rate is not settled. Amendments added to biochar are discussed as a way to lift its effect. The conclusion calls for long-term field studies, standard protocols, economic assessments before wide adoption. It is a useful orientation paper, not a source of new field data.

documents.title: Biochar as a negative emission technology: A synthesis of field research on greenhouse gas emissions
documents.summary: A synthesis of field trials, not pots, on how biochar changes soil greenhouse gas emissions, covering studies published before 2022. Across studies biochar cut nitrous oxide by 18 per cent, methane by 3 per cent, while carbon dioxide rose 1.9 per cent. Paired with nitrogen fertiliser, it reduced nitrous oxide in 84 per cent of observations, so results depend on how it is used.
documents.abstract: Shrestha, Jacinthe, Lal and colleagues reviewed field studies published before 2022 on biochar and greenhouse gases, setting aside the laboratory, glasshouse, mesocosm work dominating earlier reviews. Effects ranged from a decrease to an increase to no change. On average biochar cut nitrous oxide by 18 per cent, methane by 3 per cent, and raised carbon dioxide by 1.9 per cent. Combined with nitrogen fertiliser, it lowered carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide in 61, 64, 84 per cent of observations. Combined with other amendments, the figures were 78, 92, 85 per cent. The spread of results means rate, depth, frequency of application remain unsettled. Long-term trials are needed to explain the discrepancies between sites.

documents.title: Biochar benefits carbon off-setting in blue-green infrastructure soils - A lysimeter study
documents.authors: Wang, Manning, Stirling, López‐Capél and Werner
documents.summary: A three-year outdoor lysimeter trial of urban landscaping soil, comparing wheat straw pellets with biochar made from the same straw, each at 2 per cent carbon by dry soil weight. Biochar soil held 28.8 per cent more organic carbon, 41.5 per cent more inorganic carbon, despite 17.2 per cent less vegetation. Estimated storage was 30 tonnes of carbon a hectare. Council stakeholders worried about production cost.
documents.abstract: Two large lysimeters were filled with urban landscaping soil, one amended with wheat straw pellets, one with biochar from wheat straw. Both received pellets mixed into the top 15 centimetres at an initial carbon input of 2 per cent of dry soil weight. Over three years the team tracked soil carbon, carbon isotopes, dissolved carbon in leachate, carbon dioxide emissions, plant growth, soil water, infiltration. Biochar soil held 28.8 per cent more organic carbon and 41.5 per cent more inorganic carbon than the straw soil, even with 17.2 per cent less vegetation. Isotope analysis confirmed the biochar carbon was more stable. Infiltration rates did not differ between the lysimeters. Wheat straw biochar could store an estimated 30 tonnes of carbon a hectare in city blue-green spaces. Interviews with institutional stakeholders found interest in carbon offsetting, with concern about producing biochar, applying it, the extra maintenance. Two lysimeters means no replication, so treat the figures as indicative.

documents.title: Scoping the potential for biochar in a Scottish context
documents.summary: A Scottish Government scoping report from 2026, built on a literature review and nine stakeholder interviews. A pilot with Scotland's Rural College in 2023 to 2025 lifted grassland yields by 16 to 18 per cent and arable yield by 34 per cent when biochar was applied with organic fertiliser, compared with fertiliser alone. It was a limited pilot.
documents.abstract: ClimateXChange, the Scottish Government's climate research centre, commissioned this scoping report from Logika Group and the University of Edinburgh. It reviews published evidence and draws on nine stakeholder interviews. Forestry residues are the most feasible feedstock for Scotland, and each tonne of woody biochar removes roughly 3 tonnes of carbon dioxide after production emissions. The Scotland's Rural College pilot (2023 to 2025) lifted grassland yields by 16 to 18 per cent, with arable yield up 34 per cent against fertiliser alone. Biochar also raised soil pH, which would help about half of Scottish agricultural soils. Nitrous oxide from mineral soils fell by 12 to 38 per cent. Application to peat should be avoided. Local yield data are thin, so most of the evidence comes from tropical or degraded soils. The report draws policy lessons from Denmark, Sweden and Germany.

documents.title: Biochar and Methane (IBI white paper)
documents.summary: A 2023 International Biochar Initiative white paper arguing biochar can cut methane from farms, landfills, oilfields. It cites a 2022 study in which composting manure with biochar reduced methane by 79 per cent compared with composting without it. The paper is advocacy built on cited work, not new trial data.
documents.abstract: The paper opens with the methane push at COP27 in Egypt in November 2022 and the Global Methane Pledge, signed by 130 countries in 2021, which aims to cut 2020 methane emissions by at least 30 per cent by 2030. It notes methane traps heat more than 25 times as strongly as carbon dioxide over its first 20 years. Biochar is presented as a way to keep methane out of the atmosphere, from dairy farms to landfills. The one farm figure given comes from a 2022 study: composting manure with biochar cut methane by 79 per cent against composting without it. Dairy or feedlot operators with manure heaps will want the original study for conditions, rates before banking that number.

documents.title: A review of evidence for the potential role of biochar to reduce net GHG emissions from New Zealand agriculture
documents.publisher: New Zealand Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Centre (Hedley and Hedley)
documents.summary: A 2020 report for the New Zealand Ministry for Primary Industries on whether biochar can cut net greenhouse gas emissions from the country's farms.
