It models forestry-residue biochar at 0.8 tonnes a hectare each year on dairy farms, then estimates how much of the carbon stays locked in the soil beyond 100 years. The result depends on the share of stable carbon in the char.
documents.abstract: Massey University's New Zealand Biochar Research Centre wrote this report of about 100 pages for the Ministry for Primary Industries. It reviews the evidence on biochar as a way to lower net greenhouse gas emissions from New Zealand agriculture. The modelling case is forestry-residue biochar spread on dairy farms at 0.8 tonnes a hectare each year, with the stable fraction (the share of biochar carbon lasting more than 100 years) used to work out the climate benefit. Other sections cover feedstock choice, test methods, soil water retention, plus the cost of making char from kiwifruit orchard prunings in a flame curtain kiln. A closing section looks at how biochar carbon could be counted in national greenhouse gas inventories under international guidance. It is a desk review and model, not a field trial.

documents.title: Conservation Practice Standard: Soil Carbon Amendment (Code 808)
documents.summary: An interim US Natural Resources Conservation Service standard, Soil Carbon Amendment (Code 808), dated September 2020 and marked under evaluation. It makes biochar eligible for conservation funding as a carbon amendment, specifying biochar above 60 per cent carbon where the aim is to cut nitrogen or phosphorus losses. Application is barred on slopes steeper than 15 per cent on cropland.
documents.abstract: Code 808 defines carbon-based amendments used to raise soil carbon, improving soil physical, chemical, biological properties. Stated purposes include organic matter, aggregate stability, soil organism habitat, plant productivity, irrigation water efficiency, lower emissions. It excludes native grasslands, plus fallow fields without a cover crop or cash crop. Operators must document the amendment's analysis, testing it in a credentialed laboratory when the supplier has none. They must not apply more nitrogen or phosphorus than the next crop will take up. Rates adding 100 pounds of nitrogen an acre (about 112 kilograms a hectare) or more trigger a full nutrient management plan. High carbon to nitrogen amendments need extra nitrogen to avoid immobilisation. No application in high wind, on frozen or saturated ground, near wetlands, or on slopes over 8 per cent on rangeland or forest. On grazing land, apply once, in autumn. This is an interim standard, not final.

documents.title: Biochar 2× Soil Carbon — extended field-trial measurements
documents.summary: Field measurements of soil carbon in biochar-treated ground over the trial period. Biochar roughly doubled measured soil carbon stocks in the treated layer, and the effect held across the measurements. Compost carbon breaks down within years, but biochar carbon stays for decades to centuries. This is relevant to anyone weighing an ACCU project.
documents.abstract: Field-trial measurements show biochar amendments roughly doubled soil carbon stocks in the treated layer over the trial duration. The effect held across the whole measurement period, because biochar does not decompose on agricultural timescales. That persistence separates it from compost or cover-crop carbon, which returns to the atmosphere within years. The practical reading is a one-time build of durable soil carbon, not a yearly input. For a farmer looking at ACCU project assessment, this is the kind of field-scale verification the persistence claim rests on.

documents.title: 2019 Refinement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines, Vol 4 Ch 2, Appendix 4: Method for Estimating the Change in Mineral Soil Organic Carbon Stocks from Biochar Amendments
documents.publisher: IPCC Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories
documents.summary: A five-page appendix to the 2019 Refinement of the IPCC Guidelines giving the basis for a Tier 1 method to count soil carbon from biochar in national inventories. It covers biochar added to mineral cropland or grassland over a 100-year frame. The fraction of carbon remaining after 100 years is 0.89 for pyrolysis above 600 degrees Celsius, 0.80 at 450 to 600, 0.65 at 350 to 450.
documents.abstract: The IPCC defines biochar as solid material made by heating biomass above 350 degrees Celsius with limited oxidant, by pyrolysis or gasification. Wildfire char is excluded. The method is top-down: tonnes of biochar added to mineral soil in the year, multiplied by its organic carbon content, multiplied by the fraction left after 100 years. Application rate is not needed. Soil type is not considered either, but compilers must record feedstock and pyrolysis temperature. Carbon content factors by pyrolysis include 0.77 for wood, 0.74 for nut shells, 0.65 for herbaceous material, 0.49 for rice husks, 0.38 for manure, 0.35 for biosolids; gasification gives much lower values. Persistence was fitted with a two-pool model to field plus laboratory studies, adjusted to 20 degrees Celsius, which is conservative. It does not apply to forest land, settlements, wetlands. The appendix says plainly it is a basis for future development, not complete guidance.

documents.title: The Big California Biochar Model (v1.1)
documents.summary: A 2019 statewide model from Pacific Biochar for turning California's excess forest biomass into biochar. At 10 per cent conversion it yields 1.43 million tonnes of char a year, for carbon drawdown, drought resilience and nitrogen conservation. It cites biochar cutting emissions from dairy manure composting by 27 to 32 per cent.
documents.abstract: Josiah Hunt and Charlie McIntosh of Pacific Biochar Benefit Corporation published version 1.1 of this model in September 2019. It starts from California's overstocked forests, where excess fuel loads feed catastrophic wildfires, and asks what happens if the biomass becomes biochar for valley farmland. The headline figures are about 1.5 million tonnes of biochar a year, applied to 160,000 acres at a rate lifting soil organic matter by 1 per cent. That adds 13,000 acre feet of water holding capacity each year, with carbon dioxide drawdown of roughly 9.2 million tonnes at $35 a tonne. It cites biochar cutting dairy manure composting emissions by 27 to 32 per cent. A biochar producer built this scenario, with a worksheet for testing the assumptions. It seeks partners to build the plants.

documents.title: Biochar as a strategy for sustainable land management and climate change mitigation (Global Symposium on Soil Organic Carbon)
documents.publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
documents.summary: A five-page paper for the FAO Global Symposium on Soil Organic Carbon in Rome, March 2017, by Cowie, Van Zwieten, Singh, de la Rosa. Biochar is most useful for rehabilitating degraded land, or low-fertility soils with defined constraints. A cited meta-analysis found soil nitrous oxide emissions fell by an average 54 per cent. Carbon stabilisation is certain; other effects vary widely.
documents.abstract: The paper reviews biochar for sustainable land management. Biochar properties depend on feedstock, pyrolysis temperature, post-production treatment. Biochar from woody material at higher temperature tends to be more stable. Negative priming, where biochar slows loss of native soil carbon, has been seen especially in clay-dominated soils. The nitrous oxide result is from Cayuela and colleagues in 2014, reflecting less substrate for denitrifying organisms, tied to the biochar's hydrogen to carbon ratio. Enriched biochar, made by adding minerals during pyrolysis or reacting the char with organic matter, has worked as a fertiliser. Limits to scale are biomass supply in drylands, high capital cost, few large production facilities, low awareness. Risks are polluting production sites, unsustainable biomass harvest, weak quality control, all manageable through certification, training, shared practice. Benefits are not universal, so biochar should be designed for a specific constraint.

documents.title: Biochar Systems for Smallholders in Developing Countries: Leveraging Current Knowledge and Exploring Future Potential for Climate-Smart Agriculture
documents.summary: A 231-page World Bank study with Cornell authors on biochar systems for smallholders in developing countries. Life-cycle case studies in Kenya, Vietnam, Senegal found greenhouse gas reductions of 0.4 to 2.0 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of dry feedstock. It also weighs soil benefits, social impacts, competing uses for biomass.
documents.abstract: Scholz, Sembres, Roberts, Whitman, Wilson, Lehmann reviewed the opportunities and risks of biochar systems in low-income farming. The report covers soil health, productivity, climate change effects, social impacts, competing uses of biomass. A survey of existing projects produced a typology of biochar systems, then three life-cycle assessments (Kenya, Vietnam, Senegal) put numbers on emissions: a net reduction of 0.4 to 2.0 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of dry feedstock, depending on the system. Later chapters cover economics, carbon markets, sociocultural barriers to adoption, then the role development institutions could play and what research is still needed. The report sets out where scientific opinion differs on biochar, trying to reconcile it. The settings are smallholder systems with cookstoves and local kilns, so transfer to Australian commercial farming is limited.

documents.title: Bio-char sequestration in terrestrial ecosystems: a review (Lehmann, Gaunt, Rondon)
documents.publisher: Cornell University (Lehmann lab), Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change
documents.summary: A 25-page foundational review by Johannes Lehmann, John Gaunt and Marco Rondon of Cornell University from 2006. Converting biomass to biochar retains about 50 per cent of the initial carbon, against 3 per cent after burning and under 10 to 20 per cent after 5 to 10 years of natural decomposition.
documents.abstract: Lehmann, Gaunt and Rondon published this review in Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change, and it set out the case for biochar as a carbon store. It compares what happens to the carbon in plant biomass under three fates. Burning leaves about 3 per cent of the carbon as ash. Natural decomposition leaves under 10 to 20 per cent after 5 to 10 years. Converting the biomass to char keeps about 50 per cent. It points to the age of charcoal in soils, including the Amazonian terra preta, as evidence that the carbon persists for centuries or longer. It predates most of today's field trials, so the retention figures are estimates from the literature of its time. Later work has refined them by feedstock and pyrolysis temperature.

documents.title: Permanence of soil applied biochar (Schmidt et al.)
documents.summary: An executive summary for Global Biochar Carbon Sink certification by Schmidt, Abiven, Hagemann and Meyer zu Drewer. Biochar made above 550 degrees Celsius with a molar H:C ratio below 0.4 holds 75 per cent of its carbon in stable polycyclic aromatic form, lasting more than 1000 years in any soil or climate. The other 25 per cent is semi-persistent, with a mean residence time of 50 to 100 years.
documents.abstract: Schmidt, Abiven, Hagemann and Meyer zu Drewer prepared this executive summary to support certification of biochar as a carbon sink. They set two conditions for high persistence: a pyrolysis temperature above 550 degrees Celsius and a molar H:C ratio below 0.4. Biochar meeting both is 75 per cent stable polycyclic aromatic carbon, which persists for more than 1000 years whatever the soil type or climate. The remaining 25 per cent is semi-persistent, with a mean residence time of 50 to 100 years depending on soil or climate. Soil-applied biochar thus holds two carbon pools with different permanence, each with its own sink value. For anyone planning to sell carbon credits, the practical consequence is that the production temperature and the H:C test, not the feedstock label, decide how much of the carbon can be counted. Check the current methodology of the registry you plan to use.

documents.title: The Carbon Farming Experiment (Lotz)
documents.summary: A long-term trial on 7 hectares of abandoned terraces at Ratanpur, Nepal, set up in 2023. Nine carbon farming systems, each built around the same number of coffee trees, are compared across 27 plots of 2,500 square metres. The interim report covers the first two years of establishment, so yield and carbon results are still to come.
documents.abstract: The Ithaka Institute set up the Ratanpur Carbon Farming Experiment in the mid-hills of Nepal, between Kathmandu and Pokhara, at 500 to 2,000 metres above sea level. Seven hectares of fallow terraces were divided into 27 plots of 2,500 square metres in a randomised block design: three blocks, each holding all nine systems. Every system carries coffee, planted two metres apart in rows six metres apart, with the gap given to fruit trees, lentils, ginger, broomgrass or bamboo. Baseline sampling in March 2023 took more than 400 soil samples to 60 centimetres. Weeds cleared from the terraces were pyrolysed in a Kon-Tiki kiln, about five tonnes of weeds giving one tonne of biochar, which was mixed with goat manure for the tree seedlings. Planting began with the monsoon in June 2023. The report covers design, baseline and establishment only. The trial is planned to run for three decades, so the comparison between systems will take years to read.

documents.title: Feedstock choice, pyrolysis temperature and type influence biochar characteristics: a comprehensive meta-data analysis review
documents.summary: A meta-analysis of about 5,400 papers with 50,800 data points on how feedstock, pyrolysis temperature and kiln type shape biochar. Feedstock has the biggest effect on properties. Temperatures above 500 degrees Celsius generally give half-lives beyond 1,000 years, while fast or slow pyrolysis matters little.
documents.abstract: Drawing on about 5,400 peer-reviewed papers, the work sorts biochar properties by feedstock, temperature, pyrolysis type. Fast against slow pyrolysis made little difference to physical or chemical traits. Temperature drove longevity: above 500 degrees Celsius, half-lives generally exceeded 1,000 years. Hotter pyrolysis also raised carbon content and specific surface area. Feedstock mattered most overall. Wood biochars had the greatest specific surface area, while crop and grass biochars had higher cation exchange capacity, which points to better nutrient holding in soil. Nutrient availability (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, iron, copper) could be predicted reasonably from feedstock plus total nutrient content. For a buyer, the practical point is to ask for the feedstock and the peak temperature before the price. Data come from lab and field papers of varying quality.

documents.title: Emissions and Char Quality of Flame-Curtain 'Kon Tiki' Kilns for Farmer-Scale Charcoal/Biochar Production
documents.authors: Cornelissen, Pandit, Taylor, Pandit, Sparrevik, Schmidt
documents.summary: Flame-curtain Kon-Tiki kilns tested for farmer-scale biochar production, across several feedstocks. The char averaged 76 per cent carbon, met the European Biochar Certificate threshold, and gave lower CO and NOx emissions than earth or retort kilns. A soil-pit kiln can cost as little as 30 euros. This is the documented source for the method.
documents.abstract: Cornelissen and colleagues measured char yield, carbon content, gas emissions from flame-curtain Kon-Tiki kilns across several feedstocks, then compared the results with traditional earth kilns, retort kilns, industrial pyrolysis reactors. Carbon content averaged 76 per cent (plus or minus 9). Char quality fully complied with the European Biochar Certificate, the strictest published standard. CO and NOx emissions were well below those of other small-scale methods. A soil-pit kiln can cost as little as 30 euros, against more than US$500,000 for an industrial reactor. Industrial reactors have negligible emissions but are out of reach for most farms. For Australian operators with storm debris, shelterbelt trimmings or orchard prunings, the paper documents on-site conversion instead of chipping, burning or hauling.

documents.title: Influence of pyrolysis temperature on physico-chemical properties of corn stover biochar and feasibility for carbon capture and energy balance
documents.authors: Rafiq, Bachmann, Rafiq, Shang, Joseph, Long
documents.summary: Corn stover biochar made across a range of pyrolysis temperatures, assessed for properties, carbon capture and energy balance. At 500 degrees the char kept 29 per cent of the feedstock mass at 64.5 per cent carbon. Potassium concentrated in the char as temperature rose.
documents.abstract: A team from Lanzhou University, with Stephen Joseph of the University of New South Wales, produced biochar from corn stover at different pyrolysis temperatures. They measured physical and chemical properties, then assessed carbon capture and energy balance. At 500 degrees Celsius the char retained 29 per cent of the feedstock mass, with a carbon content of 64.5 per cent. Potassium concentrated in the char as temperature rose. For a producer the trade is plain: hotter pyrolysis gives less char per tonne of stover but a char with different chemistry. This is a laboratory study of a single feedstock, so the figures will shift with other crop residues or a different kiln design. It is useful for choosing a target temperature.

documents.title: Biochar physicochemical properties: pyrolysis temperature and feedstock kind effects
documents.publisher: Reviews in Environmental Science and Bio/Technology
documents.summary: A review of how pyrolysis temperature and feedstock set biochar properties. Higher temperatures give more surface area, porosity, pH, ash and carbon, but lower cation exchange capacity. Chars from animal litter or solid waste have less surface area and carbon but more exchange capacity than chars from crop residue or wood. Lignin, cellulose and moisture in the raw biomass drive the difference.
documents.abstract: This review covers how the pyrolysis temperature and the feedstock decide what a biochar is like. Higher temperatures build a char with a well-developed surface area, high porosity, high pH, plus more ash and carbon. Cation exchange capacity and volatile matter drop, probably because more of the organic matter breaks down. Chars from animal litter and solid waste show lower surface area, carbon content, volatile matter, with higher exchange capacity, than chars from crop residue or woody biomass, even when made hot. Lignin, cellulose and moisture content in the raw material explain much of the gap. The review ties these properties to three uses: pollution remediation, liming of soil, carbon storage. For a buyer, the lesson is to ask for the feedstock and the production temperature before the price.

documents.title: Life-cycle assessment of biochar production systems in tropical rural areas: Comparing flame curtain kilns to other production methods
documents.summary: A life-cycle assessment of making and burying one kilogram of biochar in tropical rural settings, across five methods. Flame curtain kilns came out environmentally neutral, as sequestered carbon offset the production emissions. Earth mound kilns did worst, while cookstoves and gasifiers did best.
documents.abstract: The assessment compared flame curtain kilns, earth mound kilns, retort kilns with off-gas burning, pyrolytic cookstoves, gasifiers making electricity. It scored climate change, particulate matter, land use, minerals, fossil fuels together. Earth mound kilns had negative impacts from gas and aerosol emissions. Flame curtain kilns scored slightly better than retort kilns, far better than earth mound kilns, since they need no start-up wood, use little material, give off less gas. Over the full life cycle they were neutral: the carbon locked in the biochar offset what the kiln emitted. Cookstoves scored best through avoided firewood use, gasifiers through avoided grid electricity. On its own, flame curtain biochar gave no direct environmental gain, so its case rests on rural fit, low cost, soil benefits.

documents.title: Waste timber pyrolysis in a medium-scale unit: Emission budgets and biochar quality
documents.publisher: The Science of The Total Environment
documents.summary: Three batches of waste timber plus one of clean wood and leaves were run through a Pyreg-500 unit (750 tonnes a year) with after-combustion. Methane was zero, PAH-16 averaged 0.00002 g a kilogram of biochar. The waste timber biochar failed European Biochar Certificate limits for zinc and PAH.
documents.abstract: Emissions and biochar quality were measured for lightly contaminated waste timber in a medium-scale unit with after-combustion of pyrolysis gases. Mean emission factors per kilogram of biochar were carbon monoxide 7 g, non-methane volatile organics 0.86 g, particulates (PM10) 0.6 g, nitrogen oxides 0.65 g, with methane at zero. Total products of incomplete combustion came to 9 g. Emissions from waste timber matched the clean reference batch, except that PM10, volatile organics, PAH-16 were lower for waste timber. The biochar still missed both basic and premium European Biochar Certificate criteria because of zinc and PAH. Leachable metals were under 0.1 per cent of the total. Use is limited to applications outside soil, such as stabilising contaminants ex situ, with no role in improving fertility. A single unit, three timber batches.

documents.title: Systematic evaluation of pyrolysis processes and biochar quality in the operation of low-cost flame curtain pyrolysis kiln for sustainable biochar production
documents.summary: Real-time monitoring of a low-cost flame curtain kiln, logging emissions, temperatures, mass loss during operation. Adjusting how fast feedstock was layered onto the fire gave a 28 per cent biochar yield with 65 per cent fixed carbon. A continuous-scale pyrolysis unit gave comparable output from the same feedstock.
documents.abstract: The work tracked a flame curtain kiln as it ran, logging emissions, temperatures, mass loss, then sampled the biochar thoroughly afterwards. Operators who changed the rate at which feedstock was layered on got a yield of 28 per cent by weight with fixed carbon at 65 per cent. A continuous-scale pyrolysis unit gave comparable output from the same feedstock. The result makes the case for written operating guidelines: the kiln is simple, but the product depends on how it is fed. For a farm or a council making its own biochar, the person at the kiln matters as much as the kiln.

documents.title: Emerging trends in appropriate kiln designs for small-scale biochar production in low to middle income countries
documents.summary: A review of small-scale kilns for low and middle income countries, sorted into flame curtain, drum, cookstove, retort, masonry designs. Yields range from 10 to 46 per cent, with fixed carbon from 26 to 87 per cent. Drum retort kilns suit most low-income settings.
documents.abstract: Kilns are grouped into flame curtain kilns, drum kilns, top-lit updraft cookstoves, retort kilns, masonry kilns, a few others. Across the designs, yield efficiency ran from 10 to 46 per cent, fixed carbon in the biochar from 26 to 87 per cent, calorific value from 14 to 40 MJ a kilogram. Direct comparison is difficult, as some data are missing, many experiments use only one feedstock. A qualitative comparison puts drum retort kilns ahead for most low-income applications. The review expects better kilns could come from combining features of different designs, nearer to the theoretical maximum yield with cleaner burns. Its value for a reader is a map of what each kiln type delivers, with the gaps in the evidence marked.

documents.title: Methane Emissions From Flame Curtain Pyrolysis (Kon‐Tiki)
documents.summary: Flame curtain kilns (Kon-Tiki) were compared with open burning of five crop residues, with flue gas measured for CO2, CO, methane and propane. Kon-Tiki gave lower CO and methane than open burning, most clearly for wheat straw. Dry feedstock at or below 15 per cent moisture kept methane under 5 grams per kilogram of biochar, while wet feedstock gave up to ten times more.
documents.abstract: Five crop residues were burned in a flame curtain kiln (Kon-Tiki) across a range of moisture contents, then compared with open burning, the usual baseline for crop residues. Temperature plus flue gas (CO2, CO, methane, propane) were logged continuously, with emission factors worked out from a carbon mass balance. Kon-Tiki produced less CO and methane than open burning, with the biggest gap for wheat straw. Feedstock at 15 per cent moisture or below gave methane under 5 grams per kilogram of biochar. Feedstock at 25 per cent or above gave up to ten times as much. Flue gas temperature explained methane best, with emissions falling exponentially as the flame got hotter. For anyone making biochar in a kiln on farm, the rules are simple: dry the residue first, then keep the burn hot. Carbon credit claims rest on getting this right.

documents.title: Operational performance and cost–performance trade-offs of low-cost, farmer-scale biochar kilns
documents.summary: Sixty batch trials of three low-cost kilns on Midwestern US agroforestry residues. Biochar yield averaged 22.3 per cent in an open flame-curtain kiln, 31.5 per cent in a controlled-draft version, 46.5 per cent in an indirect-heat retort. Peak temperature explained 92 per cent of yield variation. Build costs ran from US$360 to US$1,280.
documents.abstract: Three kilns a farmer could build locally were tested over sixty batches (five per kiln and feedstock combination) on four agroforestry residues from the US Midwest. Type A was an open flame-curtain kiln (Traditional Oregon Kiln), Type B a controlled-draft flame-curtain kiln, Type C an indirect-heat retort. Mean yields were 22.3, 31.5 and 46.5 per cent, at mean peak temperatures of 510, 460 and 385 degrees Celsius. Kiln design explained 92.4 per cent of yield variance, while feedstock plus its interaction with the kiln explained under 1 per cent. Yield was most repeatable in Type B (coefficient of variation 6.8 per cent) and Type C (7.6 per cent), least in Type A (13.2 per cent). Build cost rose with control, from about US$360 for Type A to US$1,280 for Type C. The cheapest kiln wastes the most feedstock, so paying more buys more biochar per tonne of residue.

documents.title: Converting shelterbelt biomass to biochar — practical guide
documents.summary: A practical guide to turning shelterbelt trees and woody waste into biochar on the farm, using flame-curtain methods. It covers feedstock preparation, kiln operation, expected yield, and fitting production around grazing or cropping. Wilson's work is the usual source for the 70 to 80 per cent cut in biomass weight, which shrinks a cleared shelterbelt to a few pallets of char.
documents.abstract: Kelpie Wilson documents how to convert shelterbelt and other woody-waste biomass into biochar using on-farm flame-curtain methods. The guide moves through feedstock preparation, kiln operation, yield expectations, plus how production fits around grazing or cropping work. Its main figure is the 70 to 80 per cent reduction in biomass weight, quoted widely in biochar discussions. In practice it means a shelterbelt that takes a day to clear, or a pile of storm debris, becomes a volume of char small enough to sit on a single pallet. Wilson has long worked on flame-curtain production, the same approach used on Australian farms by Possible Agriculture. Written for farmers weighing up their own kiln.

documents.title: Biochar Pyrolysis Plant Guidelines
documents.summary: A 32-page technical guide from the International Biochar Initiative, version 1.1 of June 2010, on the components and design of pyrolysis plants for biochar. Jane Lynch with Stephen Joseph wrote it. It points to sound engineering practice, professional engineers, rather than offering a full safety manual.
documents.abstract: The guidelines open with the components of a pyrolysis plant, then walk through the design phase: a functional specification, a process flow diagram with mass balances, piping diagrams, hazard review (HAZOP), detailed design with costing. The text is explicit about its limits. It is advice on equipment design and testing, not an exhaustive review of hazards. The International Biochar Initiative accepts no responsibility for outcomes, recommends professional engineers for system design. Cordner Peacocke, Robert Brown, KC Das reviewed it. The document is 2010 vintage, so check emissions rules plus current kiln designs before relying on it. It suits anyone weighing up whether to build or buy a plant.

documents.title: Kon-Tiki: the democratization of biochar production
documents.summary: Hans-Peter Schmidt and Paul Taylor describe the Kon-Tiki, a flame-curtain kiln for making biochar on the farm. With some charmaking skill, a farmer can produce a cubic metre of biochar in an afternoon. Commercial biochar will stay dear while construction, electronics, textiles and other industries compete for it, so on-site production is the cheaper route for small farmers.
documents.abstract: Schmidt and Taylor present the Kon-Tiki as a simple invention allowing any farmer or gardener to make enough high quality biochar for their own use. The flame-curtain design builds on lessons from open-fire charmaking. With a reasonable investment plus some know-how, a cubic metre of biochar can be produced in one afternoon. Their reasoning is economic: industrially produced biochar may become a key raw material for the bio-based economy, with construction, electronics, paper making, wastewater treatment, textiles, 3D printing all competing for supply, so commercial biochar will remain an expensive input for farmers. They see on-site production as the way for small farmers to close the production loop. Note the article is a design description. Emissions, quality control and local rules on open burning differ between sites, so check these before building one in Australia.

documents.title: Methane emissions from artisanal biochar production
documents.summary: Methane measured from flame curtain (Kon-Tiki) kilns across a range of feedstocks and moisture contents, against open burning of the same biomass. Methane fell by 36 per cent on average in the kiln. Dry woody feedstock gave around 5 kilograms of methane per tonne of biochar, so drying material before it goes in is the main control.
documents.abstract: Flame curtain pyrolysis burns the gas from layered feedstock in an open kiln, the Kon-Tiki. Methane and carbon monoxide escape when the flame misses some gas. This white paper measured methane, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide from the kiln for several feedstocks and moisture classes: dry (15 per cent or less), semi-moist (16 to 24 per cent) and moist (25 per cent or more). Against open burning of the same biomass, the kiln cut methane by 36 per cent and carbon monoxide by 35 per cent on average. Dry and semi-moist feedstock came in well below the 30 kilograms of methane per tonne of biochar assumed in the Global Artisan C-Sink Standard. Woody biomass under 25 per cent moisture averaged about 5 kilograms, semi-moist wheat straw reached 20, and moist feedstock gave 30 to 40. The very high figures reported earlier for wet twigs and leaves were not reproduced. The work is published in Global Change Biology Bioenergy (2026).

documents.title: Quantitative Assessment of the Effect of Agency-Led Prescribed Burns and Cultural Burns on Soil Properties in Southeastern Australia
documents.authors: Murramarang Country, Davis, Simmons, Snelson, Channell, Haynes, Deutscher, Brook, Dosseto
documents.summary: A trial on the NSW South Coast comparing cultural cool-fire burns, agency prescribed burns and unburnt controls. Soil organic carbon reached 6.5 per cent under cool-fire burns, against 4.3 per cent on prescribed burns and 3.8 per cent on controls. Nitrogen stocks were 1.6 times the unburnt baseline. Cooler fire leaves char in the soil.
documents.abstract: A trial on the NSW South Coast compared three regimes: agency-led hazard-reduction burns, cool-fire cultural burns, unburnt control sites. Soil organic carbon was 6.5 per cent (plus or minus 0.4) under cool-fire burns, 4.3 per cent under prescribed burns and 3.8 per cent on the unburnt controls. Nitrogen stocks under cool-fire sites were 1.6 times the unburnt baseline. The mechanism is temperature: cooler fire preserves charred biomass in the soil profile instead of combusting it to CO2. The 1.7 times difference in carbon between cool-fire and unburnt sites shows how much char survives at the right temperature. Flame-curtain biochar production applies the same principle in a controlled form. Cool-fire burning on country is uneven across a landscape, while a kiln gives a measured, repeatable output.

documents.title: Does Biochar Improve Establishment of Tree Seedlings in Saline Sodic Soils?
documents.authors: Drake, Cavagnaro, Cunningham, Jackson and Patti
documents.summary: Glasshouse trial in South Australia testing 5 tonnes a hectare of Acacia pycnantha biochar on saline sodic soil with Eucalyptus viminalis, Acacia mearnsii seedlings. After 108 days biochar raised Eucalyptus height in the highly saline sodic soil. Effects on plant nutrition differed by soil and species. One simulated season in pots, not paddocks.
documents.abstract: Drake, Cavagnaro, Cunningham with colleagues asked whether biochar helps tree seedlings establish on saline sodic soil, a common reforestation problem. Biochar from Acacia pycnantha was applied at 5 tonnes a hectare, against no biochar, to low, moderate and high saline sodic soils (electrical conductivity 4.75, 27.6 and 49.4 dS per metre; exchangeable sodium 6.9, 29.3 and 45.1 per cent). Eucalyptus viminalis plus Acacia mearnsii tubestock grew for 108 days. In the highly saline sodic soil, biochar increased E. viminalis height, reduced its root to shoot ratio, lowered manganese, nitrogen and sulfur in the plant. In the low saline sodic soil, leaf boron rose in E. viminalis, while phosphorus, potassium and sulfur rose in A. mearnsii. The trial is a single glasshouse season, so field establishment is untested.

documents.title: The effect of biochar management on soil and plant community properties in a boreal forest
documents.summary: A replicated field experiment on 0.05-hectare plots in boreal forest in northern Sweden, with biochar, soil mixing, both, or neither. After two growing seasons biochar raised net nitrogen mineralisation but left most soil microbial measures, respiration, ground vegetation almost untouched. Soil mixing cut ground cover and microbial activity, and biochar softened some of those effects.
documents.abstract: The trial used a randomised block design on 0.05-hectare plots in northern Sweden, with six plots per treatment: control, soil mixing only, biochar only, biochar plus mixing. After two growing seasons, biochar raised net soil nitrogen mineralisation whether or not the soil was mixed. It did not change most microbial community measures or soil respiration. Vegetation barely responded, apart from a small drop in species richness of the ground layer. Mixing the soil cut graminoid and total ground cover, reduced net nitrogen mineralisation, lifted seedling survival of Scots pine, lifted seed germination of four tree species. Where biochar was added too, the harsher effects of mixing on nutrients and microbes were milder. Biochar can store carbon in boreal forest soil, and may pair well with the scarification used in site preparation. Two seasons is short for a forest, so long-term tree growth is untested.

documents.title: Soil greenhouse gas, carbon content, and tree growth response to biochar amendment in western United States forests
documents.summary: Field trials in Idaho, Montana and Oregon forests with biochar at 0, 2.5 or 25 tonnes a hectare spread on the soil surface. Soil carbon rose by 41 per cent. Tree growth, methane, carbon dioxide fluxes were unchanged, with nitrous oxide not detected at these unfertilised, nitrogen-limited sites. Biochar did no harm to trees or soil.
documents.abstract: Sarauer, Page-Dumroese, Coleman with colleagues tested biochar in managed forest in the western United States, where thinning overstocked stands produces residual biomass suitable for pyrolysis. Sites in Idaho, Montana, Oregon received 0, 2.5 or 25 tonnes a hectare on the soil surface. Carbon dioxide, methane fluxes changed with season but not with biochar. Nitrous oxide was not detected, which fits unfertilised, nitrogen-limited forest soil. Soil carbon content rose by 41 per cent, while tree growth was unaffected. The team concludes biochar can be used in forests to store carbon without detrimental effects on trees or soils. The trials were short, so long-term tree response is untested. Tree growth did not improve, so the case rests on carbon storage and low risk, not on productivity.

documents.title: Biochar Effects on Two Tropical Tree Species and Its Potential as a Tool for Reforestation
documents.summary: A six-month nursery trial with two tropical tree species, Guazuma crinita and Terminalia amazonia, 240 seedlings each, under six biochar and fertiliser treatments. Biochar at 1 tonne a hectare plus fertiliser gave the best height, diameter, leaf number, biomass in both species. Biochar at 5 tonnes lowered early survival, as did fertiliser alone.
documents.abstract: Seedlings of an early successional species (Guazuma crinita) and a late one (Terminalia amazonia), 240 of each, were grown for six months under six treatments of biochar and fertiliser. Survival was highest at 1 tonne a hectare of biochar. Treatments with fertiliser, or with biochar at 5 tonnes a hectare, lowered survival of both species against the control. Biochar plus fertiliser raised height, stem diameter, leaf number, above-ground biomass, root biomass above every other treatment. The 1 tonne rate outperformed 5 tonnes, with or without fertiliser. Guazuma, the early successional species, responded more strongly than Terminalia. The combination could cut afforestation costs against conventional fertilising while giving better growth. This is a nursery experiment, so field survival after planting out remains to be shown, and the slightly lower early survival deserves attention.

documents.title: Amending mine tailing cover with compost and biochar: effects on vegetation establishment and metal bioaccumulation in the Finnish subarctic
documents.summary: Two field experiments on old iron mine tailings at Rautuvaara in northern Finland, where nothing had grown since 1989. Spruce biochar added to a till and composted sewage sludge mix raised grass biomass by 71 to 250 per cent over two growing seasons. Metal uptake in the plants stayed negligible.
documents.abstract: Cover till placed over closed iron mine tailings in the Finnish subarctic was amended with composted sewage sludge, with or without spruce (Picea abies) biochar. It was planted with Scots pine, a willow (Salix myrsinifolia), a grass mix of red fescue, perennial ryegrass, white clover. Plant survival and growth were tracked over two growing seasons. Composted sludge markedly lifted growth, and was needed wherever only transported till was used. Biochar added to the till-sludge mix raised grass biomass by 71 to 250 per cent. Pine and willow showed no biochar response in the first seasons. Metal accumulation in the cover plants was negligible. Cool temperatures and a short growing period are part of this site, so results suit boreal conditions, with the grass response the main finding.

documents.title: Positive Effects of Biochar on the Degraded Forest Soil and Tree Growth in China: A Systematic Review
documents.authors: Zhang, Zhang, Niu, Jiang and Sun
documents.summary: A systematic review of 96 Chinese studies, from pots to field plots, on biochar in degraded forest soil. Biochar generally improved compacted, acidified or eroding soil by raising porosity plus pH, strengthening erosion resistance, cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Trees grew better in most cases. Long-term effects remain thinly studied.
documents.abstract: Researchers at Nanjing Forestry University reviewed 96 studies from China, ranging from pot experiments to field investigations, on biochar made from agroforestry waste or biomass and applied to degraded forest soil. Biochar generally helped restore soils affected by compaction, acidification or erosion. The main effects were higher porosity, higher pH, better resistance to erosion, lower greenhouse gas emissions. Tree growth improved in most of the cases reviewed. The reviewers attribute this to nutrients supplied directly by the biochar, better soil physical and chemical properties, stronger root nutrient uptake, more room for roots. Mechanisms and long-term effects are the weakest parts of the evidence. Because the review covers Chinese studies only, the results suit similar acid, degraded soils best. Alkaline or fertile forest soils may respond differently.

documents.title: Biochar in agriculture – A systematic review of 26 global meta‐analyses
documents.summary: A review of 26 meta-analyses published since 2016 on biochar in agriculture, covering yield, root biomass, water use efficiency, microbial activity, soil carbon and greenhouse gas emissions. All 26 report an overall beneficial effect on every agronomic parameter studied. Poor biochar characterisation remains a gap. Low-quality biochars may explain the adverse results in individual studies.
documents.abstract: Agronomic biochar research grew from fewer than 100 publications in 2010 to more than 15,000 by the end of 2020. Schmidt and colleagues selected 26 rigorous meta-analyses published since 2016, covering yield, root biomass, water use efficiency, microbial activity, soil organic carbon, greenhouse gas emissions. Every one reported a beneficial overall effect on all the agronomic parameters it examined. Uses range from animal feed to manure treatment, fertiliser components, direct soil application. Because the carbon in biochar was fixed from the atmosphere by plants, applying it also removes carbon dioxide, so farm benefits are what make wide adoption workable. Basic biochar analysis is still not standardised. Adverse results inside the meta-analyses may come from low-quality biochars with high contaminants, high salinity or incomplete pyrolysis, which would not pass certification.

documents.title: Pyroligneous Acid Effects on Crop Yield and Soil Organic Matter in Agriculture—A Review
documents.summary: A review of 65 studies on pyroligneous acid (wood vinegar), with 171 yield sets across 33 crops. Yield rose 21 per cent on average, biomass 25 per cent, reaching 31 per cent at the optimum concentration of 0.5 to 1 per cent. Yield falls above that range.
documents.abstract: Pyroligneous acid is a liquid co-product of pyrolysis. The review pooled 65 studies covering 33 crops in six plant groups, with 171 yield and 123 biomass data sets. Positive, curved responses appeared from concentrations as low as 0.1 per cent, peaking around 0.5 to 1 per cent, with gains continuing up to 6 to 11 per cent depending on how it was applied. Beyond that yield declined, which suggests a herbicidal effect. Average yield gain was 21 per cent, biomass 25 per cent, 31 per cent at the optimum rate. Gains were largest under salt, drought or disease pressure, with no difference between plant groups. Soil organic matter rose slightly, on very little data. Experiments typically ran one or two seasons, with applied rates and composition reported inconsistently, so long-term effects are unknown.

documents.title: How biochar works, and when it doesn't: A review of mechanisms controlling soil and plant responses to biochar
documents.authors: Joseph, Cowie, Van Zwieten, Bolan, Budai, Buss, Cayuela, Graber, Ippolito, Kuzyakov, Luo, Ok, Palansooriya, Shepherd, Stephens, Weng, Lehmann
documents.summary: A 34-page review of how biochar changes soils and plants, written by a large international team. At 1 per cent application it reports plant productivity up 10 to 42 per cent, plant-available phosphorus up to 4.6 times, non-CO2 greenhouse gases down 12 to 50 per cent, and plant heavy-metal uptake down 17 to 39 per cent. It also covers when biochar does not work.
documents.abstract: This review draws together the mechanisms behind biochar's effects on soils and plants, with a long author list from research groups across the world. Its headline figures apply at 1 per cent biochar application: plant productivity up 10 to 42 per cent, plant-available phosphorus up to 4.6 times, non-CO2 greenhouse gas emissions (nitrous oxide plus methane) down 12 to 50 per cent, and heavy-metal concentrations in plant tissue down 17 to 39 per cent. Just as useful, it sets out the conditions under which biochar gives no benefit, which matters as much as the gains when an agronomist, council or auditor is judging a proposal. The 12 to 50 per cent figure is the correct source for emissions claims once labelled as volatile organic compound reductions.

documents.title: Environmental Benefits of Biochar
documents.summary: An overview of a 2010 conference session and the special collection built from it. The papers cover biochar's effects on nutrient leaching, contaminant availability, carbon storage, greenhouse gas emissions and crop growth on weathered or degraded soils. Contributions map what is known, the gaps, and future research needs.
documents.abstract: This introduces a special collection built from a 2010 American Society of Agronomy and Soil Science Society of America session, with papers from other biochar conferences held that year. The common aim is better environmental quality: less nutrient leaching, lower bioavailability of contaminants, carbon sequestration, fewer greenhouse gas emissions, higher crop productivity on highly weathered or degraded soils. Individual papers lay out the current knowledge base, the gaps, the research needs. It reports no trial data of its own, no application rates. The main point for a reader is that biochars can be tailored for a specific job, so a char chosen for filtering water would differ from one chosen for a depleted pasture. It is a 2012 snapshot, early in the field.

documents.title: Biochar as a tool for the improvement of soil and environment
documents.summary: A 2023 review of recent biochar work on soil, crops and pollution control. Biochar improved fertility, nutrient retention, water holding, with the clearest crop gains in coarse-textured soils. It also stores carbon in the soil, though the risks need weighing before use.
documents.abstract: Review published in Frontiers in Environmental Science in 2023, drawn from recent literature rather than new trials. Biochar is a stable, carbon-rich material with a porous structure, which explains its effect on fertility, nutrient retention and water holding capacity. Plant growth and yield gains are tied to greater microbial activity, strongest in coarse-textured soils. Biochar also works as a sorbent, pulling heavy metals, organic contaminants or excess nutrients out of soil and water. On climate, it stores atmospheric carbon, improves soil quality, lowers some greenhouse gas emissions. Results shift with feedstock, production conditions, soil type, rate. The review calls for careful evaluation of risks before wide use. Read it as a map of what biochar can do, not a rate recommendation.

documents.title: A Review of Biochar Properties and Their Utilization in Crop Agriculture and Livestock Production
documents.summary: A review of a decade of research on biochar in crop and livestock farming. Most work treats biochar as a soil amendment or remediation tool, with better soil quality, higher yields, stored carbon. Composting with biochar and pyrolysing farm waste, manure included, are also well studied. Odour control from manure and feeding biochar to animals are the gaps.
documents.abstract: This review sums up ten years of research on biochar in crop agriculture and livestock production. Most studies treat it as a soil amendment or a remediation tool, with better soil quality, higher crop yields, carbon stored in the soil. Two other strands are well covered: composting agricultural waste with biochar added, then making biochar from agricultural waste, manure included. The properties of biochar suit other uses too, and the review flags two where evidence is thin. One is cutting odorous emissions from manure. The other is feeding biochar to animals. No single trial or rate is reported. For a livestock operator, the manure and feed uses are the open questions, so treat early claims there with care.

documents.title: Biochar for ameliorating soil fertility and microbial diversity: From production to action of the black gold
documents.summary: A 2024 review of production methods for biochar, with effects on soil fertility, microbes. Newer routes such as hydrothermal or retort carbonisation run at lower temperatures yet give high yields. Biochar's alkalinity eases soil acidity, while its pores give microbes a home.
documents.abstract: Review published in iScience on how biochar is made, how it behaves, what it does in soil. Newer production methods, including hydrothermal and retort carbonisation, run at lower minimum temperatures but still give high yields. They improve heating value, oxygen functionality and carbon content over traditional methods. Temperature, feedstock type and moisture content shape the product. Surface functional groups make biochar alkaline, which addresses soil acidity. Its porous structure lets microbes attach, which affects soil health and nutrient availability. Reported plant benefits include better root morphology, photosynthetic pigments, enzyme activities, growth, even under salinity stress. The review closes by calling for more research, with testing specific to each application, since a biochar suited to one soil or crop may not suit another.

documents.title: A Critical-Systematic Review of the Interactions of Biochar with Soils and the Observable Outcomes
documents.summary: A critical-systematic review of biochar and soil interactions covering physical, chemical and biological properties and plant performance. Biochar surface area, charge and nutrient content decide its role in the soil. How much changes depends on the soil it goes into, so the pairing matters.
documents.abstract: This review works through what biochar does in soil at the particle level, because many meta-analyses sum up effects without separating biochar type from soil type. It covers physical, chemical and biological properties, then functions such as plant performance and nutrient cycling. Biochar interacts with minerals, organic matter, gases, liquids and nutrients, and shifts the microbial community. Its specific surface area, surface charge and nutrient content determine its role. The size of the change depends on soil properties, so biochar and soil need matching before an application. Biochar generally improved soil and plant performance. No single rate or feedstock wins, since the answer depends on the pairing. It is a guide for choosing a product for a particular paddock.

documents.title: European Biochar Certificate: Guidelines for a Sustainable Production of Biochar (v10.5E)
documents.summary: The European Biochar Certificate guideline, version 10.5E of August 2025, runs to about seventy pages. It sets rules for feedstock, pyrolysis, sampling, lab testing, labelling, inspection. It also defines the EBC-Feed class for biochar in animal feeding, which needs pure plant feedstock made above 500 degrees Celsius.
documents.abstract: Written by the Ithaka Institute with Agroscope and several European universities, this is the basis for biochar certification in Europe. Producers register each production batch, which lasts at most 365 days. Pyrolysis temperature and feedstock mix may not drift more than 20 per cent within a batch. The molar H/Corg ratio must sit below 0.7 for standard grades, or below 0.4 for feed grade. Producers declare nutrients, pH, salt, water content, with limits on heavy metals, PAHs, PCBs, dioxins. Pyrolysis gases must be captured or burned. Feed-grade biochar needs approval as a feed producer, impurities removed, a fluorine limit of 150 milligrams per kilogram. Companies that only process or trade certified biochar follow a separate chapter. Buyers can check a product against a published quality basis.

documents.title: European Biochar Certificate Standard 10.5E
documents.summary: The European Biochar Certificate Standard, version 10.5E of September 2025, runs to fifty-four pages. It defines the certification classes (Feed, Agro, Urban, Materials, Basic) with limit values for each. It is the shorter rulebook beside the full EBC guidelines, written for producers who need the pass marks without the technical detail behind them.
documents.abstract: This standard is the certification document for biochar producers or processors, drawn from the same Ithaka Institute authors as the EBC guidelines. Contents run from the definition of biochar through the certification classes, feedstock rules, batch registration, sampling, biochar properties. Each batch must declare organic carbon, nutrients, pH, salt, bulk density, water content, water holding capacity. The molar H/Corg ratio must sit below 0.7, or below 0.4 for feed grade, with O/Corg below 0.4. Heavy metal, PCB, dioxin, PAH limits apply. Further chapters cover pyrolysis, work safety, the feed additive class, certification of processing companies, labelling. Feed-grade biochar must come from pure plant biomass, made above 500 degrees Celsius. It is a European scheme, so Australian buyers should read it beside local rules.

documents.title: A Report on the Value of Biochar and Wood Vinegar
documents.authors: ANZBI (Australia and New Zealand Biochar Industry Group)
documents.summary: An industry overview of biochar production and use across Australia and New Zealand, written in 2020. It sets out the economic, agronomic and carbon-market context, with a section on wood vinegar, a pyrolysis byproduct. It carries no headline trial numbers. Councils weighing biochar can use it to show the sector is established.
documents.abstract: A 2020 report from the Australia and New Zealand Biochar Industry Group. It surveys biochar production and use across both countries, with the economic, agronomic and carbon-market background. Wood vinegar gets its own treatment. This liquid byproduct of pyrolysis has uses in agriculture as well as remediation, which most operators overlook. The report is not the place to look for headline yield or carbon figures. Its value is breadth: it shows where the industry sat in 2020, with the picture pulled together in one place. Councils weighing biochar as a procurement category will find the policy framing useful. So will grant assessors asking whether biochar is a real sector in Australia.

documents.title: Australian Biochar for Soils Standard: ANZBI Draft for Comment
documents.summary: A draft Australian standard for biochar used on soils, released for comment in July 2019 by the ANZBI task force of Joseph, Cowie, Bagnall and colleagues. It was written as the starting point for a Standards Australia process. It draws on the Australian Compost Standard AS4454, the European Biochar Certificate, the IBI product guidelines.
documents.abstract: The draft sets out scope, product classification, process criteria, physical and chemical requirements, toxicity tests, testing, packaging. Process criteria include heating and cooling temperature. Optional plant tests sit beside the required toxicity tests. The task force built it on AS4454-2012, the 2019 European Biochar Certificate guidelines, the IBI Standardised Product Definition for biochar used in soil. The preface notes that local, state or federal rules not cited may add requirements, and a production facility may need site approval before it is built. It went to ANZBI members first, then to Standards Australia as the basis for a possible national standard. It is a draft, so check whether a later version has replaced it before quoting limits.

documents.title: Biochar Field Trial Guide
documents.summary: A 2009 International Biochar Initiative guide by Julie Major to designing and running an on-farm biochar trial. It takes the grower through seven steps, from forming a hypothesis to analysing results. Control plots, replication and randomisation get the most attention.
documents.abstract: The guide sets out seven steps: generating hypotheses, planning the design, planning measurements, sampling, carrying out the trial, then analysis. Its design section explains why a trial needs control plots, replicated plots, a randomised layout, using commonly adopted layouts. A measurement section covers yield sampling as well as soil sampling. All figures and tables in the guide are fictitious examples for illustration, not real data. Photos show a maize trial in New York, plus lump charcoal prepared for soil in Honduras. It is version 1.2 from April 2009, reviewed by the IBI Science Advisory Committee. Anyone testing biochar on their own paddock should read it first, since an unreplicated strip without a control tells you very little.

documents.title: Biochar for Environmental Management (Lehmann and Joseph, book proof)
documents.summary: The 2009 reference book edited by Johannes Lehmann of Cornell University and Stephen Joseph, which runs to 438 pages in this proof. It opens with the case that biochar has properties making it a valuable soil amendment. The chapters cover how char forms, how it is made, what it does in soil, and where it sits in climate policy.
documents.abstract: Biochar for Environmental Management was the first full-length reference on the subject. Johannes Lehmann at Cornell University and Stephen Joseph edited it, with chapters from soil scientists, engineers and climate policy specialists. It opens by describing biochar as a material with unusual properties, which make it a valuable soil amendment. The book draws on the dark, carbon-rich terra preta soils of the Amazon as the historical model for what char can do over centuries. Much of the field evidence it relied on has since been overtaken by newer trials, so the book is best read for the foundations: how char forms, what it is made of, and why it persists in soil. This copy is the publisher's proof.

documents.title: IBI Biochar Standards: Standardized Product Definition and Product Testing Guidelines for Biochar That Is Used in Soil (V2.1)
documents.summary: Version 2.1 of the IBI Biochar Standards, dated 23 November 2015, the product definition and testing guidelines for biochar used in soil. It gave producers, buyers a basis for quality claims, laboratory testing. The International Biochar Initiative retired the standard in April 2024 without a successor edition.
documents.abstract: The document is a product definition standard, reference code IBI-STD-2.1, licensed under Creative Commons for sharing with attribution, for non-commercial use, without derivatives. It was a common reference for what counted as biochar in soil use, how to test it. Readers should know the standard is closed: it was retired in April 2024 and will not be updated. It remains useful for reading older test reports, for tracing where later certification schemes came from. Anyone buying biochar should ask what testing the supplier actually holds, whether the results come from an accredited laboratory, rather than treat a reference to this standard as proof of current quality.

documents.title: The 55 uses of biochar (Schmidt and Wilson)
documents.summary: A catalogue by Hans-Peter Schmidt and Kelpie Wilson of 55 uses for biochar beyond the garden bed, spanning farming, building, water treatment, clothing. The porous carbon holds water, air, metals, organic chemicals, and gives microbes a home. The idea running through it is cascading use: one batch of biochar doing several jobs before it ends up in soil.
documents.abstract: Schmidt and Wilson list 55 uses of biochar in The Biochar Journal, from the compost heap to building materials, clothing, electronics and consumer products. They argue the stable carbon matrix has properties worth using in their own right: it holds water, air, metals, organic chemicals, it has unusual thermal and electrical behaviour still being explored, and its porous structure suits microorganisms. From these properties they build the case for cascades, where biochar is used in one setting, then moved along to the next, finally applied to soil, so material, nutrient and energy flows are recycled. For a livestock or turf operator the practical entry points are the farm-scale items such as feed, litter, composting and water filtration. The article is a survey of ideas rather than a set of measured results, so each use needs its own evidence before you commit money to it.
